[6]. For each pair, a linear baseline was drawn between the two local absorbance minima flanking both bands, following the baseline method of Rochas et al. [7] as adapted for alginate by Gómez-Ordóñez & Rupérez [8]. The transmittance at the baseline (Tb) and at the actual peak (Tp) were read at each diagnostic wavenumber, the baseline-corrected absorbance was calculated as A = log₁₀(Tb/Tp), and the M/G ratio was obtained as A(M band)/A(G band). Band assignments in the fingerprint (anomeric) region, 950–750 cm⁻¹, were further supported by comparison with the literature values reported by Leal et al. [9].

The expected outcome was to determine whether the raw alginate was mannuronic- or guluronic-rich, providing an initial indication of its expected gelling behaviour. If mannuronic residues predominated, a comparatively softer, more elastic calcium-alginate gel would be expected, potentially requiring closer control of crosslinking parameters (alginate concentration, CaCl₂ concentration, crosslinking time) to achieve sufficient mechanical integrity. Conversely, if guluronic residues predominated, a stiffer, more rigid gel would be expected, favouring mechanical stability but potentially requiring adjustment of other parameters (e.g. flow rate, drop height) to avoid excessive brittleness. This information was intended to guide the interpretation of the mechanical and preservation behaviour observed in the subsequent bead and core-shell experiments.
- Bead optimisation: alginate concentration and drop height

The aim of this experiment was to identify the alginate concentration and drop height that produced the most homogeneous and reproducible alginate beads. As the first step in developing our encapsulation platform, establishing a robust bead synthesis protocol was essential before introducing the additional complexity of a core-shell architecture.

Alginate concentration was evaluated because it directly determines solution viscosity, influencing droplet formation. Drop height was investigated because it affects the impact velocity of the droplets entering the calcium chloride bath, thereby influencing their final geometry and increasing the likelihood of deformation if not properly controlled.

To evaluate these variables, sodium alginate solutions of different concentrations were dripped into a calcium chloride crosslinking bath from several predefined heights while all remaining synthesis parameters were kept constant. The parameters for the experiment were set as follows:

For each condition, 10 beads were imaged after crosslinking and analysed using ImageJ, following the image-taking and image-analysis protocols described on the Protocols page. Bead size was characterised through the projected area, perimeter, equivalent diameter (Deq) and maximum (Dmax) and minimum (Dmin) Feret diameters, while bead shape was characterised through sphericity (s = minor axis / major axis). The variability of these parameters between the beads of each condition was used as an indicator of reproducibility.

Higher alginate concentrations were expected to produce more spherical and mechanically stable beads, as the increased viscosity helps the droplet retain its shape on impact and the higher polymer content provides more sites for calcium crosslinking. However, excessively viscous solutions could hinder droplet detachment from the outlet and produce elongated or tailed beads. Drop height was expected to show an intermediate optimum: if the height was too low, droplets might not detach cleanly or penetrate the bath surface, whereas if it was too high, the greater impact velocity could flatten or deform the droplets before gelation. The combination providing the highest sphericity and lowest variability between beads would be selected for the subsequent optimisation steps.
- Bead optimisation: flow rate

The aim of this experiment was to determine the range of flow rates compatible with stable bead production, once the optimal alginate concentration and drop height had been established. Flow rate was investigated because it governs the rate of droplet formation at the needle outlet: at low flow rates, droplets form and detach individually under gravity, whereas excessively high flow rates can lead to the formation of a continuous liquid jet rather than discrete drops, preventing bead formation. Identifying whether, and at which flow rate, this transition occurred would establish the operating window for bead production.

To evaluate this variable, beads were synthesised using the previously optimised alginate concentration and drop height while varying only the flow rate at which the alginate solution was dispensed through the infusion pump. All remaining synthesis parameters were kept constant. The flow rate was progressively increased up to 3200 μL/min; the range was not extended further, as this value was already far above the flow rates typically reported in the literature for alginate bead extrusion [10].

Droplet formation at the outlet was monitored visually for each flow rate to determine whether stable dripping was maintained or whether a transition to jetting occurred. In addition, 10 beads per condition were imaged after crosslinking and analysed using ImageJ, following the image-taking and image-analysis protocols described on the Protocols page, so that any effect of flow rate on bead size and shape could be quantified rather than only observed. Bead size was characterised through the projected area, perimeter, equivalent diameter (Deq) and maximum (Dmax) and minimum (Dmin) Feret diameters, while bead shape was characterised through sphericity (s = minor axis / major axis), with the variability between beads of each condition used as an indicator of reproducibility.

The expected outcome was to identify the maximum flow rate at which stable dripping could be maintained without transition to jetting, and to establish whether bead morphology changed within that range. A flow rate within the stable range would then be carried forward as a constant parameter for the subsequent optimisation of crosslinking time.
- Bead optimisation: crosslinking time

The aim of this experiment was to determine whether the duration of calcium-mediated crosslinking influenced the morphology of the alginate beads. Once the optimal alginate concentration and drop height had been established, crosslinking time was evaluated to determine whether longer exposure to calcium ions produced more compact and structurally stable beads.

Crosslinking time was investigated because calcium ions progressively diffuse into the alginate matrix, promoting the formation of calcium-mediated junction zones between polymer chains according to the egg-box model. Although gelation occurs rapidly at the bead surface, extending the crosslinking period could potentially increase the degree of crosslinking throughout the bead, affecting its dimensions, structural integrity and handling properties.

To evaluate this variable, beads were synthesised using the previously optimised alginate concentration drop height and flow rate while varying only the residence time in the calcium chloride bath. All remaining synthesis parameters were kept constant. The experimental conditions were as follows:

For each condition, 10 beads were imaged after crosslinking and analysed using ImageJ, following the image-taking and image-analysis protocols described on the Protocols page. Bead size was characterised through the projected area, perimeter, equivalent diameter (Deq) and maximum (Dmax) and minimum (Dmin) Feret diameters, while bead shape was characterised through sphericity (s = minor axis / major axis). Changes in bead size were used to assess compaction of the alginate network with increasing crosslinking time, and the variability between the beads of each condition was used as an indicator of reproducibility.

The expected outcome was to determine whether extending the crosslinking time produced measurable changes in bead morphology or compaction. If no significant differences were observed, a crosslinking time of 30 min, within the range commonly reported in the literature [3,10,11], would be retained, as it would provide fully formed beads without unnecessarily extending production time.
- Bead preservation under different storage media

The aim of this experiment was to evaluate the preservation of alginate beads under conditions representative of those they would encounter during storage and application. Following the optimisation of bead production, it was necessary to assess whether the capsules maintained their morphology over time when exposed to different aqueous environments.

Three storage media were investigated: distilled water, industrial wastewater and phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). These media differ in ionic composition, ionic strength and phosphate content, all of which can influence alginate swelling, calcium ion exchange and hydrogel integrity. Water served as a control with minimal ionic interference, industrial wastewater (provided by Bio-Oils Huelva) represented the intended application environment, and PBS was included as a phosphate-rich medium with a well-defined ionic composition and ionic strength. PBS could promote alginate degradation because sodium ions compete with calcium ions within the alginate matrix [12], progressively disrupting the ionic crosslinks that stabilise the hydrogel. Evaluating preservation in these media allowed us to assess the effect of different storage media on alginate integrity.

10 beads synthesised under the previously optimised conditions were transferred to a container with 8 mL of each storage medium immediately after crosslinking, and kept at room temperature. Their morphology was monitored by photographs taken after 0, 24, 48 and 72 h, and after one week. Beads stored in PBS lost their structural integrity during the first days, and once a bead had broken each fragment was measured as a separate bead, so this medium was followed qualitatively rather than quantified; images from the remaining conditions were analysed quantitatively to compare the evolution of bead morphology over time.
The experimental conditions were as follows:

The expected outcome was to identify storage conditions that best preserved bead morphology while determining whether specific media promoted hydrogel degradation. In particular, this experiment was expected to reveal whether PBS adversely affected alginate stability, providing the rationale for the more detailed preservation studies later performed with core-shell capsules.
alginate encapsulation::core shell forma: Building on the optimised bead protocol, the system was translated into a core-shell architecture, in which a liquid calcium chloride core is surrounded by an alginate shell. Because capsule formation now depends on two coaxial flows meeting and gelling simultaneously rather than a single phase, the outer alginate and inner calcium chloride concentrations were first screened to identify a viable window, and the outer-to-inner flow-rate ratio was then optimised within that window. The resulting configuration was tested against the three requirements it must meet in operation: chemical stability under the ionic environments the capsules will encounter, physical containment of their contents, and mechanical resistance to the compression and handling expected in the bioreactor.
- Core-shell screening: alginate and CaCl₂ concentrations

The aim of this experiment was to identify combinations of alginate and calcium chloride concentrations capable of producing stable core-shell capsules. Unlike conventional beads, core-shell encapsulation requires the simultaneous extrusion of an outer alginate solution and an inner calcium chloride solution. As calcium ions begin diffusing into the alginate shell immediately after the two solutions meet, inappropriate concentration combinations can lead to premature gelation, clogging of the coaxial nozzle or jet formation (continuous stream, caused by a partially clogged nozzle, which prevents detachment of the drop from the nozzle), preventing successful capsule production.

For this reason, an initial screening was carried out before optimising any additional process parameters. The outer alginate concentration and inner calcium chloride concentration were systematically varied while maintaining all remaining synthesis conditions constant. This approach allowed us to identify the concentration ranges compatible with stable capsule formation and establish suitable starting conditions for the subsequent optimisation of flow-rate ratios and capsule properties.
*Not all calcium chloride concentrations were evaluated for every alginate concentration. The screening was refined based on capsule or jet formation, as shown in the experimental matrix below.

Capsule formation was assessed qualitatively by monitoring the stability of the dripping regime, the appearance of premature gelation at the nozzle tip and the transition from dripping to jetting. Conditions capable of producing stable core-shell dripping were selected for subsequent optimisation experiments.

The expected outcome was to identify a concentration window that allowed stable core-shell production while avoiding premature gelation and nozzle obstruction. Establishing these conditions was essential before investigating additional variables, as successful capsule formation depends primarily on the physicochemical compatibility of the inner and outer solutions.
- Core-shell optimisation: outer-to-inner flow-rate ratio

The aim of this experiment was to optimise the outer-to-inner flow-rate ratio (Qe/Qi) for the production of homogeneous and mechanically robust core-shell capsules. Following the identification of suitable alginate and inner calcium chloride concentrations, the flow-rate ratio became the main process variable governing capsule formation, as it determines the relative volumes of the core and shell, influences shell thickness and affects the stability of the coaxial flow during encapsulation. Although several Qe/Qi ratios have been reported in the literature for coaxial core-shell systems [3,4,13], their performance depends strongly on the physicochemical properties of each encapsulation system. Therefore, rather than adopting published conditions directly, we evaluated two literature-based ratios (4:1 and 6:1) to determine which provided the best performance under our synthesis conditions.

The same 4:1 or 6:1 proportion can be delivered at different paces, so each ratio was tested at two outer flow rates to separate the effect of the proportion from that of the flow itself. 600 μL/min was carried over from the optimised bead protocol. 300 μL/min was included to test whether slower drop formation benefits the core-shell architecture, since the longer the drop takes to detach, the more time the inner phase has to settle symmetrically within the surrounding alginate; at 6:1 this setting already requires an inner flow of 50 μL/min, which we considered too slow to reduce further. Flow rates above 600 μL/min were not investigated, as the bead experiments had shown that drops grow with increasing flow and the drop now has to accommodate a liquid core in addition to its shell.

Because preliminary attempts to visualise the alginate shell using conventional photographs and optical microscopy were unsuccessful, magnetite particles were incorporated into the alginate solution to increase contrast. Consequently, all capsules evaluated in this experiment were synthesised with magnetite-labelled alginate, enabling the shell boundaries to be clearly distinguished during microscopic observation.

Following synthesis, the resulting core-shell capsules were frozen with liquid nitrogen, cut in two, and imaged under an optical microscope to evaluate shell continuity, overall morphology and the presence of defects such as deformation, rupture or incomplete shell formation. Micrographs were subsequently analysed using ImageJ to measure shell thickness, allowing a quantitative comparison between the different outer-to-inner flow-rate ratios. Ten capsules were analysed per condition, six for 3.5% (w/v) alginate at 300/75 μL/min, with ten thickness measurements per capsule, five on each half, so that variation around a single capsule and variation between capsules of the same condition could be distinguished. The most promising conditions would then be selected for mechanical resistance testing.

The expected outcome was to determine the outer-to-inner flow-rate ratio that consistently produced reproducible core-shell capsules with a uniform shell thickness and well-defined morphology, with the higher ratio anticipated to yield thicker shells since it delivers a larger proportion of alginate per capsule. The lower outer flow rate was expected to produce more consistent capsules if the time available for the two streams to arrange themselves before detachment is a limiting factor. These conditions would subsequently be used for the remaining preservation and characterisation experiments.
- Mechanical resistance of core-shell capsules

The aim of this experiment was to compare the mechanical resistance of the core-shell capsule formulations and identify the configuration best suited for handling, transport and operation inside the bioreactor. Besides maintaining a well-defined morphology, the capsules must withstand external loads without collapsing or undergoing permanent deformation, so compression-based assays are a standard way to compare the mechanical robustness of alginate capsules [3,4,13].

Mechanical resistance also served a second purpose. The shell-thickness measurements had proved too variable to distinguish the two outer-to-inner flow-rate ratios, and resistance to compression measures the property that shell thickness was only a proxy for. It also captures the uniformity of the shell as well as its average thickness, since a capsule with a thick but uneven shell has a weak point that a mean value does not reveal.

Core-shell capsules produced under the eight conditions carried forward from the previous experiments were subjected to increasing compressive loads by placing calibrated masses (1, 2, 5, 10 and 20 g) on a microscope coverslip (0.4 g) resting on groups of three capsules. Each mass was applied independently, and after every loading step the capsules were photographed before removing the weight and replacing it with the next mass.

Two independent batches were tested: one on the day of synthesis and one after one week of storage in distilled water. This would allow the effect of storage time to be observed, which is relevant because capsules will not be used on the day they are produced.

The photographs obtained at each loading step were analysed using ImageJ following the image-analysis protocol described on the Protocols page, using sphericity as the descriptor of deformation. Each condition was expressed as the fraction of its own unloaded sphericity retained at each load, since capsules do not all start out equally spherical and an absolute comparison would confound resistance to compression with initial shape.

The expected outcome was to identify the formulation that best resisted compressive loading while preserving its geometry and shell integrity. The 6:1 ratio was anticipated to perform better, since a higher proportion of outer phase delivers more alginate per capsule, whereas no difference was expected between the 300 and 600 μL/min outer flow rates, as these change the rate of production rather than the composition of each capsule. Any difference between freshly synthesised capsules and stored ones would be useful in predicting their behaviour inside of the bioreactor. This information would support the selection of the most mechanically robust capsule design for subsequent biological experiments and integration into the modular bioreactor.
- Core-shell containment assessed with magnetite

The aim of this experiment was to evaluate the containment capacity of the optimised core-shell capsules by determining whether encapsulated particulate material was retained during capsule synthesis and subsequent storage. As the encapsulation platform is intended to immobilise engineered *Pseudomonas putida*, demonstrating effective cargo retention was an essential validation step before introducing biological material.

Magnetite nanoparticles (50–100 nm in diameter; Aldrich, 637106) were selected as a surrogate cargo because they darken the material visibly and absorb across the ultraviolet and visible range, which allows them to be detected by UV-Vis spectroscopy. At that size they are an order of magnitude smaller than *P. putida* cells, which are roughly a micrometre across, so successful retention of the nanoparticles represents a conservative assessment of capsule containment: particles significantly smaller than bacterial cells are more likely to escape through structural defects.

Three capsule formulations were prepared using the optimised encapsulation conditions: control capsules without magnetite, capsules containing magnetite in the calcium chloride core, and capsules containing magnetite dispersed in the alginate shell. Although localisation within the core more closely resembles the intended encapsulation of the bacterial suspension, preliminary observations suggested that the limited core volume would provide insufficient visual contrast, and that maintaining magnetite nanoparticles homogeneously suspended in the calcium chloride solution throughout the encapsulation process would be difficult because of particle sedimentation inside the syringe. Magnetite dispersed in the alginate shell was therefore included as an alternative formulation, expected to provide a more homogeneous particle distribution and a more reliable detection of leakage. Control capsules without magnetite were included to account for the absorbance of the capsule material itself, which was subtracted from the spectra of the magnetite-containing samples.

Capsules were synthesised on Day 0, and the calcium chloride crosslinking bath was collected immediately after encapsulation. The capsules were subsequently transferred to distilled water for storage. On Day 1, UV-Vis spectra were acquired from the recovered calcium chloride bath, to evaluate particle loss during synthesis, and from the storage water, to assess leakage during storage. On Day 3, the storage water was measured again to evaluate whether additional leakage occurred during prolonged storage, and capsules taken from it were deliberately dissolved in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and the resulting solution measured, to confirm the presence of magnetite inside the capsules. Reference spectra of a magnetite suspension and of a diluted magnetite suspension were also recorded.

Absorbance measurements were performed using a GENESYS 10S UV–Vis spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific) with quartz cuvettes, as the spectra extended into the ultraviolet range, where conventional plastic cuvettes exhibit significant background absorbance. Full spectra between 200 and 1000 nm were recorded for each sample, using the corresponding medium (calcium chloride solution, distilled water or PBS) as the instrumental blank. Capsules without magnetite and a magnetite suspension were measured as references, to establish the spectral regions in which each component absorbs. Since the capsule material was expected to absorb mainly in the ultraviolet, whereas magnetite absorbs broadly across the ultraviolet and visible range, the presence of magnetite was to be assessed in the visible region, where the contribution of the capsule material should be negligible. For each medium, the spectrum of the corresponding control (capsules without magnetite) was subtracted from those of the magnetite-containing samples, and the mean absorbance difference between 450 and 600 nm was used as an indicator of the amount of magnetite present.

The expected outcome was that negligible magnetite would be detected in the calcium chloride bath and storage medium, whereas the highest absorbance would be observed after dissolution of the capsules in PBS, indicating that the encapsulated material remained effectively retained until intentional degradation of the alginate matrix. This would demonstrate that the optimised core-shell architecture provides effective physical containment throughout synthesis and storage, supporting its suitability for the encapsulation of engineered bacteria.
- Core-shell preservation under different chemical environments

The aim of this experiment was to identify a storage composition, beyond distilled water alone, that would not degrade alginate core-shell capsules. The initial preservation experiment, performed with conventional beads, showed that PBS compromised structural integrity, but it remained unclear whether this effect resulted from the presence of sodium ions, phosphate ions, ionic strength or pH. Previous reports on alginate beads show that, under acidic conditions, ion exchange between the sodium ions of an external medium and the calcium ions crosslinking the gel is accelerated, weakening the gel to varying degrees **[14]**, with the underlying competition between monovalent counterions such as Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ for the alginate carboxylate groups also described mechanistically for alginate gelation more broadly **[12]**. This experiment was therefore designed to isolate which of these chemical factors was responsible for the degradation observed, so that a preservation medium avoiding it could be identified.

Preservation was also evaluated in the industrial wastewater supplied by Bio-Oils Huelva, as this is the medium the capsules must actually withstand during operation. Because this wastewater is highly acidic, it requires pH adjustment before it can be used with encapsulated bacteria. Three bases (NaOH, KOH and NH₄OH) were compared for this purpose, allowing any effect of the basifying agent itself, beyond pH, to also be assessed.

Core-shell capsules synthesised under the optimal encapsulation conditions were incubated in five groups of media: distilled water adjusted to different pH values (1.73, 3.00, 5.00 and 5.78) using HCl, serial dilutions of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS: 1×, 1/2×, 1/4× and 1/8×), an equivalent sodium-free phosphate buffer with the same ionic strength and matching dilutions, untreated industrial wastewater, and the same wastewater basified to pH 5 with each of the three bases mentioned. All remaining synthesis and storage conditions were kept constant throughout the study.

Capsule integrity was monitored by photographing the capsules after 0, 24, 48 and 72 h, and 1 week of incubation, allowing qualitative and quantitative comparison of the progression of degradation under each chemical environment.

The expected outcome was to isolate the specific effect of each variable on capsule integrity. For pH alone, using the pH-adjusted water, lowering pH was expected to protonate the carboxylate groups of alginate and reduce swelling independently of any monovalent cation exchange [15]. For PBS and the sodium-free buffer dilutions, comparing the two was expected to distinguish whether degradation was driven specifically by sodium ions or by overall ionic strength, since only the PBS series contains sodium while both series share the same ionic strength at each dilution. For the industrial wastewater, changing the basifying agent was expected to reveal whether the choice of base, beyond its effect on pH, had any measurable impact on capsule stability.
alginate encapsulation::final physical c: With a validated configuration in hand, the encapsulation platform was characterised further by TGA-DSC and SEM, to establish its thermal behaviour, water content and microstructure ahead of integration with the biological module.
- Thermal characterisation (TGA-DSC)

The aim of this experiment was to characterise the thermal behaviour and water content of the optimised core-shell capsules using thermogravimetric analysis coupled with differential scanning calorimetry (TGA-DSC), completing the physical characterisation of the encapsulation platform ahead of its integration with the biological module.

Two capsule states were compared: hydrated core-shell capsules, taken directly from distilled water storage with no additional treatment, and dried core-shell capsules, obtained by placing capsules on absorbent paper and leaving them to air-dry overnight. Comparing these two states allows the mass loss attributable to free and bound water to be distinguished from the mass loss and thermal transitions associated with the alginate polymer itself, since the dried sample retains substantially less water than the hydrated one.

Because a hydrated capsule weighs an order of magnitude more than a dried one, a single capsule provided enough material for the hydrated runs, whereas two capsules were needed for the dried sample. Two independent hydrated capsules were analysed as replicates.

For each sample, mass loss was recorded as a function of temperature by TGA, and the corresponding heat flow was recorded simultaneously by DSC, allowing thermal events (for example, water evaporation, polymer decomposition) to be correlated with the mass-loss steps observed in the same run. The water content of each sample was estimated from the mass remaining after the first mass-loss step, and the residue at the end of the run was used as an indication of the inorganic fraction left after decomposition of the polymer.

Literature characterisations of alginate by TGA-DSC are typically performed on the raw sodium alginate powder rather than on a hydrated hydrogel structure [3]. The dried core-shell capsules were therefore expected to yield a thermal profile broadly consistent with these literature values for alginate powder, since drying was intended to bring the capsule's water content closer to that of a dry polymer sample. The hydrated capsules, by contrast, were expected to show a substantially larger initial mass-loss step than both the dried capsules and the literature values, reflecting the high water content retained within the core-shell structure under normal storage conditions. A contribution from the internal calcium chloride was also anticipated, since its hydrates lose water over ranges that overlap those of the hydrogel [16]. Comparing the three profiles (hydrated capsule, dried capsule and literature powder data) was intended to provide an estimate of how much water the core-shell architecture retains relative to the starting raw material.
- Microstructural, surface and elemental characterisation (optical microscopy, SEM and EDS)

The aim of this experiment was to examine the surface morphology, microstructure and composition of the optimised core-shell capsules. Capsules were first imaged dry optically, and then analysed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), which required drying and coating them beforehand.

A dried capsule was imaged first by optical microscopy. This is non-destructive and requires neither a vacuum nor a conductive coating, so the capsule could be imaged with no preparation beyond the drying itself. It provided a reference view of the dried structure that would later be examined by SEM. A single capsule was examined: one image was taken at 5× to frame the whole capsule, and four further images at 20× at separate positions on its surface.
The expected outcome was a clear view of the capsule outline and of the appearance of its surface to judge whether the surface was smooth and intact.

SEM was then used to obtain the topographical detail that optical microscopy cannot provide. Only dried core-shell capsules were analysed. A hydrated capsule cannot be imaged directly, as the high vacuum required for SEM is incompatible with a sample retaining substantial free water: the water would evaporate inside the chamber, collapsing the structure and degrading the vacuum [17]. Air-drying the capsules overnight on absorbent paper removes that water, at the cost of the shrinkage and surface collapse that are expected for any alginate hydrogel dried without a solvent-exchange or critical-point step. The micrographs therefore describe the dried polymer network rather than the hydrated capsule as it exists in operation, and this has to be kept in mind when interpreting them.

The dried capsules were inspected under an optical microscope, at a magnification high enough to judge how far the drying had deformed them and whether the surface was intact, so that a suitable specimen could be chosen before committing it to the coating step. Because alginate is not intrinsically conductive, the dried capsules required a conductive coating before imaging to prevent charging artefacts. Gold was used, as it gives a uniform conductive layer and good image quality on an irregular, collapsed surface.

Micrographs were acquired at five magnifications spanning more than two orders of magnitude. The lowest (90×) gives a whole-capsule view that shows the overall shape and the extent of drying-induced collapse; the intermediate magnifications (400× and 2000×) cover the outer surface and, where a capsule had fractured, the exposed cross-section; and the highest (7000× and 20000×) resolve the texture of the dried polymer itself. The expected outcome was to observe a surface morphology consistent with the alginate hydrogel network, and to describe the porosity and texture of the dried material at a resolution that optical microscopy cannot reach.

The elemental composition of the capsule surface was then measured by EDS on the same instrument. The electron beam excites characteristic X-ray emission from the elements present in the interaction volume, so the spectrum provides a direct check on whether the species expected from the encapsulation chemistry are actually there, and in what proportion. Two questions motivated the measurement: whether calcium is present in the material, as it must be if the alginate is ionically crosslinked; and how much chloride remains from the CaCl₂ bath after washing, which indicates how much unreacted salt the capsule retains. A single spectrum was acquired from a representative area of the capsule surface.

Two limitations apply to the interpretation. EDS does not detect hydrogen, and quantification is normalised across the elements that are detected, so the reported percentages describe the heavy-element composition rather than the true composition of the polysaccharide. The gold coating also contributes to the spectrum and consumes part of that normalised total, which lowers the apparent weight of every other element to a comparable extent; relative comparisons between elements remain meaningful, absolute mass fractions do not. The expected outcome was to detect carbon and oxygen as the dominant elements, together with calcium at a level consistent with ionic crosslinking, and to establish whether chloride persisted after washing.
Conclusion

The experiments on this page were chosen to answer a fixed sequence of questions rather than to characterise the system exhaustively, and each one exists because the next decision could not be made without it. The raw material was characterised first because every later result depends on what the alginate is. Beads came before capsules because four production variables can be separated in a single-phase system and cannot be separated in a coaxial one. Each variable was then tested until it either proved to matter or demonstrably did not, and the ones that did not, crosslinking time and the upper end of the flow-rate range, were dropped rather than optimised further. Where a measurement failed to discriminate, as shell thickness did, the response was to change the measurement rather than to repeat it with more replicates.

The scope was also set by the circumstances of the project rather than by what would be ideal. A mechanical assay built from calibrated masses, a coverslip and a camera replaced an instrumented compression tester we did not have, and it answered the comparative question that needed answering even though it yields no modulus. Magnetite stood in for bacteria because the encapsulation setup sits in a physics laboratory with no biosafety containment, which is also why containment was validated with a conservative surrogate rather than with live cells. Dried specimens were used for thermal and electron imaging because no cryogenic or critical-point preparation was available, and the resulting limitations are stated rather than glossed. What is missing from this page is therefore missing for stated reasons, and in each case the experiment that would close the gap is named alongside the one that was done.
enzymatic immobilisation::intro abstract: Phosphorus is at once a finite, critical resource (fertilisers, with no chemical substitute) and a key wastewater pollutant that drives eutrophication. In vegetable oil refining, the **acid degumming** step (typically 85% v/v phosphoric acid) generates effluents loaded with organic phosphorus: partially hydrolysed phospholipids, phytate and free phosphate. Conventional chemical precipitation cannot reach phosphorus that is covalently bound to organic matrices, so these effluents systematically exceed the discharge limits set by Directive (EU) 2024/3019, and the phosphorus is lost instead of recovered.

**RePhlow** closes this loop with modular spheres whose alginate core holds the engineered phosphorus-accumulating organism (PAO, see the **Genetic engineering** block) and whose surface is **functionalised with a panel of phosphohydrolases**. These surface enzymes mineralise organic phosphorus into free orthophosphate, which the encapsulated *Pseudomonas putida* KT2440 then imports and locks away as polyphosphate. In other words, this block builds the enzymatic layer that feeds the engineered chassis.

- **Produce** the enzyme panel, we mine candidate phosphohydrolases (phospholipases, non-specific acid phosphatases and phytases), express them heterologously in *Escherichia coli*, purify them by IMAC and characterise them under simulated industrial conditions (pH 5.0, 30 ºC). *(Enzyme production block)*
- **Immobilise** them, we work out the immobilisation chemistry on a simple, previously optimised model support (MANAE-agarose), using the commercial chimera **Lecitase Ultra** as a demanding model enzyme, before transferring the winning strategy to the alginate-chitosan-genipin sphere. *(Immobilisation chemistry block)*
In one sentence: we **make the enzymes that release phosphate from the degumming waste, and we work out how to fix them onto the sphere without killing their activity**.
enzymatic immobilisation::the four parts: The degumming stream is not hydrolysed by a single enzyme, but by a **cocktail that acts synergistically**, each activity attacking a different bond of the substrate. Four catalytic activities were targeted, all selected to retain function at the pH 5.0 and 30 ºC of the acid-degummed effluent.
enzymatic immobilisation::pla type a pho: **What it does:** these hydrolases cleave the carboxylic ester bonds of glycerophospholipids. PLA1 (EC 3.1.1.32) acts at the sn1 position and PLA2 (EC 3.1.1.4) at the sn2 position, releasing free fatty acids and lysophospholipids. Removing these acyl chains reduces the hydrophobicity and viscosity of the gums, so the rest of the cocktail can reach the phosphate head group with less steric impediment.

**What we do to it and why:** we cover this activity with the commercial chimera **Lecitase Ultra** (a fusion of lipase from *Thermomyces lanuginosus* and phospholipase A1 of *Fusarium oxysporum*), chosen as the **immobilisation model** because it is the hardest enzyme to stabilise: its active site is occluded by a lid that requires interfacial activation, and it tends to form bimolecular aggregates. In parallel, a metagenomic esterase (EstE1) was produced recombinantly as a candidate PLA activity.
**GIF (storyboard):** a phospholipid with two acyl chains; scissors snip the ester bonds at sn1 and sn2; the fatty acids drift off and a lysophospholipid is left behind, the gum visibly thinning.
enzymatic immobilisation::plc type c pho: **What it does:** phospholipase C (EC 3.1.4.3) is a phosphodiesterase that breaks the ester bond between glycerol and the phosphate group. Its action releases a diacylglycerol (DAG), which stays in the oil phase and increases refined-oil yield, and a water-soluble phosphorylated head group (for example phosphocholine or phosphoethanolamine) that passes into the aqueous phase in a much easier form to process.

**What we do to it and why:** two candidates were selected, plc from *Thermococcus kodakarensis* and cerA from *Bacillus cereus*. Recombinant expression was attempted but both proved **cytotoxic to *E. coli***, since PLCs with alpha-toxin homology hydrolyse essential membrane phospholipids of the host. This activity is therefore redirected to cell-free **IVTT (In Vitro Transcription–Translation)**, a system suited to toxic, membrane-associated proteins because it does not rely on host viability.

In this block we build and validate the enzymatic toolbox: we identify candidate phosphohydrolases by data mining, express them heterologously in *E. coli*, purify them by immobilised metal-ion affinity chromatography (IMAC) and characterise their activity under the operating conditions of the reactor (pH 5.0, 30 ºC).

Because heterologous expression carries inherent risks (insoluble aggregates, proteolysis, loss of active conformation), a parallel search for **commercial homologues** was kept for each activity as a contingency plan. The workflow runs from database mining, through in-silico construct design and cloning, to expression, solubilisation, purification and functional characterisation, aiming to reach **soluble, active and characterised enzymes with the fewest possible steps**.
enzymatic immobilisation::bioinformatic: The aim was to assemble a shortlist of phosphohydrolases able to dismantle the organophosphorus in the degumming effluent while remaining expressible in *E. coli*. Because the effluent is not a single compound but a mixture of phospholipids, phytate and phosphomonoesters, no single enzyme can mineralise it, so four complementary activities were targeted: type A and type C phospholipases (PLA, PLC), non-specific acid phosphatases (NAP) and phytases. The substrate composition itself was taken from the European patent describing industrial degumming [1], so that the activities were matched to the real stream rather than to a generic phospholipid.

Candidates had to satisfy four constraints, each chosen to de-risk the downstream work. First, a sequence deposited in a public database (GenBank or UniProt), so it could be synthesised or amplified. Second, suitability for *E. coli*, meaning no dependence on post-translational modifications such as glycosylation that a prokaryote cannot perform. Third, at least one literature report of recombinant expression and kinetics. Fourth, retention of at least 30% of maximum activity at pH 5.0 and 30 ºC, the window imposed by the acid-degummed effluent and the mesophilic PAO. Screening on these criteria before any wet work concentrated effort only on enzymes that could realistically be made and would survive the process.

The search combined **EnzymeMiner** [2], a platform that ranks candidate sequences by predicted solubility and expressibility, with targeted queries in **BRENDA** [3] and **UniProt** [4], applied as four sequential filters (initial pool, prokaryotic origin, literature support, catalytic profile). In parallel, a commercial homologue was identified for every activity as a contingency, so that a failure to express any one enzyme would not stall the panel.

The screen was expected to yield a small, redundant panel with at least two representatives per activity. It reduced 3,741 candidates to **7**: EstE1 (PLA), Plc and CerA (PLC), AppA and PhyA (phytase), and M2-32 and AphA (NAP). *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*
enzymatic immobilisation::in silico stru: Before ordering any DNA, we decided for each enzyme where to place the purification tag and whether it would need a special folding environment, because both decisions are far cheaper to make on a model than to correct after cloning.

Each sequence without a resolved structure was modelled by homology on **SWISS-MODEL** [5] and inspected in **PyMOL** [6] for two things. First, the accessibility of the N- and C-termini: the polyhistidine tag must sit on an exposed terminus so it can reach the resin without occluding the active site, so the more exposed terminus set the vector, **pET-28a(+)** for an N-terminal tag (introduced at the NdeI site with a downstream STOP codon) or **pET-22b(+)** for a C-terminal tag [7]. Second, the presence of structural disulphide bridges: pairs of cysteine sulphur atoms closer than 2.5 Å were flagged, because a disulphide-dependent enzyme will not fold in the reducing cytoplasm of a standard strain and will instead need an oxidising chassis. Mapping this in silico told us in advance which enzymes would later require Rosetta-gami 2 or Origami 2, so the folding strategy was planned rather than discovered by trial and error.

The expected outcome was a per-enzyme decision (tag position, vector and disulphide dependence) that pre-empted the main causes of insolubility. *Protocol and PyMOL scripts: see the Protocols page [link pending].*
enzymatic immobilisation::obtaining the: The aim was to obtain each gene inside its chosen pET backbone, using two routes according to availability so as to minimise cost. Sequences held in no repository were ordered as de novo gene synthesis directly in the pET vector (GCAT Bio, Changzhou, China), with codon optimisation used only when the nucleotide sequence was unavailable but the amino acid sequence was, since unnecessary optimisation can introduce its own expression artefacts. Sequences already validated in Addgene were amplified by PCR and cloned, which is far cheaper than synthesis.

For amplification, primers carried NdeI (5') and HindIII (3') sites matching the pET multiple cloning site. A small amount of donor plasmid (50 ng) was used as template with the high-fidelity polymerase **Pfu Ultra II** [8], chosen to avoid mutations in the coding sequence, and DMSO was added to help denature GC-rich regions. Because the Addgene genes arrived in different backbones, cloning them into the **same** pET vectors as the synthesised genes was a deliberate choice, so that any later difference in expression would reflect the enzyme and not the vector.

Inserts and vectors were then cut with FastDigest NdeI and HindIII, and the linearised vector was dephosphorylated with the thermosensitive alkaline phosphatase FastAP, a step included specifically to stop the vector re-circularising on itself without an insert and inflating the background. Fragments were gel-purified, and ligation was set at a 1:5 vector:insert molar ratio (NEBioCalculator) with T4 DNA ligase overnight at 16 ºC, a temperature that balances ligase activity against the annealing stability of the short cohesive ends.
The expected outcome was a set of recombinant pET plasmids for each gene, in matched backbones and ready to transform. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*
enzymatic immobilisation::transformation: The aim was to introduce the plasmids into bacteria, confirm the correct insert and hand a validated construct to the expression host. The plasmids were introduced by **transformation**, the direct uptake of naked plasmid DNA by permeabilised competent cells, which is the appropriate route for purified plasmid DNA, as opposed to conjugation or transduction. Cloning was done first in *E. coli* DH5α, a recA and endA deficient strain that gives a high yield of stable plasmid but carries no T7 polymerase, so it propagates the construct without expressing it.

Immediately after heat shock (42 ºC, 90 s) or electroporation, the cells were recovered in **LB-SOC**, a rich medium supplemented with glucose, and incubated for one hour at 37 ºC before plating. This recovery step is essential: it lets the permeabilised cells repair their envelopes and, above all, transcribe and translate the antibiotic-resistance gene, so that they survive the subsequent selection. Plating straight onto antibiotic would kill successfully transformed but not-yet-resistant cells and collapse the apparent efficiency.

Transformants were screened by colony PCR with universal T7 primers flanking the insert, resolved on a 1% agarose gel; since the amplicon sizes matched the SnapGene simulation, sequencing was not required. Positive clones were grown and their plasmid recovered by alkaline-lysis **miniprep** (NZY), which denatures and precipitates genomic DNA and protein while keeping the supercoiled plasmid in solution, giving clean DNA to re-transform. The verified plasmid was finally moved into a **(DE3)** expression strain, which carries T7 RNA polymerase under the IPTG-inducible lacUV5 promoter, the element absent from DH5α that actually drives transcription of the cloned gene.
The expected outcome was verified clones in the expression host, ready for induction. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*
enzymatic immobilisation::recombinant ex: The aim was to find the induction regime that maximises production of each enzyme, comparing chemical induction with IPTG against ZY auto-induction, both at 20 ºC.

For IPTG, cultures were grown in LB to mid-exponential phase (OD₆₀₀ 0.4 to 0.6), where the cells are healthiest and most metabolically active, and induced with 1 mM IPTG, a saturating concentration that fully derepresses lacUV5 and therefore T7 transcription. Induction was continued overnight at a reduced **20 ºC** rather than 37 ºC, because slowing translation gives the nascent chains more time to fold and reduces the accumulation of inclusion bodies. Auto-induction instead uses a medium whose glucose is consumed first and whose lactose then induces the system automatically as the culture reaches high density [9], so it needs no OD monitoring or timed addition. Every culture was started from a single colony in a 5 mL overnight pre-inoculum and seeded at OD₆₀₀ 0.05, so that all conditions began from the same low density. Expression was read by SDS-PAGE of the total and soluble fractions against a prestained standard.

The expected outcome was to select the higher-yielding regime. IPTG gave the stronger overexpression and was carried forward; it also revealed that the enzymes accumulated as inclusion bodies and that the two phospholipases C were cytotoxic to the host, which set up the next two experiments. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*
enzymatic immobilisation::solubilisation: Since none of the targets appeared in the soluble fraction, the aim here was to recover folded, soluble enzyme, applying three levers that each address a different cause of misfolding.

Induction at **30 ºC** was tried as a compromise that slows synthesis relative to 37 ºC while keeping growth reasonable, giving chains more time to fold. **Molecular chaperones** were co-expressed, the ribosome-associated Trigger factor, which stabilises the emerging chain and prevents premature aggregation, and the GroES/GroEL complex, which encapsulates partly folded protein and lets it fold in an ATP-dependent cage away from the crowded cytoplasm. Finally, for the disulphide-dependent enzymes flagged in Experiment 2, expression was moved to strains with an oxidising cytoplasm and rare-codon tRNAs (**Origami 2, Rosetta-gami 2 and SHuffle T7**, the last also co-expressing a disulphide isomerase); a codon analysis motivated this, since rare codons throttle both yield and folding. The cytotoxic phospholipases C were not forced through this pipeline but earmarked for cell-free IVTT, which does not depend on host viability.

The expected outcome was soluble enzyme for the tractable targets. GroES/GroEL solubilised **M2-32**, Rosetta-gami 2 solubilised **PhyA**, and **AphA** was obtained in BL21 (DE3). *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*
enzymatic immobilisation::purification b: The aim was to obtain each soluble enzyme clean enough for kinetic characterisation and, ultimately, immobilisation. Purification used immobilised metal-ion affinity chromatography on Ni-NTA [10], which exploits the coordinate bond between the engineered polyhistidine tag and nickel ions held on the resin.

The two membrane cut-offs are chosen deliberately so that small solutes pass during dialysis while the enzymes are retained during concentration. The expected outcome was homogeneous preparations; PhyA and M2-32 reached electrophoretic homogeneity and AphA was recovered at lower yield but sufficient for characterisation. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*

Activity was measured with **bis(p-nitrophenyl) phosphate (bis-pNPP)** rather than the usual pNPP [11], because bis-pNPP is a phosphodiester that better mimics the bulky, stable organophosphates of a real effluent (phytate, phospholipids), whereas pNPP carries a single, easily hydrolysed phosphate.

The end-point design (sampling into NaOH) is necessary precisely because pNP cannot be followed continuously at acidic pH, a constraint that later dictated a different assay for the immobilisation work. An enzyme-free well corrected for spontaneous substrate hydrolysis. Protein was quantified by Bradford against a BSA standard, and specific activity (U/mg, one unit releasing 1 µmol pNP per minute) was taken from the initial linear rate; normalising by protein mass is essential, since two enzymes releasing the same amount of product can differ greatly in efficiency once their loading is accounted for.

The expected outcome was a definitive order of intrinsic efficiency in acid medium, **AphA (0.222 U/mg) > M2-32 (0.161 U/mg) > PhyA (0.141 U/mg)**, identifying AphA and PhyA as the key components. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*

**Conclusion.** These experiments take the panel from database to characterised biocatalyst with no redundant step: activities were matched to the real effluent, constructs were designed to pre-empt insolubility, and only the rescue strategies actually needed were used.

In this block we establish **how to fix the enzymes onto the support** while keeping them active. Rather than testing directly on the more complex and costly alginate-chitosan-genipin sphere, the chemistry is first optimised on a simple, well-characterised **MANAE-agarose** model support, and the more reactive genipin of the final sphere is emulated by **glutaraldehyde**, which plays the same crosslinking role.

The model enzyme is **Lecitase Ultra**, chosen because it is the most demanding case: its active site is capped by a mobile lid that requires **interfacial activation**, and it forms **bimolecular aggregates** in solution. Mastering its immobilisation without losing activity is a strong indication that the more hydrophilic, structurally simpler enzymes of the panel can be accommodated afterwards. Two covalent strategies are compared, with and without detergent, and the results are rationalised by in-silico modelling of the enzyme's open and closed conformations.
enzymatic immobilisation::characterisati: The immobilisation chemistry needs a well-quantified enzyme available in bulk, so the commercial chimera Lecitase(R) Ultra was characterised before any immobilisation. It was chosen not only for availability but because it is the hardest case in the panel: its active site is capped by a lid that opens only on contact with a hydrophobic interface (interfacial activation), and it aggregates into dimers in solution [12], [13], so a chemistry that preserves its activity should generalise to the simpler, soluble enzymes.

Activity was followed with **p-nitrophenyl butyrate (pNPB)** [14] read continuously at **348 nm**, giving ΔA₃₄₈/min directly. A continuous assay is needed here because immobilisation is monitored in real time as enzyme leaves solution, and 348 nm was used instead of 405 nm because, unlike the acidic phosphatase assay, this wavelength lets pNP be read continuously without the pH-dependent colour problem. Protein was quantified by Bradford using serial dilutions to bring the reading into the linear range of the standard.

The expected outcome was a characterised stock (approximately **40 mg/mL** and **981 U/mg**) to serve as the baseline for every immobilisation yield. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*
enzymatic immobilisation::preparation of: The aim was to build a cheap, reproducible model support on which to compare immobilisation chemistries before committing to the alginate-chitosan-genipin sphere. MANAE-agarose was chosen because it is well characterised and previously optimised [14], and because glutaraldehyde on it plays the same amino-crosslinking role that genipin will play on the final sphere, so the conclusions transfer.

Starting from BCL agarose, the hydroxyls were first converted to epoxides with glycidol under alkaline reducing conditions, then oxidised with sodium periodate to give a glyoxyl (aldehyde) agarose. The aldehydes were reacted with an excess of ethylenediamine at pH 10, and the resulting Schiff bases were reduced with sodium borohydride, leaving the support decorated with positively charged secondary amino groups. Amination was carried out in an ice bath to control the exothermic reaction, and the support was washed sequentially at pH 9, pH 4 and with water to strip loosely bound reagents. The result is a positively charged support that adsorbs the acidic patches of a protein surface by ion exchange and, once activated with glutaraldehyde, can also bind it covalently.
The expected outcome was a MANAE-agarose support ready to serve as the common base for both immobilisation strategies. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*
enzymatic immobilisation::immobilisation: The aim was to test the classic route, direct multipoint covalent attachment, expected to give rigid, reusable derivatives. One gram of MANAE-agarose was activated with 10% glutaraldehyde overnight and used **immediately**, because the reactive aldehydes oxidise on standing and would otherwise lose reactivity before the enzyme is added.

The enzyme was offered at a deliberately low loading of **1 mg per g support**, to avoid crowding and diffusional limitation and so keep the experiment in the regime where the immobilisation chemistry, not mass transfer, governs the outcome. Attachment occurs through the ε-amino groups of the surface lysines. The run was performed both in plain buffer and with 0.1% Triton X-100 (see Experiment 5).
The expected outcome was covalent derivatives whose activity depends strongly on the enzyme's conformation at the moment of attachment. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*

The aim was to test a gentler two-step route in which the enzyme is first allowed to orient itself on the support and only then fixed covalently [15], [16]. The enzyme (1 mg/g) was first adsorbed on the bare, positively charged support in 25 mM potassium phosphate at pH 7 and 25 ºC, with adsorption followed by the fall in supernatant activity.

Only once adsorbed and oriented was it crosslinked, with a mild **0.5% glutaraldehyde** for 1 h and then a **20 h maturation**. The low glutaraldehyde concentration and the long maturation let the already-bound crosslinker react intra- and intermolecularly to consolidate a multipoint attachment without over-rigidifying the enzyme at the outset. Letting the dimers pre-orient before fixation is the whole point of the two-step design, and is what distinguishes it from strategy A.

The expected outcome was derivatives in which the enzyme retains the mobility its lid needs to open, provided its orientation on the support is right. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*
enzymatic immobilisation::effect of dete: Because Lecitase(R) Ultra aggregates through the hydrophobic regions exposed when its lid opens [13], a surfactant was introduced as a deliberate variable to control the open/closed equilibrium during immobilisation. Both strategies were run in parallel in plain buffer and in **0.1% Triton X-100**.

The detergent was expected to help or harm depending on the anchoring geometry, so it was tested against both strategies rather than assumed to act the same way. To interpret the results at the residue level, the open and closed conformations were also modelled (Experiment 7).
The expected outcome was opposite optima for the two strategies, the detergent helping the preactivated route and harming the adsorption route. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*
enzymatic immobilisation::evaluation of: The aim was to quantify how much active enzyme is actually bound, on an equal enzyme-and-support basis, so the strategies can be compared fairly. At intervals, activity was measured in the whole **suspension** (free plus bound enzyme) and in the clarified **supernatant** after a brief 604 × g spin that sediments the beads (free enzyme only). Their difference is the immobilised activity, and its ratio to the total is the yield.

A **free-enzyme control** incubated without support under the same conditions ran in parallel, so that any drop in activity could be attributed to immobilisation and not to buffer effects or thermal denaturation. This control is what allows the kinetic data to be trusted.

The expected outcome was that ionic adsorption followed by crosslinking, without detergent, would immobilise more active enzyme than the preactivated covalent route, from the same amount of enzyme and support. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*
enzymatic immobilisation::computational: The aim was to explain, at the residue level, why the detergent effect reverses between the two strategies. The open and closed conformations of Lecitase(R) Ultra were aligned and coloured in PyMOL, mapping the catalytic triad (Ser146, Asp201, His258), the lid (residues 80 to 95), the reactive lysines nearest the active site (Lys24, Lys259) and the acidic crown at the base (Asp27, Glu56, Asp57, Asp62).

On the preactivated support, the detergent holds the lid open so the enzyme is locked in its active form, whereas without detergent the closed enzyme is fixed through Lys24 and Lys259, jamming the lid shut and explaining the low activity [17]. In the adsorption route the acidic crown anchors the enzyme with its active site projected away from the surface, so without detergent the lid stays free to open, whereas the detergent scrambles that electrostatic orientation and the subsequent crosslinking then freezes a distorted arrangement [18].

The expected outcome was a structural model that fully accounts for the measured yields and points to the closed-form adsorption route as the strategy to transfer to the sphere. *PyMOL scripts: see the Protocols page [link pending].*

**Conclusion.** Using an inexpensive model support and glutaraldehyde as a stand-in for genipin let the two anchoring strategies be compared without spending resources on the full sphere; the detergent variable and the free-enzyme control were the minimum needed to interpret the yields, and the modelling was added only to explain the result.
enzymatic immobilisation::conclussion: The experiments on this page are both necessary and sufficient for the objective of the block, and they were ordered so that each one answered the question the next decision depended on. The mining was done before anything was expressed, because committing to seven heterologous enzymes is only worth it once the panel is matched to the real effluent and to the operating window, which is why the catalytic-profile filter at pH 5.0 and 30 ºC, and not sequence availability, drove the selection. The constructs were then designed in silico before any DNA was ordered, so that the folding environment each enzyme would need could be anticipated rather than discovered from a failed expression round. Expression separated what could be made from what could be folded, and the solubilisation effort was escalated only as far as each target required and stopped once three enzymes were soluble, rather than pursued to completeness: the enzymes that resisted, EstE1 and AppA, were left as the stated limit of the panel, and the cytotoxic phospholipases C were rerouted to cell-free expression rather than forced through a host that could not make them. Nothing was characterised beyond what the system required, a single affinity step rather than a full purification train, and activities reported as specific activities normalised by protein, which is the measurement that actually ranks the biocatalysts and the one that reversed the apparent order.

The scope of the immobilisation work was set by the circumstances of the project as much as by what would be ideal. The chemistry was developed on an inexpensive, previously optimised MANAE-agarose support with glutaraldehyde standing in for the genipin of the final sphere, rather than on the costly alginate-chitosan sphere itself, and on the commercial Lecitase Ultra, chosen as the most demanding model enzyme so that a chemistry able to preserve its activity would generalise to the simpler, more hydrophilic members of the panel. Each comparison carried the control that makes it interpretable: an enzyme-free spontaneous-hydrolysis control in the activity assay, and a free-enzyme inactivation control run alongside every immobilisation, so that a loss of activity could be attributed to the anchoring and not to the buffer or to thermal denaturation. The two sub-blocks are mutually dependent and converge in a single downstream step, since enzymes with no way to immobilise them for reuse, or an immobilisation chemistry with no enzymes to fix, would each fall short of a functionalised sphere: the panel of phosphohydrolases produced in the first is fixed, by the chemistry established in the second, onto the surface of the PAO-loaded alginate-chitosan sphere, with genipin replacing glutaraldehyde as a far less cytotoxic crosslinker. What is left undone is left for stated reasons, and in each case the experiment that would close the gap is named: the winning strategy has been validated on the model enzyme and support but not yet transferred to the panel enzymes on the real genipin sphere, and the phospholipase activity still awaits its cell-free production.
