Screening on these criteria before any wet work concentrated effort only on enzymes that could realistically be made and would survive the process.

The search combined **EnzymeMiner** [2], a platform that ranks candidate sequences by predicted solubility and expressibility, with targeted queries in **BRENDA** [3] and **UniProt** [4], applied as four sequential filters (initial pool, prokaryotic origin, literature support, catalytic profile). In parallel, a commercial homologue was identified for every activity as a contingency, so that a failure to express any one enzyme would not stall the panel.

The screen was expected to yield a small, redundant panel with at least two representatives per activity. It reduced 3,741 candidates to **7**: EstE1 (PLA), Plc and CerA (PLC), AppA and PhyA (phytase), and M2-32 and AphA (NAP). *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*

Before ordering any DNA, we decided for each enzyme where to place the purification tag and whether it would need a special folding environment, because both decisions are far cheaper to make on a model than to correct after cloning.

Each sequence without a resolved structure was modelled by homology on **SWISS-MODEL** [5] and inspected in **PyMOL** [6] for two things. First, the accessibility of the N- and C-termini: the polyhistidine tag must sit on an exposed terminus so it can reach the resin without occluding the active site, so the more exposed terminus set the vector, **pET-28a(+)** for an N-terminal tag (introduced at the NdeI site with a downstream STOP codon) or **pET-22b(+)** for a C-terminal tag [7]. Second, the presence of structural disulphide bridges: pairs of cysteine sulphur atoms closer than 2.5 Å were flagged, because a disulphide-dependent enzyme will not fold in the reducing cytoplasm of a standard strain and will instead need an oxidising chassis. Mapping this in silico told us in advance which enzymes would later require Rosetta-gami 2 or Origami 2, so the folding strategy was planned rather than discovered by trial and error.

The expected outcome was a per-enzyme decision (tag position, vector and disulphide dependence) that pre-empted the main causes of insolubility. *Protocol and PyMOL scripts: see the Protocols page [link pending].*

The aim was to obtain each gene inside its chosen pET backbone, using two routes according to availability so as to minimise cost. Sequences held in no repository were ordered as de novo gene synthesis directly in the pET vector (GCAT Bio, Changzhou, China), with codon optimisation used only when the nucleotide sequence was unavailable but the amino acid sequence was, since unnecessary optimisation can introduce its own expression artefacts. Sequences already validated in Addgene were amplified by PCR and cloned, which is far cheaper than synthesis.

For amplification, primers carried NdeI (5') and HindIII (3') sites matching the pET multiple cloning site. A small amount of donor plasmid (50 ng) was used as template with the high-fidelity polymerase **Pfu Ultra II** [8], chosen to avoid mutations in the coding sequence, and DMSO was added to help denature GC-rich regions. Because the Addgene genes arrived in different backbones, cloning them into the **same** pET vectors as the synthesised genes was a deliberate choice, so that any later difference in expression would reflect the enzyme and not the vector.

Inserts and vectors were then cut with FastDigest NdeI and HindIII, and the linearised vector was dephosphorylated with the thermosensitive alkaline phosphatase FastAP, a step included specifically to stop the vector re-circularising on itself without an insert and inflating the background. Fragments were gel-purified, and ligation was set at a 1:5 vector:insert molar ratio (NEBioCalculator) with T4 DNA ligase overnight at 16 ºC, a temperature that balances ligase activity against the annealing stability of the short cohesive ends.
The expected outcome was a set of recombinant pET plasmids for each gene, in matched backbones and ready to transform. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*

The aim was to introduce the plasmids into bacteria, confirm the correct insert and hand a validated construct to the expression host. The plasmids were introduced by **transformation**, the direct uptake of naked plasmid DNA by permeabilised competent cells, which is the appropriate route for purified plasmid DNA, as opposed to conjugation or transduction. Cloning was done first in *E. coli* DH5α, a recA and endA deficient strain that gives a high yield of stable plasmid but carries no T7 polymerase, so it propagates the construct without expressing it.

Immediately after heat shock (42 ºC, 90 s) or electroporation, the cells were recovered in **LB-SOC**, a rich medium supplemented with glucose, and incubated for one hour at 37 ºC before plating. This recovery step is essential: it lets the permeabilised cells repair their envelopes and, above all, transcribe and translate the antibiotic-resistance gene, so that they survive the subsequent selection. Plating straight onto antibiotic would kill successfully transformed but not-yet-resistant cells and collapse the apparent efficiency.

Transformants were screened by colony PCR with universal T7 primers flanking the insert, resolved on a 1% agarose gel; since the amplicon sizes matched the SnapGene simulation, sequencing was not required. Positive clones were grown and their plasmid recovered by alkaline-lysis **miniprep** (NZY), which denatures and precipitates genomic DNA and protein while keeping the supercoiled plasmid in solution, giving clean DNA to re-transform. The verified plasmid was finally moved into a **(DE3)** expression strain, which carries T7 RNA polymerase under the IPTG-inducible lacUV5 promoter, the element absent from DH5α that actually drives transcription of the cloned gene.
The expected outcome was verified clones in the expression host, ready for induction. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*
The aim was to find the induction regime that maximises production of each enzyme, comparing chemical induction with IPTG against ZY auto-induction, both at 20 ºC.

For IPTG, cultures were grown in LB to mid-exponential phase (OD₆₀₀ 0.4 to 0.6), where the cells are healthiest and most metabolically active, and induced with 1 mM IPTG, a saturating concentration that fully derepresses lacUV5 and therefore T7 transcription. Induction was continued overnight at a reduced **20 ºC** rather than 37 ºC, because slowing translation gives the nascent chains more time to fold and reduces the accumulation of inclusion bodies. Auto-induction instead uses a medium whose glucose is consumed first and whose lactose then induces the system automatically as the culture reaches high density [9], so it needs no OD monitoring or timed addition. Every culture was started from a single colony in a 5 mL overnight pre-inoculum and seeded at OD₆₀₀ 0.05, so that all conditions began from the same low density. Expression was read by SDS-PAGE of the total and soluble fractions against a prestained standard.

The expected outcome was to select the higher-yielding regime. IPTG gave the stronger overexpression and was carried forward; it also revealed that the enzymes accumulated as inclusion bodies and that the two phospholipases C were cytotoxic to the host, which set up the next two experiments. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*
Since none of the targets appeared in the soluble fraction, the aim here was to recover folded, soluble enzyme, applying three levers that each address a different cause of misfolding.

Induction at **30 ºC** was tried as a compromise that slows synthesis relative to 37 ºC while keeping growth reasonable, giving chains more time to fold. **Molecular chaperones** were co-expressed, the ribosome-associated Trigger factor, which stabilises the emerging chain and prevents premature aggregation, and the GroES/GroEL complex, which encapsulates partly folded protein and lets it fold in an ATP-dependent cage away from the crowded cytoplasm. Finally, for the disulphide-dependent enzymes flagged in Experiment 2, expression was moved to strains with an oxidising cytoplasm and rare-codon tRNAs (**Origami 2, Rosetta-gami 2 and SHuffle T7**, the last also co-expressing a disulphide isomerase); a codon analysis motivated this, since rare codons throttle both yield and folding. The cytotoxic phospholipases C were not forced through this pipeline but earmarked for cell-free IVTT, which does not depend on host viability.

The expected outcome was soluble enzyme for the tractable targets. GroES/GroEL solubilised **M2-32**, Rosetta-gami 2 solubilised **PhyA**, and **AphA** was obtained in BL21 (DE3). *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*

The aim was to obtain each soluble enzyme clean enough for kinetic characterisation and, ultimately, immobilisation. Purification used immobilised metal-ion affinity chromatography on Ni-NTA [10], which exploits the coordinate bond between the engineered polyhistidine tag and nickel ions held on the resin.

The two membrane cut-offs are chosen deliberately so that small solutes pass during dialysis while the enzymes are retained during concentration. The expected outcome was homogeneous preparations; PhyA and M2-32 reached electrophoretic homogeneity and AphA was recovered at lower yield but sufficient for characterisation. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*

The aim was to confirm that the purified enzymes are active at process conditions and to rank them by intrinsic efficiency. Activity was measured with **bis(p-nitrophenyl) phosphate (bis-pNPP)** rather than the usual pNPP [11], because bis-pNPP is a phosphodiester that better mimics the bulky, stable organophosphates of a real effluent (phytate, phospholipids), whereas pNPP carries a single, easily hydrolysed phosphate.

The end-point design (sampling into NaOH) is necessary precisely because pNP cannot be followed continuously at acidic pH, a constraint that later dictated a different assay for the immobilisation work. An enzyme-free well corrected for spontaneous substrate hydrolysis. Protein was quantified by Bradford against a BSA standard, and specific activity (U/mg, one unit releasing 1 µmol pNP per minute) was taken from the initial linear rate; normalising by protein mass is essential, since two enzymes releasing the same amount of product can differ greatly in efficiency once their loading is accounted for.

The expected outcome was a definitive order of intrinsic efficiency in acid medium, **AphA (0.222 U/mg) > M2-32 (0.161 U/mg) > PhyA (0.141 U/mg)**, identifying AphA and PhyA as the key components. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*

**Conclusion.** These experiments take the panel from database to characterised biocatalyst with no redundant step: activities were matched to the real effluent, constructs were designed to pre-empt insolubility, and only the rescue strategies actually needed were used.

In this block we establish **how to fix the enzymes onto the support** while keeping them active. Rather than testing directly on the more complex and costly alginate-chitosan-genipin sphere, the chemistry is first optimised on a simple, well-characterised **MANAE-agarose** model support, and the more reactive genipin of the final sphere is emulated by **glutaraldehyde**, which plays the same crosslinking role.

The model enzyme is **Lecitase Ultra**, chosen because it is the most demanding case: its active site is capped by a mobile lid that requires **interfacial activation**, and it forms **bimolecular aggregates** in solution. Mastering its immobilisation without losing activity is a strong indication that the more hydrophilic, structurally simpler enzymes of the panel can be accommodated afterwards. Two covalent strategies are compared, with and without detergent, and the results are rationalised by in-silico modelling of the enzyme's open and closed conformations.

The immobilisation chemistry needs a well-quantified enzyme available in bulk, so the commercial chimera Lecitase(R) Ultra was characterised before any immobilisation. It was chosen not only for availability but because it is the hardest case in the panel: its active site is capped by a lid that opens only on contact with a hydrophobic interface (interfacial activation), and it aggregates into dimers in solution [12], [13], so a chemistry that preserves its activity should generalise to the simpler, soluble enzymes.

Activity was followed with **p-nitrophenyl butyrate (pNPB)** [14] read continuously at **348 nm**, giving ΔA₃₄₈/min directly. A continuous assay is needed here because immobilisation is monitored in real time as enzyme leaves solution, and 348 nm was used instead of 405 nm because, unlike the acidic phosphatase assay, this wavelength lets pNP be read continuously without the pH-dependent colour problem. Protein was quantified by Bradford using serial dilutions to bring the reading into the linear range of the standard.

The expected outcome was a characterised stock (approximately **40 mg/mL** and **981 U/mg**) to serve as the baseline for every immobilisation yield. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*

The aim was to build a cheap, reproducible model support on which to compare immobilisation chemistries before committing to the alginate-chitosan-genipin sphere. MANAE-agarose was chosen because it is well characterised and previously optimised [14], and because glutaraldehyde on it plays the same amino-crosslinking role that genipin will play on the final sphere, so the conclusions transfer.

Starting from BCL agarose, the hydroxyls were first converted to epoxides with glycidol under alkaline reducing conditions, then oxidised with sodium periodate to give a glyoxyl (aldehyde) agarose. The aldehydes were reacted with an excess of ethylenediamine at pH 10, and the resulting Schiff bases were reduced with sodium borohydride, leaving the support decorated with positively charged secondary amino groups. Amination was carried out in an ice bath to control the exothermic reaction, and the support was washed sequentially at pH 9, pH 4 and with water to strip loosely bound reagents. The result is a positively charged support that adsorbs the acidic patches of a protein surface by ion exchange and, once activated with glutaraldehyde, can also bind it covalently.
The expected outcome was a MANAE-agarose support ready to serve as the common base for both immobilisation strategies. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*

The aim was to test the classic route, direct multipoint covalent attachment, expected to give rigid, reusable derivatives. One gram of MANAE-agarose was activated with 10% glutaraldehyde overnight and used **immediately**, because the reactive aldehydes oxidise on standing and would otherwise lose reactivity before the enzyme is added.

The enzyme was offered at a deliberately low loading of **1 mg per g support**, to avoid crowding and diffusional limitation and so keep the experiment in the regime where the immobilisation chemistry, not mass transfer, governs the outcome. Attachment occurs through the ε-amino groups of the surface lysines. The run was performed both in plain buffer and with 0.1% Triton X-100 (see Experiment 5).
The expected outcome was covalent derivatives whose activity depends strongly on the enzyme's conformation at the moment of attachment. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*

The aim was to test a gentler two-step route in which the enzyme is first allowed to orient itself on the support and only then fixed covalently [15], [16]. The enzyme (1 mg/g) was first adsorbed on the bare, positively charged support in 25 mM potassium phosphate at pH 7 and 25 ºC, with adsorption followed by the fall in supernatant activity.

Only once adsorbed and oriented was it crosslinked, with a mild **0.5% glutaraldehyde** for 1 h and then a **20 h maturation**. The low glutaraldehyde concentration and the long maturation let the already-bound crosslinker react intra- and intermolecularly to consolidate a multipoint attachment without over-rigidifying the enzyme at the outset. Letting the dimers pre-orient before fixation is the whole point of the two-step design, and is what distinguishes it from strategy A.

The expected outcome was derivatives in which the enzyme retains the mobility its lid needs to open, provided its orientation on the support is right. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*

Because Lecitase(R) Ultra aggregates through the hydrophobic regions exposed when its lid opens [13], a surfactant was introduced as a deliberate variable to control the open/closed equilibrium during immobilisation. Both strategies were run in parallel in plain buffer and in **0.1% Triton X-100**.

The detergent was expected to help or harm depending on the anchoring geometry, so it was tested against both strategies rather than assumed to act the same way. To interpret the results at the residue level, the open and closed conformations were also modelled (Experiment 7).
The expected outcome was opposite optima for the two strategies, the detergent helping the preactivated route and harming the adsorption route. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*

The aim was to quantify how much active enzyme is actually bound, on an equal enzyme-and-support basis, so the strategies can be compared fairly. At intervals, activity was measured in the whole **suspension** (free plus bound enzyme) and in the clarified **supernatant** after a brief 604 × g spin that sediments the beads (free enzyme only). Their difference is the immobilised activity, and its ratio to the total is the yield.

A **free-enzyme control** incubated without support under the same conditions ran in parallel, so that any drop in activity could be attributed to immobilisation and not to buffer effects or thermal denaturation. This control is what allows the kinetic data to be trusted.

The expected outcome was that ionic adsorption followed by crosslinking, without detergent, would immobilise more active enzyme than the preactivated covalent route, from the same amount of enzyme and support. *Protocol: see the Protocols page [link pending].*

The aim was to explain, at the residue level, why the detergent effect reverses between the two strategies. The open and closed conformations of Lecitase(R) Ultra were aligned and coloured in PyMOL, mapping the catalytic triad (Ser146, Asp201, His258), the lid (residues 80 to 95), the reactive lysines nearest the active site (Lys24, Lys259) and the acidic crown at the base (Asp27, Glu56, Asp57, Asp62).

On the preactivated support, the detergent holds the lid open so the enzyme is locked in its active form, whereas without detergent the closed enzyme is fixed through Lys24 and Lys259, jamming the lid shut and explaining the low activity [17]. In the adsorption route the acidic crown anchors the enzyme with its active site projected away from the surface, so without detergent the lid stays free to open, whereas the detergent scrambles that electrostatic orientation and the subsequent crosslinking then freezes a distorted arrangement [18].

The expected outcome was a structural model that fully accounts for the measured yields and points to the closed-form adsorption route as the strategy to transfer to the sphere. *PyMOL scripts: see the Protocols page [link pending].*

**Conclusion.** Using an inexpensive model support and glutaraldehyde as a stand-in for genipin let the two anchoring strategies be compared without spending resources on the full sphere; the detergent variable and the free-enzyme control were the minimum needed to interpret the yields, and the modelling was added only to explain the result.

The experiments on this page are both necessary and sufficient for the objective of the block, and they were ordered so that each one answered the question the next decision depended on. The mining was done before anything was expressed, because committing to seven heterologous enzymes is only worth it once the panel is matched to the real effluent and to the operating window, which is why the catalytic-profile filter at pH 5.0 and 30 ºC, and not sequence availability, drove the selection. The constructs were then designed in silico before any DNA was ordered, so that the folding environment each enzyme would need could be anticipated rather than discovered from a failed expression round. Expression separated what could be made from what could be folded, and the solubilisation effort was escalated only as far as each target required and stopped once three enzymes were soluble, rather than pursued to completeness: the enzymes that resisted, EstE1 and AppA, were left as the stated limit of the panel, and the cytotoxic phospholipases C were rerouted to cell-free expression rather than forced through a host that could not make them. Nothing was characterised beyond what the system required, a single affinity step rather than a full purification train, and activities reported as specific activities normalised by protein, which is the measurement that actually ranks the biocatalysts and the one that reversed the apparent order.

The scope of the immobilisation work was set by the circumstances of the project as much as by what would be ideal. The chemistry was developed on an inexpensive, previously optimised MANAE-agarose support with glutaraldehyde standing in for the genipin of the final sphere, rather than on the costly alginate-chitosan sphere itself, and on the commercial Lecitase Ultra, chosen as the most demanding model enzyme so that a chemistry able to preserve its activity would generalise to the simpler, more hydrophilic members of the panel. Each comparison carried the control that makes it interpretable: an enzyme-free spontaneous-hydrolysis control in the activity assay, and a free-enzyme inactivation control run alongside every immobilisation, so that a loss of activity could be attributed to the anchoring and not to the buffer or to thermal denaturation. The two sub-blocks are mutually dependent and converge in a single downstream step, since enzymes with no way to immobilise them for reuse, or an immobilisation chemistry with no enzymes to fix, would each fall short of a functionalised sphere: the panel of phosphohydrolases produced in the first is fixed, by the chemistry established in the second, onto the surface of the PAO-loaded alginate-chitosan sphere, with genipin replacing glutaraldehyde as a far less cytotoxic crosslinker. What is left undone is left for stated reasons, and in each case the experiment that would close the gap is named: the winning strategy has been validated on the model enzyme and support but not yet transferred to the panel enzymes on the real genipin sphere, and the phospholipase activity still awaits its cell-free production.

genetic engineering::ppk1 polyphosphate: **What it does:** the enzyme that **builds polyphosphate**. It takes the terminal (γ) phosphate from ATP and adds it, residue by residue, to a growing polyP chain. It is the engine of polyP synthesis in PAOs.

**What we do to it and why:** we **express it heterologously** (cloned into a pSEVA vector), using the *Ca.* Accumulibacter version. We add extra synthesis capacity so that all the incoming phosphate is turned into stored polyP, the heart of accumulation.
**GIF (storyboard):** ATP molecules coming in; the phosphate is clipped off ATP (ATP → ADP) and attached to the end of a polyP chain that grows into a granule.
genetic engineering::pstscab high affini: **What it does:** a high-affinity **phosphate import pump**. PstS captures phosphate in the periplasm; PstC and PstA form the membrane channel; PstB is the ATPase supplying the energy. It brings phosphate into the cell **even when very little is left outside**.

**What we do to it and why:** we **express it heterologously** (from *Ca.* Accumulibacter) to maximise phosphate uptake and feed polyP synthesis. Its high affinity is key to "polishing" the water down to low residual concentrations.
**GIF (storyboard):** phosphate ions from the medium captured at the membrane/periplasm and pumped through the channel into the cell, with ATP → ADP powering the pump.
genetic engineering::ppx exopolyphosphat: **What it does:** the enzyme that **degrades polyphosphate**. It hydrolyses phosphates from the end of the polyP chain and releases them as inorganic phosphate (Pi). It is the main activity that "undoes" what has been accumulated.

**What we do to it and why:** we **inactivate it with CRISPR** (base editing) so the cell cannot dismantle its polyP reserves. This locks in the accumulated phosphorus and avoids a futile synthesis/degradation cycle.
**GIF (storyboard):** a polyP chain being nibbled from the end, phosphates dropping off one by one → with a large red **X / strike-through** showing we remove this activity.
genetic engineering::ppkb ppk2 polyphosp: **What it does:** a **type-2 polyphosphate kinase**: it uses polyP as a phosphate donor to phosphorylate nucleotides (e.g. ADP → ATP, GDP → GTP), **consuming** the polyP chain. In other words, it spends polyP to regenerate nucleotides.
**What we do to it and why:** we **inactivate it with CRISPR** so polyP is not consumed by this route. We reduce polyP turnover and favour net accumulation.
**GIF (storyboard):** polyP donating a phosphate to an ADP that becomes ATP while the chain shortens → struck through with a red **X**.
genetic engineering::pitb low affinity p: **What it does:** a **low-affinity phosphate transporter** (Pit-type), a metal-phosphate/H⁺ symporter. Pit systems are bidirectional and are implicated in the **efflux/release** of phosphate from PAOs.
**What we do to it and why:** we **inactivate it with CRISPR** to reduce phosphate leakage to the outside, so the imported and stored phosphate stays inside and is not lost back to the medium.
**GIF (storyboard):** phosphate escaping from the cell through a channel → struck through with a red **X** to show we block the leak.

This set of experiments establishes, in **wild-type P. putida KT2440** [1], how much phosphorus the **cells take up and store as polyphosphate, how fast, and under which operating condition**s this is maximised. Because the engineered strains will later be judged by exactly this read-out, the experiments first build and standardise a reproducible intracellular-phosphorus assay, then use it to **characterise growth, the kinetics of accumulation across media, and the two operating variables available in the real feed**. Two variants were used: t**he wild type (WT) and an mCherry-tagged variant (Cherry)** for growth tracking. The application target is a synthetic aqueous stream mimicking the phosphorus-rich effluent of biofuel production, the context in which polyphosphate-based phosphorus recovery would operate [2], [3].
genetic engineering::growth characterisa: Before following accumulation over time, the growth trajectory of the cells in the minimal medium used as the maximal-stress reference (**M9**) had to be known, so that phosphorus values could be read against a defined biomass curve. The mCherry variant, which is easy to track, was cultured in M9 and OD600 was followed across the 240 min assay window.
The expected outcome was a defined OD600 trajectory over the assay window, confirming the cells remain measurable throughout.
genetic engineering::kinetics of polypho: With the assay standardised, the kinetics of intracellular polyphosphate were compared across three media that differ in nutrient availability. Cells grown in LB were shifted into each medium and sampled over 0 to 240 min; at each time point one aliquot gave OD600 and a paired aliquot was processed through the assay. The comparison rests on the hypothesis that polyphosphate accumulation is a **nutrient-stress response** [2], so retention should scale inversely with nutrient availability.

The **synthetic stream** was prepared to mimic a biofuel-derived industrial feed: citric acid, glycerol, soy lecithin, monopotassium phosphate (the phosphate source), ammonium sulfate, sodium chloride, filtered used vegetable oil and Tween 80, with the pH adjusted as required.
The expected outcome was a monotonic trend, with the highest normalised polyphosphate in M9, the lowest in LB and an intermediate value in the synthetic stream.
genetic engineering::operating condition: Having established the medium trend, the two variables that the industrial partner (**BioOils Huelva**) actually allows to be adjusted, **pH** and **degree of dilution**, were screened combinatorially in the synthetic stream, with dilution standing in for nutrient limitation, since a more dilute feed is a more nutrient-limited one. Four conditions crossed two pH values with two dilutions, with M9 and LB retained as controls, each followed over the assay time course.
The expected outcome was to identify the pH and dilution combination that maximises phosphorus retention in the application-relevant medium.
These steps take the two genes from design to a functionally validated, phosphate-accumulating strain, with each verification stage gating the next.

The goal of this set of experiments is a *P. putida* strain that stably expresses **ppk1** and **pstSCAB** from *Candidatus* Accumulibacter phosphatis. Because *P. putida* is far less amenable to routine cloning than *Escherichia coli* [1], [2], each plasmid is built and verified in an *E. coli* cloning host and only then moved into the final chassis. This keeps the iterative cloning steps in the fastest, most transformable host and reserves the slower work with *P. putida* for constructs we already trust.
genetic engineering::in silico design of: The first step was to design, in silico, the two expression cassettes: a promoter, a ribosome binding site (RBS), the coding sequence and the cloning sites needed to assemble each cassette into its pSEVA backbone by restriction and ligation.

Two design decisions carry most of the weight. First, the *ppk1* and *pstSCAB* coding sequences were **codon-optimised for *P. putida* KT2440**, because *Ca.* Accumulibacter has a different codon usage and its native sequences would be read inefficiently, with rare codons risking ribosome stalling and truncated product. Second, rather than modelling a bespoke RBS, we used the **canonical RBS for *P. putida*** (a strong, well-characterised Shine-Dalgarno of the form AGGAGG), which gives reliable, predictable initiation in this host without the risk of an untested sequence. The restriction sites were chosen to match the chosen backbones: **BamHI and HindIII** for the cassettes going into **pSEVA2513**, and **EcoRI and KpnI** for the promoter fragment going into **pSEVA6313**. Design and map management were done in **SnapGene**. See our parts collection to check DNA sequences.
The expected outcome was two fully annotated cassettes, compatible with the restriction and ligation strategy and ready to order or amplify.
genetic engineering::part acquisition an: The parts were obtained in the form best suited to each. The coding sequences were ordered as **synthetic genes delivered pre-cloned in carrier vectors**: **ppk1 in pMK-RQ** and **pstSCAB in pOK-RQ**, both kanamycin-resistant. Ordering genes pre-cloned gives a stable, sequence-verified stock that can be propagated and drawn on as needed. The promoter was supplied in the small synthetic promotor **pEM7**.

The promoter needed special handling because it is very short (about **77 bp**). Released by EcoRI and KpnI digestion, a fragment this small runs off the front of the gel and cannot be recovered cleanly, so it cannot simply be cut out and purified. The working solution was to move the promoter and RBS off the gel entirely and **build them into the genes through PCR primers**: the coding sequences were amplified with primers that carry the RBS and the required restriction sites as overhangs, so the cassette is completed during amplification rather than by purifying a tiny promoter band.

The amplification used **Pfu polymerase** (the enzyme available in the lab; slower than Phusion but high-fidelity, which matters because any error introduced while amplifying a coding sequence would be carried into the final construct). A high-fidelity enzyme keeps that error rate negligible. Products were checked on an agarose gel and quantified by NanoDrop before use.
The expected outcome was a sequence-verified stock of each gene in its carrier vector and clean, correctly sized amplicons carrying the RBS and cloning sites.
genetic engineering::preparative digesti: The backbones and inserts were then cut to matching ends. **pSEVA2513** (kanamycin-resistant, about **5.3 kb**) was digested with **BamHI and HindIII**, together with the *ppk1* and *pstSCAB* cassettes; **pSEVA631** (gentamicin-resistant, about **3.0 kb**) was digested with **EcoRI and KpnI** for the promoter route. These vector choices matter because *P. putida* does not maintain the ColE1 or pUC origins of standard *E. coli* vectors and requires **broad-host-range replicons**; the SEVA collection supplies exactly these, with compatible resistance and origin modules [3], [4]. All of the restriction enzymes used were casual Thermo Fisher ones.

Enzymes were used at **37 °C** variable time and buffer. The vector was **not dephosphorylated**; instead, background from re-ligation was controlled by running a vector-only ligation control in the next step and by clean preparative gel excision. For *ppk1*, whose backbone fragment co-migrates with the insert on a 1% gel, an **additional NcoI digestion** was used to separate the bands so the correct fragment could be excised. Digestions were resolved on **1% agarose** in TAE, stained with Diamond dye, and the bands of interest were excised and purified with the **Wizard SV Gel and PCR Clean-Up System** (Promega), eluting in water or the kit buffer.

To ensure the insert's identity, the restriction enzyme XhoI was used during the second attempt for ppk1. This enzyme has two internal restriction sites, which do not cut the empty vector but ensure the release of two fragments of 1126 and 6312 bp in the correct ligation product.
The expected outcome was cleanly cut, gel-purified vector and insert with compatible ends.
genetic engineering::ligation: The cassettes were joined to their backbones by **T4 DNA ligation**. Reactions used a **vector-to-insert molar ratio of about 1:5**, T4 buffer and T4 DNA ligase, incubated **overnight at 16 °C**, the standard low-temperature condition that favours intermolecular joining of sticky ends. A **vector-only control** was always run alongside: a control plate with only a few tiny colonies, as obtained here, indicates that the vector is not re-ligating on itself and that colonies on the sample plate are likely to carry insert.
The expected outcome was a ligation mixture ready to transform, with the control showing minimal background.
genetic engineering::transformation into: The ligation was introduced into chemically competent **E. coli DH5α**. The correct term is **transformation**, the uptake of naked plasmid DNA by an artificially competent bacterial cell; we avoid "transfer", which is nonspecific, and "transfection", which refers to eukaryotic cells. DH5α is used rather than the final chassis because its genotype protects the construct (*endA1* removes an endonuclease and gives cleaner minipreps, *recA1* reduces recombination and keeps inserts stable) and because it transforms far more efficiently than *P. putida*.

Cells were heat-shocked, then **recovered in non-selective rich medium** before plating, so that the resistance protein is expressed before selection; plating straight onto antibiotic would kill genuine transformants. Cells were then plated on **LB agar with kanamycin** or gentamycin depending on the antibiotic resistance gene from the backbone.
The expected outcome was colonies on the selective plates and few or none on the control.
genetic engineering::colony screening an: Candidate colonies were triaged by **colony PCR** and by **diagnostic restriction digestion** (for example, a PauI or BamHI and HindIII digest whose band pattern distinguishes a correct construct from an empty or mis-assembled one). Colony PCR is run first because it is fast and cheap and can screen many colonies directly. Positives were grown and their plasmid isolated by **miniprep**, either with the **PureYield Plasmid Miniprep System** (Promega) or by kit-free alkaline lysis; miniprep is chosen over midi or maxi preparations because only enough DNA for a digest and for sequencing is needed at this stage. Products were checked on agarose and quantified by NanoDrop.
The expected outcome was several independent clones per construct with the correct pattern.
genetic engineering::sequence confirmati: Clones that passed screening were confirmed by sequencing, because screening shows an insert of the right size and orientation but only sequencing rules out point mutations, indels or assembly scars that could inactivate the protein or shift the reading frame. Sanger sequencing of the cassette and its junctions, or whole-plasmid sequencing, was used, and only a clone matching the in-silico design exactly was carried forward.
The expected outcome was a **sequence-verified expression plasmid** for each gene.
genetic engineering::transformation into: The verified plasmids were moved into the final chassis by **electroporation of electrocompetent *P. putida* KT2440**, prepared by the standard rapid sucrose-wash method (repeated washes in 300 mM sucrose to remove salts) [5]. Electroporation is used because *P. putida* is not naturally competent and takes up DNA far less readily than *E. coli*, so more input DNA is generally needed than for a routine *E. coli* transformation [2], [5]. The pSEVA vectors are broad-host-range and are stably maintained in *Pseudomonas*. Transformants were selected on **LB with kanamycin**.
The expected outcome was resistant *P. putida* colonies carrying the expression plasmid.
These steps take the two genes from design to a functionally validated, phosphate-accumulating strain, with each verification stage gating the next.

The goal of this set of experiments is to remove, in the same strain, three native activities that oppose accumulation: **ppx** (degrades polyphosphate), **ppkB** / **ppk2** (consumes polyphosphate to phosphorylate nucleotides) and **pitB** (low-affinity phosphate transport implicated in efflux). They are inactivated by **CRISPR base editing** [6], [7], [8] rather than by conventional Cas9 cutting, because a double-strand break in *P. putida* is problematic: the organism has limited non-homologous end joining, so cuts are repaired poorly and are often lethal, and scarless deletion would otherwise require a homology-directed repair template. A cytidine base editor sidesteps this, introducing a premature stop codon by chemistry alone, an approach already validated for gene inactivation in *P. putida* KT2440 [8].

We use the **pMBEC2** base editor [9], which fuses a cytidine deaminase, a Cas9 nickase and a uracil glycosylase inhibitor, and carries a constitutively expressed **msfGFP** cassette flanked by **BsaI** sites in place of the guide. The guide RNA is installed by **Golden Gate assembly** [9], [10], replacing the msfGFP marker, so that correct constructs can be picked by **loss of green fluorescence**.
genetic engineering::in silico design of: The block opens with guide design because base editing only works within a narrow window. A cytidine base editor deaminates cytosine to uracil (read as thymine) within roughly positions 4 to 8 of the protospacer, converting a C·G pair to T·A [6]. To create a **premature stop codon** we look for a **CAA, CAG or CGA** codon, which a single C to T edit turns into **TAA, TAG or TGA** [8], placed so that the editable C falls inside the window and a suitable NGG PAM lies the correct distance away. The edit was placed **early in each gene** so the truncated protein is certainly non-functional, and candidate guides were screened for **off-targets** against the KT2440 genome, with two or three guides designed per gene. This was achieved by using the *CRISPR for Pseudomonas excel*  tool.
The expected outcome was a prioritised set of guides for *ppx*, *ppkB* and *pitB*.
genetic engineering::amplification of th: The guide fragments were generated by **PCR from the template vector pEX128**, using oligonucleotides that carry the specific spacer for each target together with the Golden Gate (BsaI) flanking motifs [7] , so the guide is assembled directly around the desired spacer. Amplification used **Pfu polymerase**. Because the amplicon is small (about **130 to 150 bp** for *ppx*, *ppkB* and *pitB*), the cycling was tuned for a short product: a short extension (about 20 to 30 s) and a short denaturation, with an annealing temperature of **60 °C** following the source protocol and a **gradient (60 to 68 °C)** tested when a larger, non-specific band appeared. A no-oligo negative control was run to confirm that the band depends on the primers. Products were checked on **1.5% agarose**, then purified with the **Wizard SV Gel and PCR Clean-Up System** (Promega).
The expected outcome was clean bands of about 130 to 150 bp for the three targets, with a blank negative control.
genetic engineering::golden gate assembl: Each guide fragment was assembled into **pMBEC2** by **Golden Gate (BsaI)** [9], [10], replacing the msfGFP marker with the guide. Golden Gate is used here, rather than the restriction and ligation of Block A, because the pMBEC design is built for it: BsaI cuts outside its recognition site, so digestion and ligation can run in one pot and the marker is swapped for the guide seamlessly. This is also what enables the fluorescence-based screen in the next step.
The expected outcome was an assembly mixture ready to transform.
genetic engineering::transformation and: The assembly was transformed into **E. coli DH5α** and plated. Because a correct construct has lost the msfGFP marker, colonies were screened by fluorescence: **non-fluorescent (white) colonies carry the guide**, whereas green colonies still hold the template. Selected white colonies were grown, miniprepped and verified. When the Golden Gate efficiency is low, the assembly is repeated using the protocol cycling as written.
The expected outcome was verified editor-plus-guide plasmids (**pMBEC2**, guide against *ppx*, *ppkB* or *pitB*).
genetic engineering::delivery into p put: The verified editing plasmids were introduced into **P. putida KT2440 by electroporation** [5], as in Block A, step 8, and selected on the vector's antibiotic. Delivery is kept separate from editing so that a clean, selected population carrying the system is established first.
The expected outcome was *P. putida* transformants carrying the editing system.
genetic engineering::editing and colony: Cells were diluted and plated to obtain **single colonies**, because a freshly induced culture is a mixture of edited and unedited cells and only clonal colonies allow an individual genotype to be read out.
The expected outcome was individual candidate colonies.
genetic engineering::screening of edits: Each candidate was genotyped by **colony PCR and Sanger sequencing** of the target region, reading the **C to T conversion** and confirming the stop codon using SnapGene. Sequencing is the only reliable read-out, since the edit is a single base change that produces no size difference.
The expected outcome was colonies carrying the edit that creates the stop codon.
genetic engineering::curing and iteratio: The editor plasmid was then **cured**, which stops further editing, yields a stable strain and, importantly, **frees the antibiotic marker** for the next round [9]. This was achieved by sucrose 5% w/v passes. The introduce, edit, screen and cure cycle was repeated for the second and third genes, each round starting from the strain of the previous one, so the three knock-outs accumulate in a single lineage. Editing was done **sequentially rather than as a single multiplex**, so each edit is verified before the next, although the pMBEC toolset also supports multiplexing [9].
The expected outcome was a **triple mutant**, *ppx⁻ ppkB⁻ pitB⁻*.
genetic engineering::verification of the: Before phenotyping, the three target regions were amplified and sequenced to confirm all three stop codons. **Whole-genome sequencing** to check for off-targets or rearrangements accumulated over three rounds was not considered because off-target cuts were bioinformatically optimized and whole-genome sequencing costs. This ensures the later phenotype can be attributed to the intended knock-outs.
The expected outcome was confirmation of the three knock-outs with no significant unwanted edits.

The steps are the minimum needed to install and prove three clean, markerless knock-outs in one strain: per-round sequencing is required by the chemistry of base editing, and curing is what makes three sequential rounds possible with a limited set of markers.
genetic engineering::closing from two mo: Taken together, the two blocks are both **necessary and sufficient** for the block objective, and they were shaped by the constraints of the project rather than added for completeness. Neither module alone produces a phosphorus-accumulating strain: adding uptake and storage capacity (Block A) is wasted if the cell still degrades and leaks what it stores, and removing the native loss routes (Block B) achieves little without the added capacity to import phosphate and fix it as polyphosphate. The verification-heavy design of both blocks, screening before sequencing and sequencing before phenotyping, reflects a deliberate choice to fail fast and cheaply in *E. coli* and to trust *P. putida* results only once the genotype is certain.

The two modules converge in a final **integration** step. The verified expression plasmids from Block A (*ppk1* and *pstSCAB*) are introduced into *P. putida* KT2440, individually and together, by electroporation, giving the strains that carry the added machinery; in parallel, the base-edited knock-out background from Block B removes the native loss routes. The complete strain is then assessed with the **intracellular phosphorus capture assay**, this time as an end-to-end validation of the full rePhlow phenotype rather than of a single module. Measuring capture inside the cell, rather than depletion from the medium, is what makes this a direct test of phosphorus accumulation.

The assay follows a **phosphate-overplus** logic. Wild type and engineered strains are grown in LB to OD600 of about 0.6 and then **starved of phosphate for 1 h** in a phosphate-free minimal medium, which empties the internal polyphosphate and derepresses the phosphate-uptake machinery, so that avid uptake is triggered when phosphate is restored. The cells are then shifted into the **test medium at pH 5** at OD600 = 1.0, which is t = 0. Over a 0 to 120 min time course (sampled at 0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90, 105 and 120 min) one aliquot is read for OD600 (at a 1/10 dilution) while a paired aliquot is pelleted and **washed three times in 0.1 M NaCl** to remove the phosphate-rich medium, which would otherwise swamp the signal. The phosphorus stored inside the cells is released by acid digestion (150 µL of 1 M HCl, 95 °C, 15 min), the lysate is neutralised (150 µL of supernatant plus 150 µL of 1 M NaOH, to about pH 7) and pre-diluted tenfold, and the free phosphate is quantified with the **Promega Non-Radioactive Phosphatase Assay System** (Serine/Threonine Phosphatase Assay System, cat. V2460), which measures phosphate as a **molybdate:malachite green complex** by absorbance in cuvette against a 0 to 1900 ng phosphate standard curve [11]. Accumulated polyphosphate is taken as the phosphorus measured at each time point normalised to OD600.
The expected outcome was **greater intracellular phosphorus accumulation in the engineered strains than in the wild type**.

genetic engineering::remove the native p: In one sentence: we make the cell **import more phosphate, lock it away as polyP, and stop losing it**.

*Schematic of P. putida KT2440 redesigned as a PAO. In **green**, the functions we **add** (PPK1 and PstSCAB); in **red**, the ones we **inactivate** (Ppx, PpkB/PPK2 and PitB). The arrows follow the phosphate: it enters through **PstSCAB**, is fixed as polyP by **PPK1**, and both the exits (**PitB**) and the degradation/consumption of polyP (**Ppx**, **PpkB**) are blocked.*

**What it does:** the enzyme that **builds polyphosphate**. It takes the terminal (γ) phosphate from ATP and adds it, residue by residue, to a growing polyP chain. It is the engine of polyP synthesis in PAOs.

**What we do to it and why:** we **express it heterologously** (cloned into a pSEVA vector), using the *Ca.* Accumulibacter version. We add extra synthesis capacity so that all the incoming phosphate is turned into stored polyP, the heart of accumulation.
**GIF (storyboard):** ATP molecules coming in; the phosphate is clipped off ATP (ATP → ADP) and attached to the end of a polyP chain that grows into a granule.

**What it does:** a high-affinity **phosphate import pump**. PstS captures phosphate in the periplasm; PstC and PstA form the membrane channel; PstB is the ATPase supplying the energy. It brings phosphate into the cell **even when very little is left outside**.

**What we do to it and why:** we **express it heterologously** (from *Ca.* Accumulibacter) to maximise phosphate uptake and feed polyP synthesis. Its high affinity is key to "polishing" the water down to low residual concentrations.
**GIF (storyboard):** phosphate ions from the medium captured at the membrane/periplasm and pumped through the channel into the cell, with ATP → ADP powering the pump.

**What it does:** the enzyme that **degrades polyphosphate**. It hydrolyses phosphates from the end of the polyP chain and releases them as inorganic phosphate (Pi). It is the main activity that "undoes" what has been accumulated.

**What we do to it and why:** we **inactivate it with CRISPR** (base editing) so the cell cannot dismantle its polyP reserves. This locks in the accumulated phosphorus and avoids a futile synthesis/degradation cycle.
**GIF (storyboard):** a polyP chain being nibbled from the end, phosphates dropping off one by one → with a large red **X / strike-through** showing we remove this activity.

**What it does:** a **type-2 polyphosphate kinase**: it uses polyP as a phosphate donor to phosphorylate nucleotides (e.g. ADP → ATP, GDP → GTP), **consuming** the polyP chain. In other words, it spends polyP to regenerate nucleotides.
**What we do to it and why:** we **inactivate it with CRISPR** so polyP is not consumed by this route. We reduce polyP turnover and favour net accumulation.
**GIF (storyboard):** polyP donating a phosphate to an ADP that becomes ATP while the chain shortens → struck through with a red **X**.

**What it does:** a **low-affinity phosphate transporter** (Pit-type), a metal-phosphate/H⁺ symporter. Pit systems are bidirectional and are implicated in the **efflux/release** of phosphate from PAOs.
**What we do to it and why:** we **inactivate it with CRISPR** to reduce phosphate leakage to the outside, so the imported and stored phosphate stays inside and is not lost back to the medium.
**GIF (storyboard):** phosphate escaping from the cell through a channel → struck through with a red **X** to show we block the leak.

This set of experiments establishes, in **wild-type P. putida KT2440** [1], how much phosphorus the **cells take up and store as polyphosphate, how fast, and under which operating condition**s this is maximised. Because the engineered strains will later be judged by exactly this read-out, the experiments first build and standardise a reproducible intracellular-phosphorus assay, then use it to **characterise growth, the kinetics of accumulation across media, and the two operating variables available in the real feed**. Two variants were used: t**he wild type (WT) and an mCherry-tagged variant (Cherry)** for growth tracking. The application target is a synthetic aqueous stream mimicking the phosphorus-rich effluent of biofuel production, the context in which polyphosphate-based phosphorus recovery would operate [2], [3].

Before following accumulation over time, the growth trajectory of the cells in the minimal medium used as the maximal-stress reference (**M9**) had to be known, so that phosphorus values could be read against a defined biomass curve. The mCherry variant, which is easy to track, was cultured in M9 and OD600 was followed across the 240 min assay window.
The expected outcome was a defined OD600 trajectory over the assay window, confirming the cells remain measurable throughout.

With the assay standardised, the kinetics of intracellular polyphosphate were compared across three media that differ in nutrient availability. Cells grown in LB were shifted into each medium and sampled over 0 to 240 min; at each time point one aliquot gave OD600 and a paired aliquot was processed through the assay. The comparison rests on the hypothesis that polyphosphate accumulation is a **nutrient-stress response** [2], so retention should scale inversely with nutrient availability.

The **synthetic stream** was prepared to mimic a biofuel-derived industrial feed: citric acid, glycerol, soy lecithin, monopotassium phosphate (the phosphate source), ammonium sulfate, sodium chloride, filtered used vegetable oil and Tween 80, with the pH adjusted as required.
The expected outcome was a monotonic trend, with the highest normalised polyphosphate in M9, the lowest in LB and an intermediate value in the synthetic stream.

Having established the medium trend, the two variables that the industrial partner (**BioOils Huelva**) actually allows to be adjusted, **pH** and **degree of dilution**, were screened combinatorially in the synthetic stream, with dilution standing in for nutrient limitation, since a more dilute feed is a more nutrient-limited one. Four conditions crossed two pH values with two dilutions, with M9 and LB retained as controls, each followed over the assay time course.
The expected outcome was to identify the pH and dilution combination that maximises phosphorus retention in the application-relevant medium.
These steps take the two genes from design to a functionally validated, phosphate-accumulating strain, with each verification stage gating the next.

The goal of this set of experiments is a *P. putida* strain that stably expresses **ppk1** and **pstSCAB** from *Candidatus* Accumulibacter phosphatis. Because *P. putida* is far less amenable to routine cloning than *Escherichia coli* [1], [2], each plasmid is built and verified in an *E. coli* cloning host and only then moved into the final chassis. This keeps the iterative cloning steps in the fastest, most transformable host and reserves the slower work with *P. putida* for constructs we already trust.

The first step was to design, in silico, the two expression cassettes: a promoter, a ribosome binding site (RBS), the coding sequence and the cloning sites needed to assemble each cassette into its pSEVA backbone by restriction and ligation.

Two design decisions carry most of the weight. First, the *ppk1* and *pstSCAB* coding sequences were **codon-optimised for *P. putida* KT2440**, because *Ca.* Accumulibacter has a different codon usage and its native sequences would be read inefficiently, with rare codons risking ribosome stalling and truncated product. Second, rather than modelling a bespoke RBS, we used the **canonical RBS for *P. putida*** (a strong, well-characterised Shine-Dalgarno of the form AGGAGG), which gives reliable, predictable initiation in this host without the risk of an untested sequence. The restriction sites were chosen to match the chosen backbones: **BamHI and HindIII** for the cassettes going into **pSEVA2513**, and **EcoRI and KpnI** for the promoter fragment going into **pSEVA6313**. Design and map management were done in **SnapGene**. See our parts collection to check DNA sequences.
The expected outcome was two fully annotated cassettes, compatible with the restriction and ligation strategy and ready to order or amplify.

The parts were obtained in the form best suited to each. The coding sequences were ordered as **synthetic genes delivered pre-cloned in carrier vectors**: **ppk1 in pMK-RQ** and **pstSCAB in pOK-RQ**, both kanamycin-resistant. Ordering genes pre-cloned gives a stable, sequence-verified stock that can be propagated and drawn on as needed. The promoter was supplied in the small synthetic promotor **pEM7**.

The promoter needed special handling because it is very short (about **77 bp**). Released by EcoRI and KpnI digestion, a fragment this small runs off the front of the gel and cannot be recovered cleanly, so it cannot simply be cut out and purified. The working solution was to move the promoter and RBS off the gel entirely and **build them into the genes through PCR primers**: the coding sequences were amplified with primers that carry the RBS and the required restriction sites as overhangs, so the cassette is completed during amplification rather than by purifying a tiny promoter band.

The amplification used **Pfu polymerase** (the enzyme available in the lab; slower than Phusion but high-fidelity, which matters because any error introduced while amplifying a coding sequence would be carried into the final construct). A high-fidelity enzyme keeps that error rate negligible. Products were checked on an agarose gel and quantified by NanoDrop before use.
The expected outcome was a sequence-verified stock of each gene in its carrier vector and clean, correctly sized amplicons carrying the RBS and cloning sites.

The backbones and inserts were then cut to matching ends. **pSEVA2513** (kanamycin-resistant, about **5.3 kb**) was digested with **BamHI and HindIII**, together with the *ppk1* and *pstSCAB* cassettes; **pSEVA631** (gentamicin-resistant, about **3.0 kb**) was digested with **EcoRI and KpnI** for the promoter route. These vector choices matter because *P. putida* does not maintain the ColE1 or pUC origins of standard *E. coli* vectors and requires **broad-host-range replicons**; the SEVA collection supplies exactly these, with compatible resistance and origin modules [3], [4]. All of the restriction enzymes used were casual Thermo Fisher ones.

Enzymes were used at **37 °C** variable time and buffer. The vector was **not dephosphorylated**; instead, background from re-ligation was controlled by running a vector-only ligation control in the next step and by clean preparative gel excision. For *ppk1*, whose backbone fragment co-migrates with the insert on a 1% gel, an **additional NcoI digestion** was used to separate the bands so the correct fragment could be excised. Digestions were resolved on **1% agarose** in TAE, stained with Diamond dye, and the bands of interest were excised and purified with the **Wizard SV Gel and PCR Clean-Up System** (Promega), eluting in water or the kit buffer.

To ensure the insert's identity, the restriction enzyme XhoI was used during the second attempt for ppk1. This enzyme has two internal restriction sites, which do not cut the empty vector but ensure the release of two fragments of 1126 and 6312 bp in the correct ligation product.
The expected outcome was cleanly cut, gel-purified vector and insert with compatible ends.

The cassettes were joined to their backbones by **T4 DNA ligation**. Reactions used a **vector-to-insert molar ratio of about 1:5**, T4 buffer and T4 DNA ligase, incubated **overnight at 16 °C**, the standard low-temperature condition that favours intermolecular joining of sticky ends. A **vector-only control** was always run alongside: a control plate with only a few tiny colonies, as obtained here, indicates that the vector is not re-ligating on itself and that colonies on the sample plate are likely to carry insert.
The expected outcome was a ligation mixture ready to transform, with the control showing minimal background.

The ligation was introduced into chemically competent **E. coli DH5α**. The correct term is **transformation**, the uptake of naked plasmid DNA by an artificially competent bacterial cell; we avoid "transfer", which is nonspecific, and "transfection", which refers to eukaryotic cells. DH5α is used rather than the final chassis because its genotype protects the construct (*endA1* removes an endonuclease and gives cleaner minipreps, *recA1* reduces recombination and keeps inserts stable) and because it transforms far more efficiently than *P. putida*.

Cells were heat-shocked, then **recovered in non-selective rich medium** before plating, so that the resistance protein is expressed before selection; plating straight onto antibiotic would kill genuine transformants. Cells were then plated on **LB agar with kanamycin** or gentamycin depending on the antibiotic resistance gene from the backbone.
The expected outcome was colonies on the selective plates and few or none on the control.

Candidate colonies were triaged by **colony PCR** and by **diagnostic restriction digestion** (for example, a PauI or BamHI and HindIII digest whose band pattern distinguishes a correct construct from an empty or mis-assembled one). Colony PCR is run first because it is fast and cheap and can screen many colonies directly. Positives were grown and their plasmid isolated by **miniprep**, either with the **PureYield Plasmid Miniprep System** (Promega) or by kit-free alkaline lysis; miniprep is chosen over midi or maxi preparations because only enough DNA for a digest and for sequencing is needed at this stage. Products were checked on agarose and quantified by NanoDrop.
The expected outcome was several independent clones per construct with the correct pattern.

Clones that passed screening were confirmed by sequencing, because screening shows an insert of the right size and orientation but only sequencing rules out point mutations, indels or assembly scars that could inactivate the protein or shift the reading frame. Sanger sequencing of the cassette and its junctions, or whole-plasmid sequencing, was used, and only a clone matching the in-silico design exactly was carried forward.
The expected outcome was a **sequence-verified expression plasmid** for each gene.

The verified plasmids were moved into the final chassis by **electroporation of electrocompetent *P. putida* KT2440**, prepared by the standard rapid sucrose-wash method (repeated washes in 300 mM sucrose to remove salts) [5]. Electroporation is used because *P. putida* is not naturally competent and takes up DNA far less readily than *E. coli*, so more input DNA is generally needed than for a routine *E. coli* transformation [2], [5]. The pSEVA vectors are broad-host-range and are stably maintained in *Pseudomonas*. Transformants were selected on **LB with kanamycin**.
The expected outcome was resistant *P. putida* colonies carrying the expression plasmid.
These steps take the two genes from design to a functionally validated, phosphate-accumulating strain, with each verification stage gating the next.

The goal of this set of experiments is to remove, in the same strain, three native activities that oppose accumulation: **ppx** (degrades polyphosphate), **ppkB** / **ppk2** (consumes polyphosphate to phosphorylate nucleotides) and **pitB** (low-affinity phosphate transport implicated in efflux). They are inactivated by **CRISPR base editing** [6], [7], [8] rather than by conventional Cas9 cutting, because a double-strand break in *P. putida* is problematic: the organism has limited non-homologous end joining, so cuts are repaired poorly and are often lethal, and scarless deletion would otherwise require a homology-directed repair template. A cytidine base editor sidesteps this, introducing a premature stop codon by chemistry alone, an approach already validated for gene inactivation in *P. putida* KT2440 [8].

We use the **pMBEC2** base editor [9], which fuses a cytidine deaminase, a Cas9 nickase and a uracil glycosylase inhibitor, and carries a constitutively expressed **msfGFP** cassette flanked by **BsaI** sites in place of the guide. The guide RNA is installed by **Golden Gate assembly** [9], [10], replacing the msfGFP marker, so that correct constructs can be picked by **loss of green fluorescence**.

The block opens with guide design because base editing only works within a narrow window. A cytidine base editor deaminates cytosine to uracil (read as thymine) within roughly positions 4 to 8 of the protospacer, converting a C·G pair to T·A [6]. To create a **premature stop codon** we look for a **CAA, CAG or CGA** codon, which a single C to T edit turns into **TAA, TAG or TGA** [8], placed so that the editable C falls inside the window and a suitable NGG PAM lies the correct distance away. The edit was placed **early in each gene** so the truncated protein is certainly non-functional, and candidate guides were screened for **off-targets** against the KT2440 genome, with two or three guides designed per gene. This was achieved by using the *CRISPR for Pseudomonas excel*  tool.
The expected outcome was a prioritised set of guides for *ppx*, *ppkB* and *pitB*.

The guide fragments were generated by **PCR from the template vector pEX128**, using oligonucleotides that carry the specific spacer for each target together with the Golden Gate (BsaI) flanking motifs [7] , so the guide is assembled directly around the desired spacer. Amplification used **Pfu polymerase**. Because the amplicon is small (about **130 to 150 bp** for *ppx*, *ppkB* and *pitB*), the cycling was tuned for a short product: a short extension (about 20 to 30 s) and a short denaturation, with an annealing temperature of **60 °C** following the source protocol and a **gradient (60 to 68 °C)** tested when a larger, non-specific band appeared. A no-oligo negative control was run to confirm that the band depends on the primers. Products were checked on **1.5% agarose**, then purified with the **Wizard SV Gel and PCR Clean-Up System** (Promega).
The expected outcome was clean bands of about 130 to 150 bp for the three targets, with a blank negative control.

Each guide fragment was assembled into **pMBEC2** by **Golden Gate (BsaI)** [9], [10], replacing the msfGFP marker with the guide. Golden Gate is used here, rather than the restriction and ligation of Block A, because the pMBEC design is built for it: BsaI cuts outside its recognition site, so digestion and ligation can run in one pot and the marker is swapped for the guide seamlessly. This is also what enables the fluorescence-based screen in the next step.
The expected outcome was an assembly mixture ready to transform.

The assembly was transformed into **E. coli DH5α** and plated. Because a correct construct has lost the msfGFP marker, colonies were screened by fluorescence: **non-fluorescent (white) colonies carry the guide**, whereas green colonies still hold the template. Selected white colonies were grown, miniprepped and verified. When the Golden Gate efficiency is low, the assembly is repeated using the protocol cycling as written.
The expected outcome was verified editor-plus-guide plasmids (**pMBEC2**, guide against *ppx*, *ppkB* or *pitB*).

The verified editing plasmids were introduced into **P. putida KT2440 by electroporation** [5], as in Block A, step 8, and selected on the vector's antibiotic. Delivery is kept separate from editing so that a clean, selected population carrying the system is established first.
The expected outcome was *P. putida* transformants carrying the editing system.

Cells were diluted and plated to obtain **single colonies**, because a freshly induced culture is a mixture of edited and unedited cells and only clonal colonies allow an individual genotype to be read out.
The expected outcome was individual candidate colonies.

Each candidate was genotyped by **colony PCR and Sanger sequencing** of the target region, reading the **C to T conversion** and confirming the stop codon using SnapGene. Sequencing is the only reliable read-out, since the edit is a single base change that produces no size difference.
The expected outcome was colonies carrying the edit that creates the stop codon.

The editor plasmid was then **cured**, which stops further editing, yields a stable strain and, importantly, **frees the antibiotic marker** for the next round [9]. This was achieved by sucrose 5% w/v passes. The introduce, edit, screen and cure cycle was repeated for the second and third genes, each round starting from the strain of the previous one, so the three knock-outs accumulate in a single lineage. Editing was done **sequentially rather than as a single multiplex**, so each edit is verified before the next, although the pMBEC toolset also supports multiplexing [9].
The expected outcome was a **triple mutant**, *ppx⁻ ppkB⁻ pitB⁻*.

Before phenotyping, the three target regions were amplified and sequenced to confirm all three stop codons. **Whole-genome sequencing** to check for off-targets or rearrangements accumulated over three rounds was not considered because off-target cuts were bioinformatically optimized and whole-genome sequencing costs. This ensures the later phenotype can be attributed to the intended knock-outs.
The expected outcome was confirmation of the three knock-outs with no significant unwanted edits.

The steps are the minimum needed to install and prove three clean, markerless knock-outs in one strain: per-round sequencing is required by the chemistry of base editing, and curing is what makes three sequential rounds possible with a limited set of markers.

Taken together, the two blocks are both **necessary and sufficient** for the block objective, and they were shaped by the constraints of the project rather than added for completeness. Neither module alone produces a phosphorus-accumulating strain: adding uptake and storage capacity (Block A) is wasted if the cell still degrades and leaks what it stores, and removing the native loss routes (Block B) achieves little without the added capacity to import phosphate and fix it as polyphosphate. The verification-heavy design of both blocks, screening before sequencing and sequencing before phenotyping, reflects a deliberate choice to fail fast and cheaply in *E. coli* and to trust *P. putida* results only once the genotype is certain.

The two modules converge in a final **integration** step. The verified expression plasmids from Block A (*ppk1* and *pstSCAB*) are introduced into *P. putida* KT2440, individually and together, by electroporation, giving the strains that carry the added machinery; in parallel, the base-edited knock-out background from Block B removes the native loss routes. The complete strain is then assessed with the **intracellular phosphorus capture assay**, this time as an end-to-end validation of the full rePhlow phenotype rather than of a single module. Measuring capture inside the cell, rather than depletion from the medium, is what makes this a direct test of phosphorus accumulation.

The assay follows a **phosphate-overplus** logic. Wild type and engineered strains are grown in LB to OD600 of about 0.6 and then **starved of phosphate for 1 h** in a phosphate-free minimal medium, which empties the internal polyphosphate and derepresses the phosphate-uptake machinery, so that avid uptake is triggered when phosphate is restored. The cells are then shifted into the **test medium at pH 5** at OD600 = 1.0, which is t = 0. Over a 0 to 120 min time course (sampled at 0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90, 105 and 120 min) one aliquot is read for OD600 (at a 1/10 dilution) while a paired aliquot is pelleted and **washed three times in 0.1 M NaCl** to remove the phosphate-rich medium, which would otherwise swamp the signal. The phosphorus stored inside the cells is released by acid digestion (150 µL of 1 M HCl, 95 °C, 15 min), the lysate is neutralised (150 µL of supernatant plus 150 µL of 1 M NaOH, to about pH 7) and pre-diluted tenfold, and the free phosphate is quantified with the **Promega Non-Radioactive Phosphatase Assay System** (Serine/Threonine Phosphatase Assay System, cat. V2460), which measures phosphate as a **molybdate:malachite green complex** by absorbance in cuvette against a 0 to 1900 ng phosphate standard curve [11]. Accumulated polyphosphate is taken as the phosphorus measured at each time point normalised to OD600.
The expected outcome was **greater intracellular phosphorus accumulation in the engineered strains than in the wild type**.
