revalorisation::dialysis of imac eluates: The goal of this stage was to remove the imidazole and excess salt carried over from the IMAC eluate and to transfer each enzyme into a simple buffer compatible with its next use. This step is essential for our workflow. DHAK depends on **Mg-ATP** for its activity, and high concentrations of imidazole and salt interfere with its assay. PPK2 is used in a coupled assay with DHAK, so any imidazole left in its eluate would end up in the same reaction [2].

Dialysis was chosen because it is gentle, inexpensive and well suited to the millilitre volumes produced by our IMAC. The eluate is sealed in a semi-permeable membrane that retains the protein, while small molecules such as imidazole and NaCl diffuse out into a much larger volume of buffer until both sides reach equilibrium. It was carried out **overnight at 4 °C**, a temperature that protects the enzymes during the long exchange. Two practical points.

The **sample volume increases during dialysis**, because water enters the bag when the eluate, rich in imidazole, has a higher solute concentration than the buffer, so free space must be left in the bag to keep it from bursting. And a single bath may not remove all the imidazole, so **the buffer is changed at least once**, which removes far more than a single bath of the same total volume.
revalorisation::choice of dialysis buffe: The dialysis buffer only needs to keep the pH stable, so its exact concentration is not critical. We used a **low-concentration sodium phosphate buffer (5 mM)** by default. This keeps the option of **freeze-drying** the enzyme for later use: freeze-drying removes the water but concentrates every salt left in the sample, so the lower the salt content beforehand, the better the enzyme is preserved. Slightly more concentrated phosphate buffers are equally suitable when the sample goes directly to the activity assays.
revalorisation::concentrating the dialys: Where the preparation came out too dilute to assay, it was concentrated after dialysis by **centrifugal ultrafiltration**, following the protocol supplied by the manufacturer. In each case the molecular weight cut-off was chosen well below the molecular weight of the enzyme, so that the protein is retained above the membrane while water and small molecules pass through. **This was not applied to every preparation**, and when it was added later to an affinity eluate of the active enzyme it made a difference worth recording, as reported in Results. The reason for concentrating differed between the two enzymes.

**DHAK.** In one purification the elution volume exceeded the volume of CFE loaded, so the eluate came out diluted, and dialysis diluted it further as water entered the bag. The dialysed sample was therefore concentrated in a device with a **30 kDa** cut-off, well below the roughly 60 kDa of the subunit, and with a capacity suited to the volumes produced by the column [11].

**PPK2.** Here the eluate was not unusually dilute; it was concentrated because we had little material and wanted to use as little of it as possible in each assay. Working with a concentrated sample means a smaller volume per reaction, so the same preparation lasts for more measurements. Since the volumes involved were much smaller, a small-format device was used with a **10 kDa** cut-off, chosen because PPK2 is a much smaller protein, at about 33 kDa, and a 30 kDa membrane would risk letting it through [12].
revalorisation::express immobilised meta: The goal of this stage was to find out, quickly and with very little material, whether the IMAC purification itself was working for DHAK. In earlier purifications the enzyme had lost activity, and we did not know where the problem lay: in expression, in binding to and recovery from the resin, or in the activity of the enzyme itself. Running the full column protocol again each time we changed a condition would have cost a lot of sample and time without isolating the cause. This small-scale test was therefore designed as a **diagnostic step**. It checks one link of the chain at a time, whether DHAK is present in the extract and whether it binds the Co²⁺-IDA resin and can be recovered from it, so that we could start ruling out possible causes and focus on the real one.
revalorisation::size exclusion chromatog: The goal of this stage was to purify DHAK from the cell-free extract by a route independent of metal affinity. Size-exclusion chromatography was adopted as an **alternative purification method for DHAK**, used instead of IMAC followed by dialysis rather than after it. The reasons for this change are described in Engineering (Iteration 6).

**Size-exclusion chromatography (SEC)**, also called gel filtration, separates proteins by size rather than by affinity. Large aggregates elute first, DHAK elutes at its characteristic volume, and smaller proteins, nucleotides and other small molecules from the extract elute last. For DHAK this approach has two advantages:

- The enzyme is never exposed to metal ions or imidazole.
- It elutes directly in the running buffer, so no dialysis is needed before the activity assays.

The runs were performed on an **ÄKTAprime plus FPLC system** with a preparative **HiLoad 26/60 Superdex 200 pg** column. Unlike the gravity-flow steps, FPLC pumps the buffer at a controlled flow rate and pressure and records the **UV absorbance at 280 nm** in real time. The DHAK peak can be followed as it leaves the column, so the fractions to keep are chosen from the chromatogram rather than blindly. On this column the **void volume is about 110 mL** and the **total volume about 320 mL**, which places the window where DHAK is expected at approximately **220 to 270 mL**.
revalorisation::enzyme activity assay: The final block answers the question the whole module exists for: does the system work. DHAP has no useful absorbance of its own, so both assays measure it through the same **coupled reporter reaction**, in which α-glycerophosphate dehydrogenase reduces the DHAP formed while oxidising NADH, followed as a fall in absorbance at 340 nm and converted into an absolute amount of product through the NADH extinction coefficient. The first assay characterises **DHAK on its own**, in continuous format, giving a quantitative activity that can be compared across variants and across purification stages. The second combines **both enzymes** in a single long reaction with polyphosphate and a substoichiometric amount of adenine nucleotide, sampled over the course of the reaction and measured in endpoint format, to test whether ATP is genuinely being recycled rather than consumed.
revalorisation::dhak activity coupled gd: The goal of this stage was a quantitative measure of DHAK activity, so that the purified enzyme could be characterised and the different variants and preparations compared on the same scale.
revalorisation::why the activity is meas: DHAK phosphorylates dihydroxyacetone (DHA) to DHAP using ATP, but **DHAP has no useful absorbance of its own**, so it cannot be followed directly. It is therefore measured through a coupled reporter reaction. **α-glycerophosphate dehydrogenase (α-GDH)** reduces the DHAP formed to glycerol-3-phosphate while oxidising NADH to NAD⁺, and **triosephosphate isomerase (TIM)** is included in the coupling mix. NADH absorbs at 340 nm and NAD⁺ does not, so the fall in absorbance at 340 nm tracks DHAP formation in real time, and its initial rate is proportional to DHAK activity (Figure 4) [2, 5].

Applying the NADH extinction coefficient (**ε₃₄₀ = 6220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹**) converts that rate into an absolute amount of DHAP. This is what makes the measurement an absolute one rather than a relative signal, so it stays comparable between instruments, between runs and between laboratories, which matters because the same assay is used to compare enzyme variants. The assay was run mostly in **1 cm cuvettes** and occasionally in **microplate** when that was more convenient, with the path length of the format used applied in the conversion. See the R**esults.**
revalorisation::coupled dhak ppk2 assay: The goal of this stage was the proof of concept of the whole system: showing that the two enzymes work together and that ATP can be **recycled** instead of consumed stoichiometrically.
revalorisation::why regeneration matters: As DHAK phosphorylates DHA to DHAP, it consumes ATP and generates ADP. **PPK2 uses polyphosphate as a phosphate donor** to convert that ADP back to ATP, returning it to DHAK to drive another round of phosphorylation. The reaction therefore runs on a small pool of adenine nucleotide that is recycled many times rather than spent once.

This changes what limits the reaction. With regeneration, the total DHAP formed is set by the DHA and the polyphosphate supplied, not by the amount of ATP added, so far more DHAP can accumulate than the initial ATP could ever yield on its own. Clearing ADP as it forms also removes a second limitation, since ADP inhibits DHAK. This matters well beyond the bench: ATP is far too expensive to be added stoichiometrically in a real revalorisation process, whereas polyphosphate is cheap, which is what makes the system viable at scale.
revalorisation::pross cycle 1: The goal of this stage was a DHAK variant with improved **thermodynamic stability** that keeps its catalytic function intact, so that the enzyme tolerates the handling, storage and reaction conditions of a revalorisation process better than the wild type. Stabilisation was pursued computationally before any bench work, because designing and ordering a stabilised gene is far cheaper than screening mutants experimentally. **PPK2 was expressed as its native sequence** and did not go through this stage.

The design started from the crystal structure of DHAK from ***C. freundii* DSM 30040** in complex with its ligands, **PDB entry 1UN9**. The complexed structure was used on purpose, because it lets the algorithm recognise where the functional residues sit and avoid mutating them.

DHAK is a homodimer built from two domains: the **K-domain**, which carries the dihydroxyacetone site, and the **L-domain**, which carries the ATP site. In the dimer, the K-domain of one subunit faces the L-domain of the other, forming two composite active sites. Three ligands mark the regions that must not be altered: the ATP analogue (**AMP-PNP**), **dihydroxyacetone (DHA)** and the **Mg²⁺ ion**. Residues within roughly **4 Å** of any ligand were flagged as protected, so that stabilising mutations are excluded from the catalytic and cofactor-binding shells.

The **PROSS** server takes the sequence and the PDB structure and returns a small set of stabilised designs, combining phylogenetic sequence information with Rosetta energy calculations to lower the free energy of the fold while conserving function [4]. The designs are numbered from the **most conservative to the most aggressive**, so they form a gradient: the higher the number, the more mutations and, in principle, the greater the predicted stabilisation, but also the greater the **risk of disturbing the enzyme**. The protected ligands were declared explicitly, so that the server **keeps the active site untouched** while it stabilises the rest of the protein.

One design from that gradient was to be taken forward, ordered as a synthetic gene and expressed in parallel with the wild-type sequence under identical conditions. The **wild type is the control** of this experiment, because the two differ only in the introduced mutations, any difference in expression, stability or activity between them is attributable to the design itself. Which position of the gradient to choose is the real decision of this stage, since it sets how much stabilisation is pursued and how much risk to catalytic function is accepted. **The design selected, and the reasoning behind that choice, are reported in** **Results.**
revalorisation::pross cycle 2: The goal of this stage was a second, **more conservative** stabilisation design, and a way of transferring it to the DHAK variant of *C. freundii* strain **CECT 4626**. Two findings from the first design made this necessary, and both are developed in Engineering (Iterations 1 and 4): the aggressive design **did not yield a usable enzyme**, which we attribute to the large number of mutations it carries, and the team moved to the **CECT 4626 enzyme**, reported as the **most catalytically efficient DHAK** described to date [2, 5].

The design question therefore changed. Instead of asking how far the fold can be stabilised, we asked **how few mutations are needed**, and whether the natural sequence of the new strain already contains part of what the algorithm had proposed.

The starting point was the same as in the first stage: the same DHAK sequence of *C. freundii* DSM 30040, the same structure (**PDB 1UN9**) and the same protected ligands, since the regions that must not be mutated do not change. What changed is which design from the returned gradient was taken forward: this time the **most conservative one, PROSS 1** [4], which introduces the **smallest number of mutations** and therefore carries the **lowest risk to catalytic function.**

A PROSS design is tied to the sequence it was generated from, so it cannot be applied directly to a homologous enzyme from another strain, even one sharing about 96% identity. An **additional comparison step** was therefore introduced: the PROSS 1 design was aligned, position by position, with the natural sequence of DHAK CECT 4626, and three categories of position were distinguished:

- **Positions that differ naturally between the two strains.** The two DHAKs share about 96% amino-acid identity, so these mark where the new enzyme already departs from the reference.
- **Positions where the natural CECT 4626 residue is the one PROSS proposed.** These are changes the algorithm predicted as stabilising and that evolution had already fixed in the other strain, which is the strongest argument for keeping them, and they need no mutation at all in the new background.
- **Positions where PROSS proposes a residue present in neither natural sequence.** These are the genuinely new mutations, and the ones that carry the real risk.

This classification is the core of the experiment, because it sets the criterion for deciding what is actually transferred. It lets the mutations be ranked by evidence rather than by predicted energy alone, so that only the changes that are both predicted to stabilise and absent from the new sequence are introduced into it, and it is what kept us from introducing mutations the new enzyme already carried naturally. Which positions fell into each category, and which mutations were finally selected, are reported in **Results**.

From this analysis a **new plasmid was designed**, carrying the selected mutations on the CECT 4626 background, and ordered as a synthetic gene. As in the first design, the **unmodified CECT 4626 sequence is the control**, so that expression, stability and activity can be compared between the natural enzyme and its stabilised version under identical conditions. Comparing the two stabilisation designs, the aggressive one and this conservative one, would also test directly whether the earlier loss of activity was caused by the number of mutations. **That comparison is set up and awaits the activity measurement**, which the arrival date of the gene left no time for, as reported in Results.
revalorisation::channelling: The goal of this stage was to design a way of physically joining DHAK and PPK2 into a **single biocatalytic complex**. In our system PPK2 regenerates the ATP that DHAK consumes, so the two enzymes depend on each other. Keeping them covalently close should favour **substrate channelling**: the ATP produced by PPK2 reaches the DHAK active site before diffusing into the bulk solution, which raises the effective local concentration of the cofactor and should make the coupled reaction more efficient than the same two enzymes free in solution.

The **SpyTag/SpyCatcher** system was chosen because it joins two proteins through a spontaneous, irreversible isopeptide bond that forms simply on mixing, with no enzyme, cofactor or chemical crosslinker. One partner carries the short **SpyTag** peptide and the other the larger **SpyCatcher** domain, so the complex assembles by itself when both purified enzymes are combined [6].

Our working hypothesis was to assign the parts by size: the **SpyTag**, the smaller element, fused to **DHAK**, which is already a large homodimer, and the **SpyCatcher**, the bulkier domain, fused to **PPK2**, which is the smaller protein. The reasoning is that adding the larger element to the larger protein increases the risk of interfering with folding, with dimerisation or with access to the composite active sites that form at the subunit interface.

Which terminus carries each element is a second decision, independent of the first, and it cannot be made from the sequence alone. The fusion has to sit away from the catalytic regions, but it also has to leave the two active sites of the assembled complex facing each other, since that geometry is what channelling depends on. Both ends of each enzyme are in principle available, so the placement has to be examined structurally, by looking at where the tag and the catcher end up relative to the active sites, before committing to a construct. The **hexahistidine tag of the expression vector sits at the C-terminus**, which constrains the available positions and has to be accounted for in any construct placing a fusion element at that end.

The size criterion is a reasonable starting hypothesis, but it is only a hypothesis. A fusion can impair an enzyme for reasons that size alone does not predict, and the geometry of the resulting complex, which determines how close the two active sites end up, depends both on which partner carries which element and on which terminus it is attached to.
The experimental design therefore has two levels. First, the two possible **assignments of the elements**:

- **SpyTag–DHAK** with **SpyCatcher–PPK2** (the arrangement designed here).
- S**pyCatcher–DHAK** with **SpyTag–PPK2** (the reciprocal arrangement, not designed yet).

Second, within each assignment, the **position of the fusion** on each enzyme. Because we cannot predict how much the attachment point affects folding, activity or the geometry of the complex, as many combinations as possible should be built and compared, placing each element at the N- or the C-terminus of its enzyme. Comparing them is the only way to tell whether the position is what limits the system and to arrive at the most favourable configuration.

Each fusion would first be checked on its own, for expression, solubility and retained activity against the corresponding unfused enzyme as a control. Only the fusions that keep their activity would then be combined, and the assembled complex compared with the **free enzyme mixture** in the coupled assay, which is the control that tells whether joining the enzymes actually helps. This is what would show which combination, if any, produces a functional channelled complex.

**This stage remained at the level of experimental design.** Only one assignment of the elements was designed, and only for part of the possible placements; the reciprocal arrangement was left as a planned comparison and has not been designed. None of the constructs was taken to the bench within the time available, so no fusion was expressed or assayed. We document the reasoning, what was designed and the comparisons that still have to be made so that a future team can take them up. **The models produced are in Results.**

With the sequences in hand, the goal of this block was simply to obtain both enzymes in soluble form, in the smallest number of steps compatible with sequence certainty. The genes were ordered **already cloned into an expression vector** rather than assembled in-house, and the usual intermediate of verifying the plasmid in a cloning strain was deliberately skipped, since the block was focused on producing and characterising the protein rather than on building the plasmid. Both enzymes then followed the same route: transformation into *E. coli* BL21(DE3), selection and growth to exponential phase, induction with IPTG under the T7 system at a lowered temperature to favour soluble folding, and finally harvest and **enzymatic lysis** to recover a clarified cell-free extract. That extract is the input for everything that follows.
revalorisation::transformation: The goal of this stage was a strain of the **expression** host carrying the **gene of interest** on an inducible plasmid. Rather than assembling the construct by restriction and ligation, the coding sequence was ordered as a **synthetic gene already cloned into an expression vector** and introduced directly into the expression host. This trades in-house cloning flexibility for speed and sequence certainty, which suited a block focused on producing and characterising the protein rather than on building the plasmid.

For the DHAK, **two natural sequence variants** of *C. freundii* DHAK were used, and they must be told apart. The gene we ordered was the sequence of the **crystallised enzyme deposited as PDB 1UN9**, which corresponds to the previously described reference variant of *C. freundii* DHAK (**strain DSM 30040**; UniProt P45510, GenBank U09771). It was synthesised, **codon-optimised for E. coli** and cloned into the pET-28a(+) vector, and we call it **DHAK DSM 30040**. The second enzyme, **DHAK (CECT 4626),** is the variant characterised by Sánchez-Moreno [2], isolated by PCR from the genomic DNA of C. freundii strain CECT 4626 and deposited as GenBank DQ473522. The two variants share about 96% amino-acid identity (92.9% at the nucleotide level), differ at 22 residues, and the CECT 4626 variant was reported as the most catalytically efficient DHAK described to date.

The gene was supplied, **codon-optimised for *E. coli**, *in a pET-28a(+) (Figure 3) expression vector and expressed in* **E. coli *BL21(DE3)** (Thermo Scientific, cat. EC0114). The pET-28a(+) backbone was appropriate for three reasons that matter downstream. It places the gene under a **T7 promoter**, giving strong, tightly controlled expression in a DE3 host. It confers **kanamycin resistance**, the selection marker used throughout this block. And it fuses a **C-terminal hexahistidine tag** to the protein, which enables the later immobilised-metal affinity purification without further engineering. BL21(DE3) was chosen because it is **protease-deficient** and carries the **T7 RNA polymerase gene under lacUV5 control**, so the plasmid's T7 promoter is only transcribed once the polymerase is induced.

Because the construct was ready for expression, the usual intermediate of amplifying and verifying the plasmid in a cloning strain such as DH5α was **deliberately skipped** to save time. The synthetic gene was diluted to about **50 ng/µL** in nuclease-free water and transformed into chemically competent BL21(DE3) by **heat shock** [7], following the strain manufacturer's protocol. The term used here is **transformation**, the uptake of naked plasmid DNA by an artificially competent bacterial cell.

**The DHAK preparations.** The DHAK work ran across **five preparations**, which were **not handled in parallel**. They entered the pipeline in successive rounds, each one prompted by what the previous round showed; the reasoning behind each change is developed in **Engineering (Iterations 1 to 5).**

- **First round.** The reference sequence **DHAK DSM 30040**, the variant crystallised as PDB 1UN9, was transformed together with its stabilised design **PROSS 5**, so that a direct wild-type-versus-variant comparison of stability and activity was possible.
- **Second round.** When neither of those two constructs gave a usable enzyme, we turned to the wild-type **DHAK(CECT 4626)**, the variant reported as the most catalytically efficient DHAK described to date. **This enzyme was not transformed by us.** Two **expressible stocks already held by the host laboratory**, from **2021 and 2012**, were recovered and taken through the same induction, harvest and lysis route as the constructs above, the 2021 stock first on the assumption that more recent material would have been better preserved.
revalorisation::selection: The goal of this stage was to obtain isolated, verified colonies of each construct and grow them to the point of induction. The transformation mixture was plated on LB agar containing kanamycin and incubated overnight at 37 °C. Only cells that took up the plasmid, and therefore express the resistance gene, form colonies, so the plate itself is the first selection.

Individual colonies were picked into LB with kanamycin (50 µg/mL) and grown overnight at 37 °C as pre-inocula. Two colonies were picked per construct, so a second independent clone is available in case one carries an unwanted mutation, which also allows a single anomalous flask to be set aside without restarting the stage. Each pre-inoculum was then diluted roughly fiftyfold into a larger volume of LB with kanamycin (for example 1 mL into 50 mL) and grown at 37 °C with shaking at 180 rpm. Diluting into fresh medium returns the cells to exponential growth, the state in which they are most transcriptionally and translationally active and therefore best prepared for induction.

Growth was followed by optical density at 600 nm until the culture reached roughly OD₆₀₀ 0.5 to 0.7. This window sets up the decision in the next stage, because inducing during exponential phase gives the highest yield of soluble protein.
revalorisation::induction: The goal of this stage was to switch on production once enough biomass had accumulated. Expression is driven by the **T7 / lacUV5 system**. In BL21(DE3) the T7 RNA polymerase gene sits in the chromosome under a lac-derived promoter, while the enzyme gene sits on the plasmid under a T7 promoter. As long as the lac repressor is bound, neither is transcribed, so the cell spends the growth phase building biomass rather than making foreign protein.

**IPTG** (isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside) is a non-hydrolysable analogue of allolactose. It binds and releases the lac repressor without being consumed, giving a stable, sustained induction. Releasing the repressor lets the cell transcribe the T7 RNA polymerase, which then transcribes the enzyme gene from the strong T7 promoter, so a small molecule triggers a large amount of protein.

When the culture reached the target optical density, **IPTG** was added to a final concentration of about **0.4 mM**, and the culture was shifted to **30 °C** and incubated overnight with shaking at 140 rpm. The temperature was lowered deliberately, because slower expression at 30 °C gives the nascent protein more time to fold correctly, favouring soluble, active enzyme over misfolded protein trapped in inclusion bodies.
revalorisation::obtaining cfe: The goal of this final stage was to break the cells open and recover a clarified soluble fraction, the cell-free extract (CFE), containing the expressed enzyme. This extract is the input for the downstream purification and activity work, so it is the endpoint of this page.

The induced cultures were transferred to pre-weighed 50 mL Falcon tubes and centrifuged at **6000 ×g, 10 °C, for 10 to 15 minutes**. The spent medium was discarded, the pellets were drained by inversion and weighed, and were then frozen at **−80 °C** until lysis. Freezing both stores the biomass conveniently and begins to weaken the cells, which assists the enzymatic lysis that follows. **The insoluble pellets were kept at −20 °C** after clarification, so that protein trapped in inclusion bodies could later be told apart from protein never made.

The frozen pellets were resuspended in **50 mM potassium phosphate buffer (KH₂PO₄), pH 7.5**, with the buffer volume scaled to the pellet, **3.5 to 4 mL per tube**, so that all extracts entered lysis at a comparable cell density, and lysed enzymatically. Three reagents were added to each resuspension. **Lysozyme** at a final concentration of 0.5 mg/mL digests the peptidoglycan cell wall. **DNase I** at 10 µg/mL degrades the genomic DNA that would otherwise make the lysate viscous and hard to handle. **MgCl₂** at 2 mM supplies the magnesium that DNase I needs as a cofactor. The suspension was agitated at room temperature, 140 rpm, for 30 minutes, after which it visibly cleared. This lysozyme-based approach follows the method used for this enzyme by Bastida et al. [8].

The lysate was centrifuged (8500 rpm, 10 °C, 10 min) and the **supernatant was retained as the cell-free extract**. The soluble enzyme stays in the supernatant, while cell debris, membranes and any insoluble misfolded protein are discarded in the pellet.

**What we did not do.** Some reference protocols for this enzyme add two further steps, mechanical disruption by sonication and removal of nucleic acids by streptomycin-sulfate precipitation. Neither was used here. The clarified extract came out clear and only slightly turbid, so the streptomycin-sulfate step to precipitate DNA fragments was judged unnecessary, and enzymatic lysis with lysozyme plus DNase gave a workable soluble extract without sonication. These steps are noted only so our procedure is not confused with the fuller protocols in the source material.

Measuring the activity of each enzyme required separating it from the hundreds of host proteins in the extract. Both constructs carry a hexahistidine tag, so **immobilised metal affinity chromatography** on **Co²⁺-IDA-agarose** was the natural first step, run by gravity flow in a disposable cartridge so that no pump or chromatography system is needed. The procedure is the same for both enzymes, but the buffers are not: DHAK is released from the resin by low concentrations of salt and imidazole, whereas PPK2 tolerates both, which allows a far more stringent wash. The eluates were then **dialysed** to remove the imidazole that would otherwise interfere with the activity assays. Three further stages were developed for DHAK alone, in response to problems with that enzyme, a **microlitre-scale express IMAC**, designed as a diagnostic to locate where activity was being lost without consuming sample, a **size-exclusion run** on an FPLC system, adopted as a purification route independent of metal affinity, and finally a **return to the affinity route** once size exclusion proved not to be reproducible.
**Immobilised Metal Affinity Chromatography (Co^2+ - IDA - Agarose)**

The goal of this stage was to isolate each enzyme from the hundreds of host proteins present in the cell-free extract (CFE), so that its activity could be measured without interference. Both constructs carry a **C-terminal hexahistidine tag** encoded by the pET-28a(+) vector, which made **immobilised metal affinity chromatography (IMAC)** the natural first purification step. The histidine residues of the tag coordinate the metal ions immobilised on the resin, so the tagged enzyme is retained while most host proteins pass through. The enzyme is then released with a high concentration of free **imidazole**, which competes with the tag for the same metal sites.

We used **Co²⁺-IDA-agarose** rather than the more common Ni²⁺ resins. Cobalt binds histidine tags less strongly than nickel, but it is more selective: fewer host proteins with surface histidines bind to it, so a single step gives a cleaner eluate. Because the goal was to compare enzyme activities rather than to maximise yield, favouring purity over quantity suited the project.

The purification was carried out by **gravity flow** in a small cartridge, with **batch binding**: the CFE and the resin were mixed and left in contact before the unbound fraction was drained. This gives the protein more time to bind than a simple flow-through and needs no pump or chromatography system, so any team can reproduce it at low cost. Two points are worth flagging for anyone repeating it. The **outlet must be capped** before the extract is loaded, since we lost a whole sample to that on the first attempt, and the protocol now marks every point where this applies. And the **elution volume should never exceed the volume of sample loaded**, because on another run the eluate came out too dilute to work with.

The column procedure was the same for both enzymes, but the buffers were not (Table 1), because the two proteins tolerate salt and imidazole very differently. All buffers were based on **50 mM sodium phosphate, pH 8.0**, a pH at which the histidines of the tag are deprotonated and can coordinate Co²⁺.

**DHAK.** DHAK is very sensitive to salt and imidazole: even low concentrations start to release it from the resin [2]. Equilibration and washing were therefore done with **phosphate buffer alone**, with no NaCl or imidazole, so that the enzyme stayed bound throughout. Elution used the same buffer with **1 M imidazole**. The price of this mild wash is that some host proteins remain bound and co-elute. We accepted this in exchange for not losing the enzyme.
**PPK2.** PPK2 binds the resin firmly and tolerates salt and imidazole without being released [3]. Its equilibration and wash buffers therefore included **150 mM NaCl and 30 mM imidazole**:

- NaCl suppresses weak ionic interactions between host proteins and the resin.
- The low imidazole concentration displaces host proteins that bind only weakly through surface histidines.
Together they give a more stringent wash and a purer eluate. As for DHAK, elution used phosphate buffer with **1 M imidazole**.

A separate cartridge and fresh resin were used for each protein to avoid cross-contamination. Each run was internally controlled by keeping all of its fractions (Load, Flow-through, Wash and Eluate) and analysing them side by side by SDS-PAGE.
*SDS-PAGE separates the proteins of each fraction by molecular weight and shows the enzyme as a band at its expected size, about 60 kDa for the DHAK subunit and about 33 kDa for PPK2 [9].*

This shows whether the enzyme bound the resin, whether any was lost during the wash, and how much the eluate was enriched compared with the starting CFE. Where the protein concentration can be measured reliably, the purification is also judged by **specific activity** (U/mg protein), which should rise after purification even though total activity always falls.

The protein concentration of the samples was measured by the Bradford assay against a BSA standard curve [10], which is what converts a measured activity into a specific activity. Readings close to the assay blank are not reliable, and where that was the case no specific activity is assigned, as reported in **Results.**
revalorisation::dialysis: The goal of this stage was to remove the imidazole and excess salt carried over from the IMAC eluate and to transfer each enzyme into a simple buffer compatible with its next use. This step is essential for our workflow. DHAK depends on **Mg-ATP** for its activity, and high concentrations of imidazole and salt interfere with its assay. PPK2 is used in a coupled assay with DHAK, so any imidazole left in its eluate would end up in the same reaction [2].

Dialysis was chosen because it is gentle, inexpensive and well suited to the millilitre volumes produced by our IMAC. The eluate is sealed in a semi-permeable membrane that retains the protein, while small molecules such as imidazole and NaCl diffuse out into a much larger volume of buffer until both sides reach equilibrium. It was carried out **overnight at 4 °C**, a temperature that protects the enzymes during the long exchange. Two practical points.

The **sample volume increases during dialysis**, because water enters the bag when the eluate, rich in imidazole, has a higher solute concentration than the buffer, so free space must be left in the bag to keep it from bursting. And a single bath may not remove all the imidazole, so **the buffer is changed at least once**, which removes far more than a single bath of the same total volume.

The dialysis buffer only needs to keep the pH stable, so its exact concentration is not critical. We used a **low-concentration sodium phosphate buffer (5 mM)** by default. This keeps the option of **freeze-drying** the enzyme for later use: freeze-drying removes the water but concentrates every salt left in the sample, so the lower the salt content beforehand, the better the enzyme is preserved. Slightly more concentrated phosphate buffers are equally suitable when the sample goes directly to the activity assays.

Where the preparation came out too dilute to assay, it was concentrated after dialysis by **centrifugal ultrafiltration**, following the protocol supplied by the manufacturer. In each case the molecular weight cut-off was chosen well below the molecular weight of the enzyme, so that the protein is retained above the membrane while water and small molecules pass through. **This was not applied to every preparation**, and when it was added later to an affinity eluate of the active enzyme it made a difference worth recording, as reported in Results. The reason for concentrating differed between the two enzymes.

**DHAK.** In one purification the elution volume exceeded the volume of CFE loaded, so the eluate came out diluted, and dialysis diluted it further as water entered the bag. The dialysed sample was therefore concentrated in a device with a **30 kDa** cut-off, well below the roughly 60 kDa of the subunit, and with a capacity suited to the volumes produced by the column [11].

**PPK2.** Here the eluate was not unusually dilute; it was concentrated because we had little material and wanted to use as little of it as possible in each assay. Working with a concentrated sample means a smaller volume per reaction, so the same preparation lasts for more measurements. Since the volumes involved were much smaller, a small-format device was used with a **10 kDa** cut-off, chosen because PPK2 is a much smaller protein, at about 33 kDa, and a 30 kDa membrane would risk letting it through [12].
revalorisation::express imac: The goal of this stage was to find out, quickly and with very little material, whether the IMAC purification itself was working for DHAK. In earlier purifications the enzyme had lost activity, and we did not know where the problem lay: in expression, in binding to and recovery from the resin, or in the activity of the enzyme itself. Running the full column protocol again each time we changed a condition would have cost a lot of sample and time without isolating the cause. This small-scale test was therefore designed as a **diagnostic step**. It checks one link of the chain at a time, whether DHAK is present in the extract and whether it binds the Co²⁺-IDA resin and can be recovered from it, so that we could start ruling out possible causes and focus on the real one.

The express protocol keeps the principle of IMAC but scales it down to **microlitre volumes in Eppendorf tubes**. A single batch of resin was washed and equilibrated, then split into separate tubes, each mixed with a small volume of a different CFE. This lets several constructs be tested in parallel under identical conditions.

The key design choice is the elution. Instead of imidazole, the bound protein is released with **SDS-PAGE loading buffer and heat**, the same treatment used to prepare CFE samples for electrophoresis. This denatures the enzyme and detaches it from the resin, so the protocol is **analytical rather than preparative**: the sample can only be used for SDS-PAGE, not for activity assays. For the same reason a simple **phosphate buffer without NaCl or imidazole** was used, since detecting the enzyme mattered more here than obtaining a pure fraction.

Each test is controlled by running the starting CFE (Load) on the same gel as the resin eluate. A band at the expected molecular weight of DHAK that is enriched in the eluate compared with the Load confirms that the construct expresses a His-tagged enzyme that binds the resin. **What the test showed, and which of the two possibilities it ruled out, is reported in Results.**

The goal of this stage was to purify DHAK from the cell-free extract by a route independent of metal affinity. Size-exclusion chromatography was adopted as an **alternative purification method for DHAK**, used instead of IMAC followed by dialysis rather than after it. The reasons for this change are described in Engineering (Iteration 6).

**Size-exclusion chromatography (SEC)**, also called gel filtration, separates proteins by size rather than by affinity. Large aggregates elute first, DHAK elutes at its characteristic volume, and smaller proteins, nucleotides and other small molecules from the extract elute last. For DHAK this approach has two advantages:

- The enzyme is never exposed to metal ions or imidazole.
- It elutes directly in the running buffer, so no dialysis is needed before the activity assays.

The runs were performed on an **ÄKTAprime plus FPLC system** with a preparative **HiLoad 26/60 Superdex 200 pg** column. Unlike the gravity-flow steps, FPLC pumps the buffer at a controlled flow rate and pressure and records the **UV absorbance at 280 nm** in real time. The DHAK peak can be followed as it leaves the column, so the fractions to keep are chosen from the chromatogram rather than blindly. On this column the **void volume is about 110 mL** and the **total volume about 320 mL**, which places the window where DHAK is expected at approximately **220 to 270 mL**.

The separation was **isocratic**, with a single buffer of **sodium phosphate with 150 mM NaCl, pH 7.2** used throughout [2]. Here the salt does not interfere with DHAK as it did during binding to the IMAC resin. Its role is to prevent weak ionic interactions between the proteins and the column matrix, so that separation depends only on molecular size. The column was equilibrated overnight before each run, so that the baseline was stable and the peaks could be read clearly.

The cell-free extract (CFE) was clarified by centrifugation before injection, to protect the column. The chromatogram served as the main control of each run, with the fractions to keep selected from it and matched to the fraction numbers recorded by the software before going on to the activity assays. **Four runs were performed in total**, and the separation did not behave the same way across them, which is reported in Results.

Three operating points are worth recording for anyone using this instrument. The ÄKTAprime always **starts a run in pause mode**, so a run that seems to have started may not be running at all, and releasing the pause is now an explicit step in our protocol. Air trapped in the system causes a noisy baseline and pressure problems, so the system must be **purged every time the mobile phase is connected or removed**, which we do the day before, when connecting the buffer for the overnight equilibration. And the **fraction collector must be started before the peak reaches the outlet**, which is now a timed step rather than a judgement made at the console, because in one run the best separation of the whole series was lost to it.

The final block answers the question the whole module exists for: does the system work. DHAP has no useful absorbance of its own, so both assays measure it through the same **coupled reporter reaction**, in which α-glycerophosphate dehydrogenase reduces the DHAP formed while oxidising NADH, followed as a fall in absorbance at 340 nm and converted into an absolute amount of product through the NADH extinction coefficient. The first assay characterises **DHAK on its own**, in continuous format, giving a quantitative activity that can be compared across variants and across purification stages. The second combines **both enzymes** in a single long reaction with polyphosphate and a substoichiometric amount of adenine nucleotide, sampled over the course of the reaction and measured in endpoint format, to test whether ATP is genuinely being recycled rather than consumed.
revalorisation::dhak activity: The goal of this stage was a quantitative measure of DHAK activity, so that the purified enzyme could be characterised and the different variants and preparations compared on the same scale.

DHAK phosphorylates dihydroxyacetone (DHA) to DHAP using ATP, but **DHAP has no useful absorbance of its own**, so it cannot be followed directly. It is therefore measured through a coupled reporter reaction. **α-glycerophosphate dehydrogenase (α-GDH)** reduces the DHAP formed to glycerol-3-phosphate while oxidising NADH to NAD⁺, and **triosephosphate isomerase (TIM)** is included in the coupling mix. NADH absorbs at 340 nm and NAD⁺ does not, so the fall in absorbance at 340 nm tracks DHAP formation in real time, and its initial rate is proportional to DHAK activity (Figure 4) [2, 5].

Applying the NADH extinction coefficient (**ε₃₄₀ = 6220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹**) converts that rate into an absolute amount of DHAP. This is what makes the measurement an absolute one rather than a relative signal, so it stays comparable between instruments, between runs and between laboratories, which matters because the same assay is used to compare enzyme variants. The assay was run mostly in **1 cm cuvettes** and occasionally in **microplate** when that was more convenient, with the path length of the format used applied in the conversion. See the R**esults.**

The assay can be run either on the **CFE** or on **purified DHAK**, which lets the same measurement follow the enzyme through the purification. The reaction is assembled with everything except DHA: buffer, ATP, MgCl₂, NADH, the two coupling enzymes and the DHAK sample. The **coupling enzymes are supplied in excess**, so that the reporter reaction is never limiting and the measured rate reflects DHAK alone. The amount of DHAK added is **titrated** for each sample until the decrease in A₃₄₀ is clearly measurable but still linear for long enough to read an initial rate.

The **control is the baseline itself**. Before DHA is added, A₃₄₀ is recorded with the complete mixture in place until the signal has stabilised. Any fall in absorbance during that window cannot come from DHAK, since its substrate is absent, and is instead due to NADH-consuming enzymes present in the sample or to spontaneous NADH degradation. This is more pronounced in cell-free extract than in purified enzyme. That baseline slope is subtracted from the slope measured after DHA addition, so that only the NADH oxidation attributable to DHAP formation is counted.

**Modification of the reference protocol.** The assay was run in **potassium phosphate buffer at pH 7.5**, whereas the reference assay uses Tris-HCl at pH 8.0 [2]. Phosphate at pH 7.5 was chosen to keep the assay consistent with the lysis and purification buffers, so that the enzyme is not exposed to a buffer change immediately before being measured. This deviation is recorded because it may affect the absolute values obtained, and should be taken into account when comparing them with published figures.
revalorisation::coupled dhak ppk2 assay: The goal of this stage was the proof of concept of the whole system: showing that the two enzymes work together and that ATP can be **recycled** instead of consumed stoichiometrically.

As DHAK phosphorylates DHA to DHAP, it consumes ATP and generates ADP. **PPK2 uses polyphosphate as a phosphate donor** to convert that ADP back to ATP, returning it to DHAK to drive another round of phosphorylation. The reaction therefore runs on a small pool of adenine nucleotide that is recycled many times rather than spent once.

This changes what limits the reaction. With regeneration, the total DHAP formed is set by the DHA and the polyphosphate supplied, not by the amount of ATP added, so far more DHAP can accumulate than the initial ATP could ever yield on its own. Clearing ADP as it forms also removes a second limitation, since ADP inhibits DHAK. This matters well beyond the bench: ATP is far too expensive to be added stoichiometrically in a real revalorisation process, whereas polyphosphate is cheap, which is what makes the system viable at scale.

The reaction contains DHA, polyphosphate, Mg²⁺, both enzymes and a **substoichiometric** amount of adenine nucleotide. Supplying less adenine nucleotide than the DHAP that can be formed is what makes the **experiment informative**: the result cannot be explained unless the nucleotide pool turns over more than once.

Two design parameters control whether the determination can be read at all. The **volume of sample taken into each well** must be small enough that the DHAP it carries stays below the NADH supplied, otherwise every well saturates at the same ceiling and the signal marks the limit of the assay rather than the product formed. And that ceiling must sit **above the ATP supplied**, since a saturated signal below it cannot show that DHAP exceeded the nucleotide. How these were set, and what happened when they were set wrongly, is reported in Results and in Engineering (Iteration 9).

DHAP was tracked by an **endpoint version** of the α-GDH/TIM assay described above. Samples were taken during the reaction and frozen immediately to stop it, then measured by adding α-GDH and TIM, which gives a fall in absorbance at 340 nm proportional to the DHAP present and is converted to concentration against a DHAP standard curve. The endpoint format is used here because the reaction runs for hours rather than minutes, so it cannot be followed continuously in a cuvette, and for the same reason it is read in **microplate**. The sampling times and the polyphosphate feeds differ between rounds and are reported in Results.

The decisive read-out is the **DHAP formed relative to the ATP supplied at the start**. A value above one means that each adenine nucleotide molecule has been turned over more than once, which is the proof of concept that the multienzymatic system works. **The control this design calls for is the same reaction without PPK2**, in which DHAP formation should stop once the initial ATP is spent, and which is what would isolate the contribution of the regeneration step from everything else in the mixture. **That condition was not run within the time available.** The regeneration reported in Results is therefore inferred from the stoichiometry of the nucleotide supplied rather than measured against a non-regenerating reaction, and running this control is the first thing a future round should do.
**Conclusion**

Taken together, the four blocks are both **necessary and sufficient** for the objective of this module. None of them produces a result on its own: a stabilised design is only a sequence until it is expressed, an expressed enzyme is unmeasurable among hundreds of host proteins, and a purified enzyme means nothing until its activity is quantified. Equally, each block stops where the next begins. We ordered the genes already cloned into an expression vector, skipped the intermediate cloning strain, used a single affinity step rather than a full purification train, and did not characterise the enzymes beyond what the system required. The goal was a **functional demonstration**, not a complete enzymological description.

The choices also reflect the resources of a student team in a shared laboratory. Stabilisation was pursued **computationally** rather than by screening mutants, the purification was designed to run **by gravity flow** with no pump or chromatography system, and when the full purification began consuming sample without telling us where the problem was, we built a **microlitre-scale diagnostic version** of it instead of repeating the whole procedure.

Each stage carries its own control, and that is what makes the set interpretable: the wild-type enzyme controls its stabilised design, every purification keeps and analyses all of its fractions, and activities are reported as rates and, where the protein concentration could be measured reliably, as specific activities in absolute units, so that measurements made on different days remain comparable. The four blocks then converge in the **coupled DHAK–PPK2 assay**, the only experiment that tests the module as a whole.

What we deliberately left undone is also part of the design. The **SpyTag/SpyCatcher complex** was designed but not built, the **PROSS 1 construct** was expressed but not assayed, the **control without PPK2** was not run, and the **bead-derived polyphosphate** was replaced by a commercial equivalent so that the biochemistry could be characterised independently of the upstream hardware. In every case the limit is stated, the reasoning is documented, and the work is left in a state where another team can take it up.

BL21(DE3) was chosen because it is **protease-deficient** and carries the **T7 RNA polymerase gene under lacUV5 control**, so the plasmid's T7 promoter is only transcribed once the polymerase is induced.

The term used here is **transformation**, the uptake of naked plasmid DNA by an artificially competent bacterial cell.
