Next experimental steps: (i) extend the characterisation from single-point specific activity to full Michaelis–Menten kinetics [6] (Kₘ, kₑₐₜ) against bis-pNPP and, ideally, against real degumming substrate, to confirm the ranking holds at industrially relevant substrate concentrations; (ii) assess pH and thermal stability across the operating window; and (iii) carry AphA and PhyA into the immobilisation work-block, re-measuring specific activity after immobilisation to quantify activity retention. Had any enzyme shown no activity, the most likely causes would have been misfolding or loss of a required metal cofactor during dialysis; this would be addressed by re-screening expression/solubilisation conditions and by supplementing the assay with the relevant divalent cation.
total protein quantification bradford co: **Total protein quantification by the Bradford (Coomassie dye-binding) assay.**

The Bradford assay is a fast, sensitive and widely used colorimetric method for quantifying total protein concentration in solution. It is based on the binding of the dye Coomassie Brilliant Blue G-250 to protein: in acidic solution the free dye is predominantly in a reddish cationic form that absorbs around 465 nm, but on binding to protein (mainly through interactions with basic and aromatic residues) it is stabilised in an anionic blue form with an absorbance maximum at 595 nm. The increase in absorbance at 595 nm is therefore proportional to the amount of protein present, and unknown concentrations are read against a calibration curve built with a protein standard [1].

**The method’s speed, its compatibility with a microplate format and its minimal reagent requirements make it ideal for routinely quantifying the many fractions generated during recombinant enzyme expression and purification**, where a mass value is needed quickly and reproducibly. Its main practical limitation is a non-linear response outside a narrow concentration window [2], which is managed by diluting concentrated samples so their signal falls within the linear range of the standard curve.
- Application of the technique to the sample

The samples measured are aqueous protein solutions: purified recombinant enzyme preparations (PhyA, AphA, M2-32) and the concentrated commercial Lecitase® Ultra stock. In general, soluble protein preparations are well suited to the Bradford assay because the dye binds proteins in solution rapidly and the read-out requires no digestion or heating [3]; the assay is, however, sensitive to some buffer components and detergents, so buffer composition must be kept consistent between samples and standards.

Our specific samples are single-protein preparations whose mass concentration must be known in order to normalise enzymatic activity: knowing U/mL alone is insufficient to compare enzymes, because it does not account for how much protein each assay contained. For the recombinant panel, the Bradford value converts volumetric activity into specific activity (U/mg); for the concentrated Lecitase® Ultra stock, the same measurement establishes the mass of enzyme used in the immobilization experiments and the reference specific activity of the free enzyme. Because these particular samples span a wide concentration range (from dilute purified enzymes to a very concentrated commercial stock), the assay is applied with an appropriate dilution series so that every reading falls within the linear range of the standard.
- Application of the technique to the project and expected results

Bradford quantification was chosen over alternatives such as the Lowry assay or absorbance at 280 nm because it is faster, more tolerant and, unlike A₂₈₀, does not require knowledge of each protein's extinction coefficient or a pure, nucleic-acid-free sample, which is important when handling several different enzymes.

The objective within the enzyme-production block is to provide the protein-mass denominator that turns raw activity measurements into mass-normalised specific activities, so enzymes of different identity and abundance can be compared on equal footing, and so the correct amount of biocatalyst can later be loaded onto the support. We expected to obtain a linear BSA calibration curve over the working range and, from it, distinct protein concentrations for each enzyme preparation; combined with the activity assays, these values were expected to reorder the enzymes by intrinsic efficiency (since raw activity and specific activity can dissociate). The information sought is simply an accurate mg/mL value per sample, which is the input required by the specific-activity and immobilization-yield calculations elsewhere in the project.
**Sample type measured:** purified enzyme (or commercial stock) in its storage/reaction buffer.

Preparation centres on dilution and standard matching. A standard calibration series was prepared with bovine serum albumin (BSA) as the reference protein [1] across a defined range (0–0.5 mg/mL for the recombinant panel; for the very concentrated Lecitase® Ultra stock a higher-range BSA series was used and the stock itself was serially diluted, e.g. 1:10 to 1:60, until an absorbance within the linear range was obtained). In the microplate format [4], a fixed small volume of sample (10 µL) was mixed with the Bradford reagent (200 µL) directly in the wells, and absorbance was read at 595 nm; all measurements were performed in triplicate to control pipetting variability at these small volumes.

It is essential that samples and standards share the same buffer and that deionised water, not the zero-protein dye blank, is used as the reference where the protocol requires, because buffer mismatch and blank choice are the main sources of error in dye-binding assays. No modification of the standardised protocol was needed beyond the dilution strategy required to bring the concentrated Lecitase® Ultra stock into the linear range; the dilution giving the lowest replicate error (1:60 for the stock) was selected as the reference for calculating the stock concentration.
The results are the BSA calibration lines and the interpolated protein concentrations for each sample.

The BSA calibration was linear across the working range (R² = 0.98), validating the interpolation. For the recombinant panel, the assay revealed substantially different protein loads (M2-32 > PhyA > AphA), which was exactly the information needed to interpret the activity data: although M2-32 and AphA released almost identical amounts of pNP, AphA did so with ≈45% less protein, so normalising by the Bradford values reordered the enzymes to AphA > M2-32 > PhyA by specific activity.

For the Lecitase® Ultra stock, the dilution with the lowest error (1:60) gave a consistent estimate of ≈40 mg/mL and, combined with the activity assay, a specific activity of ≈981 U/mg, the reference used throughout the immobilization work. These outcomes met expectations: a clean linear standard and per-sample concentrations that meaningfully changed the comparison between enzymes.

Next steps: (i) where the highest accuracy is needed, apply the linearised Bradford read-out (A₅₉₅/A₄₅₀ ratio) to widen the reliable range and reduce dilution dependence [2]; (ii) cross-check key concentrations with an orthogonal method (e.g. A₂₈₀ with the calculated extinction coefficient) for the purified single proteins; and (iii) continue to pair every activity measurement with a Bradford quantification so all downstream activities remain mass-normalised. The main source of uncertainty is the assay’s intrinsic non-linearity and buffer sensitivity; keeping standards in the same buffer and working within the linear range (as done here via dilution) is the practical mitigation, and the observed low replicate error at the selected dilutions supports the reliability of the reported values.
intracellular polyphosphate uptake assay: **Colorimetric quantification of orthophosphate by molybdate-dye complexation, applied to measuring intracellular polyphosphate accumulation in whole cells.**

The molybdate-dye assay is a fast, sensitive colorimetric method for quantifying free orthophosphate (Pi) in aqueous solution. Its principle is that, under acidic conditions, orthophosphate reacts with molybdate to form a phosphomolybdate complex which then associates with a cationic dye (malachite-green type) to give an intensely coloured product whose absorbance is proportional to the amount of phosphate present; unknown concentrations are read against a calibration curve built with a phosphate standard. Because the reaction is driven by a one-to-one stoichiometry between Pi and the coloured complex, the method is linear over a wide range and sensitive down to the nanomolar/nanogram scale [1].

This chemistry does not measure polyphosphate (polyP) directly; it measures orthophosphate. It is applied to polyP by first hydrolysing the polymer to its constituent orthophosphate units. Since polyP is a linear chain of Pi residues joined by high-energy phosphoanhydride bonds [2], hot acid cleaves it quantitatively to free Pi, so the orthophosphate measured after hydrolysis is a direct, stoichiometric proxy for the polyP that was stored in the cells. The decisive advantage exploited here is that the assay is inexpensive, simple and directly quantitative, which makes it well suited to following phosphorus accumulation across a dense time-course for several strain/condition/replicate combinations, exactly what is needed to compare the phosphorus-capturing phenotype of two strains over two hours.
- Application of the technique to the sample

The sample actually read in the cuvette is a neutralised acid hydrolysate of a bacterial cell pellet, a clarified aqueous solution containing the orthophosphate liberated from the cells’ intracellular polyphosphate. In general, molybdate-dye assays are ideally suited to clear aqueous samples in which phosphate is free in solution, because the colour develops in the liquid phase and no phase separation is required; the main precaution is that the sample must not contain large amounts of extraneous phosphate or interfering species.

Our specific sample is the whole-cell biomass of *Pseudomonas putida* KT2440, the wild-type strain and an engineered transformant, incubated in the project’s operation medium (filtered vegetable-oil degumming effluent adjusted to pH 5). Going from general to specific: the colorimetric reaction reports total soluble Pi; here that Pi comes exclusively from the hot-acid hydrolysis of the polyphosphate granules the cells accumulated, so the read-out is interpreted as intracellular polyphosphate content [3,4]. To make the value comparable between samples and strains, the phosphate measured in each pellet is normalised to the biomass in that sample (optical density at 600 nm), yielding total ng of Pi per OD₆₀₀ unit; tracking this quantity over time converts a single-point colorimetric measurement into a phosphorus-uptake rate for each strain.
- Application of the technique to the project and expected results

This technique was chosen, rather than DAPI-based polyP fluorescence, ³¹P-NMR or enzymatic (polyP-kinase-coupled) assays, because it is cheap, requires no specialised instrumentation beyond a spectrophotometer, is directly quantitative in absolute mass units (ng Pi) and scales easily to the many time-points and replicates the comparison demands; acid extraction followed by molybdate quantification is a long-established route to total cellular polyP [3].

Within the genetic-engineering work-block, the objective is to test whether the metabolic engineering of the chassis actually increases its capacity to capture phosphorus from the operation stream. rePhlow engineers *P. putida* KT2440 to hyperaccumulate polyphosphate by heterologously overexpressing polyphosphate kinase (ppk1) and the high-affinity phosphate transporter (pstSCAB) while knocking out the polyphosphate-degrading and competing routes (ppx, ppkB, pitB) by CRISPR base editing. The experiment compares the wild-type strain against this engineered transformant for intracellular polyP accumulation under operation conditions (pH 5), after a phosphate-starvation step that primes the cells for “luxury” phosphate uptake. We expected both strains to accumulate phosphorus over the two-hour assay, and we expected the engineered transformant to do so faster and/or to a greater extent, because its genetic design biases flux towards polyP synthesis and retention. The information sought is the **phosphorus-uptake rate** (ng Pi per OD₆₀₀ per minute) of each strain, since it is the quantitative phenotype that tells us whether the engineered strain is a meaningfully better phosphorus-capture agent and should be carried forward into the recovery process.

**Sample type measured:** whole-cell pellets of *P. putida* KT2440 (WT and engineered transformant), processed into a neutralised acid hydrolysate; the orthophosphate in that hydrolysate is the analyte.

Preparation follows the logic of a luxury-uptake experiment and is designed so the colorimetric signal reflects only intracellular polyphosphate. Overnight precultures of each strain (LB + the corresponding antibiotic, 30 °C) were used to inoculate fresh cultures that were grown to mid-exponential phase (OD₆₀₀ ≈ 0.6). Cells were then subjected to a 1 h phosphate-starvation step in phosphate-free minimal medium, which de-represses the phosphate regulon and primes the cells to take up phosphate avidly once it becomes available. The starved cells were washed and resuspended to OD₆₀₀ = 1.0 in filtered operation medium adjusted to pH 5 (this point is t = 0), and the assay was run for 120 min with sampling at 15 min intervals.

At each time-point two aliquots were taken: one to measure OD₆₀₀ (blanked against cell-free filtered medium) for the biomass normalisation, and one to quantify phosphorus. **The phosphorus aliquot was washed three times with 0.1 M NaCl (centrifuging at 10,000 rpm, 4 °C between washes): this step is critical because the operation medium is itself phosphate-rich, and any carry-over of extracellular phosphate would falsify the intracellular signal**, so the extracellular medium must be removed completely. Each washed pellet was then resuspended in 1 M HCl and incubated 15 min at 95 °C, which simultaneously lyses the cells and hydrolyses the intracellular polyP to orthophosphate [3]; after cooling and clarification by centrifugation, the supernatant was neutralised with an equal volume of 1 M NaOH (to ≈ pH 7) and further diluted before colour development, giving the overall dilution factor of 5000 used in the back-calculation. Colour was developed by adding the freshly prepared molybdate-dye working reagent (dye solution + additive, made up the same day) and reading absorbance after a 15 min incubation at room temperature, against a phosphate-standard calibration series run in duplicate [1].

No major deviation from a standard protocol was required; the laboratory-level points worth noting are that the molybdate-dye working reagent must be prepared fresh daily (the additive is mixed into the dye solution immediately before use), that the triple NaCl wash must be thorough, and that the acid neutralisation must bring the sample close to neutral pH so the colour chemistry behaves as in the standards.
The results are the phosphate calibration curve, the growth (OD₆₀₀) profiles, and the biomass-normalised intracellular-phosphorus profiles from which the uptake rates are derived.

The calibration curve was linear across the 0–1900 ng range (A₆₀₀ = 0.00104·[Pi] + 0.2218), validating the interpolation, and the OD₆₀₀ profiles confirmed that biomass stayed roughly constant during the assay, so the normalised signal can be read as phosphorus accumulated per unit of biomass rather than as a growth artefact.

Both strains accumulated intracellular phosphorus from the pH-5 operation medium over the two hours, with the biomass-normalised content rising from the order of 4–9.5 × 10⁵ ng Pi·OD⁻¹ at t = 0 to roughly 1.2–1.4 × 10⁶ ng Pi·OD⁻¹ at 120 min. Because the per-time-point data are noisy (sizeable replicate SD and non-monotonic early points), the robust comparator is the slope over the linear uptake window. On that metric the engineered transformant takes up phosphorus markedly faster than the wild type: 11,017 vs 6,450 ng Pi·OD₆₀₀⁻¹·min⁻¹, a 1.71-fold higher uptake rate. This matches the expectation set out above and provides functional, whole-cell validation that the metabolic design (ppk1/pstSCAB overexpression together with ppx/ppkB/pitB knockouts) does what it was engineered to do: bias the cell towards capturing and retaining phosphorus from the operation stream [4–6].

Next experimental steps: (i) extend the time-course beyond 120 min until the normalised signal plateaus, to obtain each strain’s maximal polyP storage capacity (ng Pi·OD⁻¹) in addition to the initial rate; (ii) increase the number of biological replicates and, if needed, apply a brief additional wash or an EDTA rinse to further suppress extracellular-phosphate carry-over, since incomplete removal of the phosphate-rich medium is the most likely source of the early scatter and would inflate the apparent signal; (iii) dissect the contribution of the individual genetic modifications (e.g. ppk1/pstSCAB overexpression vs the ppx/ppkB/pitB knockouts) to the observed rate gain; and (iv) repeat on genuine, non-simulated degumming effluent and couple the measurement to the downstream biomass-harvest/phosphorus-recovery step. Should a run fail to show uptake, the first things to check would be the completeness of the NaCl washes, the efficiency of the acid hydrolysis (time/temperature) and the freshness of the molybdate-dye reagent, any of which could flatten or distort the signal.
dhak activity assay: **Coupled α-GDH/TIM spectrophotometric assay, NADH-linked kinase activity**

The coupled α-GDH/TIM assay is an enzyme-linked spectrophotometric method for measuring the activity of enzymes that produce dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP). Its principle is indirect detection. **DHAP carries no chromophore and has no useful absorbance of its own, so it cannot be followed directly; it is reported instead through two auxiliary enzymes that convert it into a change in the concentration of a species that does absorb.** α-glycerophosphate dehydrogenase (α-GDH) reduces DHAP to glycerol 3-phosphate while oxidising NADH to NAD⁺, and triosephosphate isomerase (TIM) interconverts the two triose phosphates so that any D-glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate present is funnelled into the same readout rather than escaping it [1,2]. What makes the method quantitative rather than merely indicative is the stoichiometry of the reporter step: α-GDH consumes exactly one NADH per DHAP, and NADH absorbs strongly at 340 nm while NAD⁺ does not, so **the fall in absorbance at 340 nm is stoichiometric with the DHAP formed**. The molar extinction coefficient of NADH, ε₃₄₀ = 6220 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹, converts an absorbance change into an absolute amount of product, so **the calibration rests on a physical constant rather than on an internal standard of our own** [1,3], which is what allows a rate obtained here to be set against the published activity of the same enzyme. One condition has to be engineered rather than assumed: **the auxiliary enzymes must be supplied in sufficient excess that the reporter step is never rate limiting**, since otherwise the measured slope reports the coupling system instead of the kinase [4].

The assay is used in two modes, and that both share the same chemistry is a deliberate design decision rather than a convenience. **In continuous mode** the absorbance is recorded kinetically and the initial rate is taken from the linear portion of the trace, which is what distinguishes a catalytically competent enzyme from one that is present but does not work. **In endpoint mode** the same chemistry is applied to stopped aliquots of a reaction that has run for hours, and what is obtained is not a slope but a concentration. Because the two modes share the reporter chemistry, the wavelength and the extinction coefficient, a rate measured on a single enzyme and a yield measured on a cascade are expressed in the same units. The cost should be stated alongside the benefit: **the entire characterisation of the module depends on one reporter system behaving correctly**, so the controls that establish it are part of the measurement rather than an optional extra. One consequence governs the endpoint mode in particular. Since one NADH is consumed per DHAP, **the NADH placed in the well imposes a ceiling on the product that can be detected**, and the dilution applied to the aliquot is what positions that ceiling. **A ceiling below the threshold an experiment must exceed renders a saturated reading uninformative, however large the signal looks.**
- Application of the technique to the sample

Two distinct sample types are measured here, and they place different demands on the assay. The first is a soluble protein preparation of a kinase, whether a clarified cell free extract or an enzyme purified by affinity or size exclusion chromatography; it is measured in continuous mode and what is read is a rate. For these the method is undemanding, which is one reason it was chosen: **it works directly on the sample with no labelling, derivatisation or clean-up**, so an extract can be measured as readily as a purified protein. Two points nevertheless decide whether the number obtained is usable. The sample is kept cold until it is added, since what is being measured is the activity of a protein that loses it on standing. And the volume added is titrated so that the slope is measurable but not too steep: a very steep fall exhausts the NADH within the first readings and leaves no linear region to fit, while a very shallow one cannot be distinguished from baseline drift [5]. In this work the volume ranged from about 1 to about 7 µL, and it is reported with every rate, since a volumetric activity is meaningless without it.

A clarified cell free extract raises one consideration a purified enzyme does not: **it contains the whole soluble proteome of the host, which may include enzymes that oxidise NADH on their own account**, and any such activity is indistinguishable from the signal of interest once the reaction has started. The test is performed before the substrate is added — if A₃₄₀ is stable in the complete mixture lacking only dihydroxyacetone, the extract carries no appreciable NADH-consuming activity. The second sample type is an aliquot of a multienzyme reaction that has been running for hours and has been stopped; it is measured in endpoint mode and what is read is a concentration. The aliquot carries a high concentration of substrate and product, so **the dilution applied to it is the parameter that decides whether the determination lies within its linear range or above its ceiling**. The analyte is also labile, which is why aliquots are frozen at the moment of sampling and all of them measured together in a single determination, against the same standards and the same NADH. Our specific samples are the DHAK variants of *Citrobacter freundii* available to the module, as cell free extracts and as purified preparations, and the aliquots of the coupled DHAK and PPK2 reaction.
- Application of the technique to the project and expected results

The revalorisation module converts dihydroxyacetone into dihydroxyacetone phosphate with purified enzymes rather than living cells, and its central claim is that ATP regenerated from polyphosphate can drive that phosphorylation.

**Nothing about the sequences, the structures or the designs settles whether that is true. Only a measurement does**, and the measurement has to report the product of a kinase that carries no absorbance of its own, in real time and in absolute units, so that a rate obtained here means the same thing as a rate obtained in another laboratory. The whole characterisation of the module was therefore built around this single assay, applied first to each enzyme preparation on its own and then to the coupled cascade.
The alternatives were considered and rejected for reasons specific to this product and this reaction. A discontinuous quantification of DHAP by HPLC would also work, but it is slower, of lower throughput and gives no real time information about whether the reaction is linear while it is being measured. Colorimetric phosphate assays report the release of ADP or of inorganic phosphate rather than the product of interest, and in a reaction containing millimolar polyphosphate, which hydrolyses to release phosphate on its own account, such a readout would be uninterpretable. The NADH linked assay instead reports DHAP formation directly, converts to absolute units through a single known constant, and uses reagents already available in the host laboratory.
The objective within the module is twofold, and the two purposes correspond to the two modes.

1. **For a single enzyme**, it establishes whether a given variant or preparation is catalytically active and fixes a baseline rate against which the others are judged. This is what separates an enzyme that expressed from an enzyme that works, and it is the only evidence that can rank a designed variant against the wild type.
2. **For the coupled system**, it reports how much DHAP the two enzyme reaction has accumulated over hours, which, compared against the ATP supplied at the start, is what tells us whether polyphosphate driven regeneration allows the cascade to produce more product than its initial nucleotide could support.
The single enzyme measurements were not planned as a comparison of variants decided in advance.

**They form a diagnostic chain, in which the preparation measured at each point was chosen by what the previous measurement had ruled out**, and in which each result forced a decision documented in Engineering. This is why they are reported below in the order in which they were run rather than grouped by variant: the order is the argument.
The results expected were specific and were stated before the measurements were made. For an active preparation, a clear and linear fall in A₃₄₀ with a high R², convertible into a rate in nmol DHAP per minute and, with a protein quantification, into a specific activity comparable with the 10.7 U/mg reported for the fully purified enzyme [5]. For an inactive or absent enzyme, a flat trace whose fitted slope has an R² low enough to show that the fit is to noise rather than to a descending signal. For the coupled reaction, a ratio of DHAP formed to ATP supplied above unity, which is the proof of concept for regeneration. These outcomes were what decided whether a variant was carried forward, whether a purification route was retained, and whether the regeneration module works as designed.
**Technique requirements**

Two of these deserve emphasis because they are the ones most often left out. **The optical path is not 1 cm in a microplate**, where it is set by the fill volume, so a rate converted to absolute units by assuming a cuvette path is wrong by the ratio between the two. And **the fitting window is part of the result**: the same trace yields different initial rates according to the points over which the line is fitted, so a rate reported without its window cannot be reproduced exactly.
- **Sample preparation**

The preparations measured were produced by the routes described in the expression and purification blocks, and are listed here because **the identity of the preparation is part of the measurement**: the same enzyme gives different numbers as a crude extract, as an affinity eluate and as a concentrated eluate, and those differences are the subject of the analysis below.
**1. Preparations measured in continuous mode**

- **Clarified cell free extract.** Cells harvested by centrifugation, resuspended in lysis buffer scaled to the wet biomass, lysed enzymatically, clarified by centrifugation and kept on ice. Two batches of the CECT 4626 2012 stock were measured, and the extract of the 2021 stock was measured directly without purification, because activity reports on functional enzyme whether or not a band is visible on a gel.
- **Dialysed affinity eluate.** IMAC followed by dialysis against the assay buffer, which removes the imidazole and salt that would otherwise interfere with the determination.
- **Dialysed affinity eluate concentrated by centrifugal ultrafiltration.** The same route followed by concentration in a Centricon device, so that the enzyme entering the assay was concentrated rather than left dilute.
- **Size exclusion fractions.** Individual fractions from the preparative runs, assayed without further treatment since they elute in the running buffer.

Each preparation was kept on ice and a volume titrated into the reaction such that the fall in absorbance was neither too steep to fit nor too shallow to distinguish from the baseline. **The volume actually assayed is reported with every result, because the volumetric activity depends on it directly.**
**2. Protein quantification**

Specific activity requires a protein concentration, determined by the Bradford method against a BSA standard curve [6]. **Two sample volumes were loaded for each preparation**, which is what revealed that the determination was not always trustworthy: for the crude extract and for the first PPK2 preparation the readings sat just above the assay blank and the two loads disagreed by about fourfold.

**Where the two volumes did not agree, no specific activity was assigned and the activity is reported in volumetric terms only**, since a specific activity derived from an unreliable protein figure would carry that error silently.
**3. Aliquots of the coupled reaction**

Aliquots were withdrawn at the times reported and**frozen immediately in order to stop them**, then measured together in a single endpoint determination against DHAP standards prepared fresh and kept on ice. **The dilution applied to each aliquot was the parameter that changed between the two rounds**, and it is reported with each of them because it fixes the detection ceiling.
- Results

The measurements are reported in the order in which they were made, the single enzyme assays in continuous mode first and then the two rounds of the coupled assay in endpoint mode. The full data, including every absorbance trace, are on the project results page, **Results, Revalorisation**.

**The assay did what the module required of it: it separated an active enzyme from an inactive one unambiguously, on the same scale and in the same session, and expressed the difference as an absolute rate of product formation rather than as a relative signal.**
That is what turned a set of constructs into a result.

Figures 1 to 7 follow, one per row of Table 1 and in the same order. **In every trace the two vertical lines mark the window over which the initial rate was fitted, and the number of points used is stated on the figure**, so that the fit can be reproduced and not merely the result. The sample names printed on the figures are the labels carried over from the plate layout of each session and are not descriptions of the samples; where one is misleading it is explained in the caption. The vertical scale differs between figures, since what is being compared is the slope and not the absolute absorbance.
**What the continuous mode established**

The discrimination is not marginal. The active cell free extract fell at −581.1 mOD/min with R² = 1.00, while the DSM 30040 reference fell at −3.73 and the 2021 stock and PROSS design 5 gave fitted slopes of −0.080 and −0.92 with R² of 0.035 and 0.374. **Those two low R² values are themselves the result and not a defect of the measurement**: a slope fitted to a flat trace describes noise, and reporting it as a rate would be an error, which is why no rate is assigned in those rows. The criterion applied throughout is that **a rate is accepted only when the linear fit is acceptable**, so that a steep slope with a poor fit is reported as unusable rather than as activity.

The purified preparation is the measurement that completes the line. At −850.1 mOD/min with R² = 0.999, about 20 U/mL and, against a reliable protein determination, about 10 U/mg, **it sits essentially at the 10.7 U/mg reported for the fully purified enzyme** [5], which means the affinity step followed by concentration delivered DHAK at close to its maximum specific activity. It is also what allowed the coupled reaction to be charged with a known quantity of enzyme, 3 U, rather than with a volume of extract.

Read as a chain rather than as a list, these measurements decided the course of the module. The reference variant proved too weakly active to serve as a control, which removed the comparison the stabilisation line had been built around. The designed variant was therefore measured without a working counterpart of the same sequence background, and **this is where the assay reaches its limit: a flat trace establishes that a preparation has no measurable activity, but it cannot distinguish an enzyme inactivated by the purification from a design that abolished function.** Discriminating between those two requires an active enzyme of the same background taken through exactly the same procedure, and no such reference existed at that point. The measurement is conclusive about the preparation and silent about the design.
**The size exclusion fractions** were assayed by the same method and are reported separately in Table 2, since they belong to the purification block and are discussed there as well.
**Where the determination was not trustworthy**

Two of the Bradford determinations in Table 3 are unusable, and they are reported rather than quietly dropped because the conclusion depends on them. For the crude extract the two loads gave 1.35 and 0.37 mg/mL, both sitting just above the standard curve intercept of 0.319, that is, at the lower limit of the method; for the first PPK2 preparation they gave 4.83 and 1.26 mg/mL. **Values that should coincide for the same preparation and instead differ about fourfold do not become acceptable by averaging them**, so no specific activity was assigned to the crude extract, and the PPK2 supplied in round 1 is quoted as an interval rather than as a figure. The one preparation with a clean protein determination is the one that carries a specific activity, and it is the only one compared against the published value.

A second limit of the same kind applies to the calibration of the assay itself. The conversion to absolute units rests on the **published extinction coefficient of NADH rather than on a standard curve measured on our own instrument**, which is sound for a cuvette of known path length but less so in a microplate, where the path is set by the fill volume. The continuous assays reported here were made in a 1 cm cuvette, so the constant applies directly; a local NADH standard curve would nevertheless make the conversion independent of that assumption, and is listed among the next steps.
**Endpoint mode: the coupled DHAK and PPK2 reaction**

**Round 1** was run with about 3 U of DHAK as cell free extract and purified PPK2, with 50 mM dihydroxyacetone, 1.7 mM ATP and polyphosphate at 45 or 90 mM chains, equivalent to 540 and 1080 mM of transferable phosphate, sampled at 90 and 180 min. The activity of the PPK2 preparation could not be measured in house, because the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP is not read by this assay; combining the Bradford protein with the 2 U/mg reported for this enzyme by the host laboratory [7] places the PPK2 supplied at roughly 2.5 to 9.7 U/mL, the width of the interval reflecting the unreliable Bradford in Table 3. With 0.30 mM NADH in the well and a 1:4 dilution of the aliquot,**the detection ceiling corresponds to 1.2 mM DHAP in the reaction**.

**Round 1 could not answer the question, and the reason lies in the determination rather than in the biology.** Every sample drove the assay to complete consumption of the NADH and every reading matched the single standard that developed, so the values in Table 4 are nearly identical to one another not because the samples contained the same amount of product but because **they all exhausted the same amount of NADH**. A saturated endpoint is a lower bound, and whether that bound answers the question depends on where it sits relative to the threshold the experiment must exceed. With the NADH supplied and the fourfold dilution used, the ceiling fell at 1.2 mM, **below the 1.7 mM ATP**, so saturation established only that DHAP had reached at least 1.2 mM, which the initial ATP alone could have produced. Had the ceiling been placed just above the ATP, as intended, the same readings would have constituted proof of regeneration. What round 1 does establish is that **DHAP is formed in every condition and at both sampling times**, so the coupled system runs.

**Round 2** was run with both enzymes purified, 3 U of DHAK and 0.63 U of PPK2, the same 50 mM dihydroxyacetone and 1.7 mM ATP, and polyphosphate fed in seven additions over the first hour to a final 16.9 mM chains (R1) and 50.4 mM chains (R2), equivalent to 202.8 and 604.8 mM of transferable phosphate. **A much smaller aliquot was taken into each well**, which raised the detection ceiling above the 50 mM that the substrate can yield and kept the determination within the linear range. Samples were taken at 1.5 h. The negative control was the complete reaction mixture assembled without either enzyme, with the polyphosphate present, and it remained flat at ΔA₃₄₀ = 0.019, which the calibration converts to 0.00 mM.
**Round 2 answers the question the module was built around.**

With 1.7 mM ATP supplied, the reaction formed 16.44 and 49.15 mM DHAP at the two polyphosphate feeds, which is 32.9 % and 98.3 % conversion of the dihydroxyacetone and corresponds to the nucleotide pool turning over about 10 and about 29 times. Since **only about 8 % of the phosphate supplied was transferred in either condition**, the donor was never limiting, and what distinguishes the two conditions is the amount of polyphosphate fed rather than the amount of phosphate remaining within the chains. That is what the larger feed changed, carrying the conversion from a third of the substrate to near completion.

The figure of about 29 turnovers should be quoted as **a lower bound on the capacity of the system rather than as a measurement of it**. At 98.3 % conversion the reaction had exhausted its substrate, so the number of cycles was limited by the dihydroxyacetone available and not by the ability of PPK2 to return ADP to ATP.
Three limits are attached to the figures of round 2 and should be read with them.

- **Each condition is a single determination at a single time point**, so the values carry no estimate of their dispersion and no information about the rate at which the conversion was reached.
- **The control that was run omitted both enzymes rather than PPK2 alone.** It contained the complete mixture, polyphosphate included, and stayed flat at ΔA₃₄₀ = 0.019, which establishes that the signal requires the enzymes: no DHAP arises from the reagents themselves, neither by chemical phosphorylation of dihydroxyacetone nor from DHAP already present in any component. That is a necessary control and it is clean. What it cannot do is apportion the product between the two enzymes, since neither was present, so **the regeneration of ATP remains inferred from the stoichiometry of the nucleotide supplied rather than measured against a non-regenerating condition**. The inference is strong, because 49.15 mM of product cannot be obtained from 1.7 mM of nucleotide without recycling, but the direct demonstration is a reaction containing DHAK and no PPK2, which has not yet been run.
- **The activity of PPK2 was not measured in house** but estimated from its protein content and a specific activity taken from the literature [7], so the excess of PPK2 over DHAK was assumed rather than demonstrated.

Stated plainly, what this measurement does and does not do: it establishes that specific preparations of DHAK are catalytically active and quantifies them in absolute units; it establishes that the coupled system forms DHAP far in excess of the ATP supplied and that the conversion scales with the polyphosphate fed; **it does not establish** a turnover number for the system, a rate for the coupled reaction, a measured activity for the regenerating enzyme, or whether the stabilised design would function in a background whose wild type worked.
For a team repeating the measurement, the modifications we would introduce follow from the limits set out above.

1. **Replicate both polyphosphate conditions and resolve the time course.** Sampling the complete reaction and its control at several times with the dilution of round 2 would give the rate of the coupled reaction and attach a dispersion to the conversion.
2. **Run a condition containing DHAK and no PPK2**, alongside the no-enzyme control already in place. Without regeneration, DHAP formation must stop once the initial ATP is spent, so this condition bounds the product at about 1.7 mM and converts the regeneration from an inference into a measurement. It must be read at a dilution at which 1.7 mM DHAP is quantifiable, since the dilution chosen for a 50 mM signal places that value at the floor of the determination.
3. **Measure the activity of PPK2 directly**, with a readout that detects the phosphorylation of ADP rather than the formation of DHAP, so that the regenerating enzyme is quantified rather than estimated.
4. **Calibrate the readout locally.** An NADH standard curve measured on the instrument and in the vessel actually used would make the conversion to absolute units independent of the literature extinction coefficient and of any assumption about the optical path.
5. **Quantify protein by a method that works at these concentrations**, for example absorbance at 280 nm or a Bradford micro-assay with a standard curve covering the lower range, so that the extracts can be reported as specific activities and compared with the purified preparation on the same basis.
The decisions that each of these measurements forced, and the reasoning behind the changes of route they produced, are documented in **Engineering, Iterations 1 to 10**.
fplc: **Fast Protein Liquid Chromatography (FPLC), size exclusion mode**

Fast protein liquid chromatography was introduced by Pharmacia LKB in 1982 to make the resolving power of HPLC packings available for proteins and other biopolymers. It employs stationary phases of small and closely controlled particle diameter, which minimises the theoretical plate height and therefore maximises resolution, while operating them under conditions compatible with biological material: aqueous buffers, moderate back pressures and sample loads considerably higher than those tolerated by conventional HPLC columns [1]. For the purposes of this entry, however, a more elementary property of the technique is the decisive one. **The output of a run is a single trace of absorbance against elution volume, and the selection of fractions must be made from that trace alone, before any other measurement of the sample is available.** The analytical value of the technique is therefore determined by the criteria applied in reading it.

In the size exclusion mode, also termed gel filtration, separation depends exclusively on molecular size. The matrix consists of porous beads, and the mobile phase occupies both the volume external to the beads and the volume within their pores. Molecules too large to enter the pores are eluted first, in the void volume (V₀); molecules small enough to access the entire pore volume are eluted last, at the total volume (Vₜ); and molecules within the fractionation range are eluted at an intermediate volume characteristic of their size [2]. This gives the trace **a fixed coordinate system**, since V₀ and Vₜ are properties of the packed column rather than of the sample and may be determined once with a high molecular mass marker such as Blue Dextran and a small molecule such as vitamin B₁₂ [2].

Whether the material in a peak was in fact separated is then reported by **its shape rather than its height**: a species that partitions ideally leaves the column as a narrow, symmetric band returning to the baseline on both sides, whereas a broad peak, a shoulder without an apex, or two overlapping features indicate several species eluting together or protein retarded by residual charge on the matrix. The principal causes are properties of the run rather than of the protein: an excessive or insufficient flow rate, or a load exceeding 2 to 5 % of the column volume [2,3]. There is one limit on all of this: **the number of peaks is not a measure of the number of species present**. A single pure protein may elute as a double or shouldered peak depending on the resolving power of the resin [5], and several species may elute beneath one feature, recoverable only by deconvolution [3]. A chromatogram assigns material to elution volumes; it does not establish the identity of that material. Identity requires an independent determination on the collected fractions, and the agreement between the two is what demonstrates that the trace has been read correctly [4,5,6].
- Application of the technique to the sample

The sample type in which this problem of interpretation arises most acutely is the clarified extract of a cell culture, in which the protein of interest is accompanied by the entire host proteome and by the whole small molecule content of the cytoplasm. On a size exclusion column such a mixture distributes over the coordinate system described above in a predictable manner: material too large to enter the pores elutes together at V₀, so the magnitude of the void peak is a direct measure of how far the preparation had aggregated before injection; the soluble proteins elute between V₀ and Vₜ, resolved only to the extent that their hydrodynamic sizes differ; and the small molecule fraction elutes at or close to Vₜ, absorbing strongly at 280 nm on account of its nucleotide content [2]. This is what makes the reference volumes indispensable rather than merely convenient here. In a crude extract **the most intense peak of the whole chromatogram is characteristically the one nearest Vₜ, and it is not protein**: a peak of several hundred mAU at or beyond the total volume is small molecule material, while the protein of interest may appear as a few tens of mAU in the central region. Locating each peak relative to V₀ and Vₜ is the only way to tell them apart from the trace alone. The established solution to the limit of the trace is an independent determination on the collected fractions, as in the isolation of extracellular vesicles by size exclusion FPLC, where immunoblots for inclusion and exclusion markers confirmed that the markers partitioned in accordance with the elution volumes [6]; here that determination is enzymatic activity.

The sample analysed is a clarified cell free extract of *Escherichia coli* BL21(DE3) overexpressing DHAK from *Citrobacter freundii* bearing a histidine tag, obtained by enzymatic lysis followed by clarification and applied to the column **in the crude state, without any preceding chromatographic step**. DHAK is a cytoplasmic homodimeric kinase and therefore a soluble globular protein lying well within the fractionation range of a preparative matrix. The column is a Cytiva HiLoad 26/600 Superdex 200 pg, whose stated fractionation range for globular proteins extends from 1 × 10⁴ to 6 × 10⁵ Da [7], and the native mass of the DHAK dimer falls within it. The trace is read against three reference points: a total volume of approximately 320 mL, a void volume of approximately 110 mL, and an interval from approximately 220 to 270 mL within which a peak may correspond to DHAK. **All three are nominal and none was determined experimentally in this series.** The total volume is the geometric bed volume specified by the manufacturer, the void volume is the figure typical of a prepacked column of this matrix, and the interval follows from the fractionation range together with the expected native mass. No calibration run with Blue Dextran, vitamin B₁₂ or protein standards was performed, so the coordinate system is nominal in its entirety and every peak assignment in this entry is indicative rather than established. The limitation is repeated wherever the assignments are used, and the calibration that would remove it is the first of the next steps.
- Application of the technique to the project and expected results

The revalorisation module requires DHAK in a preparation sufficiently clean for kinase activity to be measured without interference, rather than a homogeneous protein. The route applied to both enzymes of the module is immobilised metal affinity chromatography (IMAC) followed by dialysis, and for PPK2 it was successful at the first attempt. For DHAK it left unresolved a question the affinity step cannot answer, since a faint eluate is equally consistent with an enzyme that was never expressed and with an enzyme lost on the resin. Size exclusion chromatography was therefore adopted as an alternative route, used in place of IMAC and dialysis rather than after them; the reasons for the change are set out in Engineering. The grounds follow from the mechanism: separation depends on hydrodynamic size, a property the folded enzyme possesses irrespective of the state of its tag, and the procedure involves neither a metal charged resin nor imidazole elution, so the enzyme is at no point exposed to either and is eluted directly in the running buffer, removing the need for dialysis before the activity assays [1,2]. Ion exchange FPLC was not adopted, since it separates according to surface charge and would have required scouting buffers, pH values and gradients before a single informative run could be obtained [1,4].
The measurement reported here is consequently not confined to the purification.
**Its object is the decision rule itself: given a single UV trace, which fractions merit assay, and on what grounds.**
Three criteria were established in advance, each of which may fail independently of the others.

1. **Position.** Every peak is located relative to the nominal V₀ (~110 mL) and Vₜ (~320 mL), and only a peak lying within 220 to 270 mL is admitted as a candidate for DHAK. Intensity is not a criterion, since in a crude extract the most intense peak is expected near Vₜ and is expected to be small molecule material.
2. **Shape.** A candidate peak is accepted as resolved only if it is narrow and symmetric and returns to the baseline on both sides. A shoulder without a defined apex, a broad feature, or overlap with an adjacent peak indicates that the corresponding fractions cannot be assumed homogeneous [2].
3. **Agreement with an independent determination.** The collected fractions are assayed by the coupled α-GDH/TIM method, which follows the formation of DHAP as a decrease in A₃₄₀. If the trace is being read correctly, activity must be detected in fractions taken from the protein region and must be absent from fractions taken at or beyond Vₜ [4,6].

The result expected of each run was a chromatogram with a small void peak, a narrow symmetric peak inside the DHAK interval and a late peak near Vₜ. The result expected of the series was that criteria 1 and 2 would predict criterion 3. It is that correspondence, rather than the purification itself, that would establish the method as transferable to other teams: if it holds, the trace may be used to select fractions before assay time is committed to them; if it fails, either the criteria are wrong or the enzyme does not survive the separation, and the activity data are what discriminate between the two.
**Technique requirements**

Two operational points belong with the parameters above, since both cost us runs. The instrument initiates every run in **pause mode**, so the pause must be released after each start, and trapped air produces a noisy baseline and pressure irregularities, so the system is **purged whenever the mobile phase is connected or disconnected** when the buffer is connected for the overnight equilibration.
- **Sample preparation**
The sample is a clarified cell free extract of *E. coli* BL21(DE3) overexpressing His-tagged DHAK from *C. freundii*.
**1. Lysis and clarification**

Cells were harvested by centrifugation and resuspended in lysis buffer, the volume scaled to the wet biomass so that every preparation entered lysis at a comparable cell density.
Lysis was enzymatic. This route avoids the local heating and shear of sonication, which matters in a preparation destined for immediate assay of a kinase. The lysate cleared on its own, so neither sonication nor streptomycin sulfate precipitation was needed. The extract was then clarified by centrifugation and kept on ice.
**2. Three measures that the reading criteria require**
Each of these follows from how the chromatogram will be read, not from any property of the enzyme.

- **Filter immediately before injection.** Particulate matter accumulates at the top of the bed and impairs partitioning, and peak shape is uninterpretable without this step [2].
- **Keep the load within the column specification.** Resolution depends on the sample reaching the bed as a narrow band, and an overloaded column broadens every peak. Where necessary the extract was concentrated by ultrafiltration rather than injected as a large dilute volume [2,6].
- **Use the running buffer as the sample buffer.** Any mismatch between the two disturbs the baseline against which peak shape is judged [1].
**3. Injection**
Manual, through the valve and its loop. Immediately beforehand:

The sample is then drawn into a syringe free of air, loaded with the valve in the **load** position, and the valve switched to **inject**, at which point the running buffer carries the sample from the loop onto the column and the software marks the injection point on the chromatogram.
- Results

Four separations were performed on the same column and buffer, reported as runs 1 to 4 in the order carried out. For each one the three criteria were applied to the trace **before** the fractions were assayed, and the activity measured afterwards is what tests the reading. The reference volumes are the nominal V₀ (~110 mL) and Vₜ (~320 mL), with the DHAK window at 220–270 mL; **none of the three was measured on this column**, so every peak assignment below is indicative. The load was not recorded run by run, so the series contains no replicate in the strict sense: what is replicated across runs is the reading, not the separation. Table 1 is placed before the figures so that the peak positions are available while the traces are examined.
The full chromatograms, the fraction records and the activity traces are available on the project results page: Revalorisation, Results.
**Run 1 — an empty window, and no usable fractions**

The trace stays below 7.5 mAU throughout, so very little left the column at all, and the collected region contains no resolved feature [2]. The reading predicted that nothing usable would be recovered, and the three fractions assayed bore it out: fraction 27 gave **−8.40 mOD/min** with an acceptable R² of 0.957, but a rate two orders of magnitude below the extract applied; fractions 46 and 56 gave −1.51 (R² = 0.571) and −0.16 (R² = 0.035), both fits to noise rather than to a descending signal.
**Run 2 — the positive case, and the run that validates the reading**

This is the only run with appreciable absorbance in the protein region. **Position** excluded the two dominant peaks without any further measurement: at 288 and 330 mL they lie at and beyond Vₜ, where small molecules that fully penetrate the matrix elute, and no retained species can appear past the total volume [2]. The small void peak indicates that little of the sample had aggregated. Activity was then found **in the protein region and nowhere else**: fraction 46 gave **−42.91 mOD/min** (R² = 0.998), the steepest and cleanest trace of any size-exclusion fraction in the study, fraction 27 gave −16.64 (R² = 0.989), and fraction 56, taken from beyond Vₜ, was flat at −0.16 (R² = 0.035).

The distribution matters as much as the rates, since it is exactly what is expected if the enzyme elutes where size exclusion predicts and the late peak is small molecule material. This is the scheme of validation applied to vesicle isolation by immunoblot [6], with catalytic activity as the independent determination here. Recovery was nonetheless modest: the extract applied gave −**581.1 mOD/min** from 5 µL, so even the best fraction accounts for a small proportion of the activity loaded.
**Run 3 — the best separation of the series, lost to the collector**

Under criteria 1 and 2 this is the best result of the series, and it yielded no data at all. The failure is instructive rather than merely unfortunate, since it follows from the collection strategy adopted: collection was begun 15 to 20 min before the **expected** elution of the enzyme, which is the economical option but presupposes that the elution volume is known, and the interval used was the nominal one taken from the matrix specification. **An uncalibrated interval does not support a timed start.** The delay between detector and collector must be determined before the run rather than assumed [2]: a trace that can be read correctly is of no value if the fractions do not correspond to it.
**Run 4 — an intense peak that shape reject**

The candidate at 261 mL sits correctly inside the window, but it is broad and its trailing edge overlaps the considerably larger peak behind it, so the fractions taken between them contain both species. The fraction assayed gave **−11.12 mOD/min** with R² = 0.566: a slope that is not small in magnitude but that cannot be interpreted as a rate. Here **the predictive variable was the shape of the feature and not its absorbance**. The void peak is considerably larger than in run 2, indicating that more of this sample had aggregated before injection.
The activity traces themselves are on the Results page; Table 2 contains the rates and the R² values on which the analysis depends.
**What the series establishes**
The criteria held in all four runs, and it is this correspondence that we would offer to other teams as the transferable result of the work.

- **Position** excluded the most intense peaks of the series without a single assay, and fraction 56 of runs 1 and 2 confirmed it, giving −0.16 mOD/min with R² = 0.035 in both cases. That these volumes are nominal rather than measured does not weaken this particular inference, since the peaks concerned lie at or beyond the total volume by a margin far larger than the uncertainty of a bed volume taken from the geometry of the column; what it does weaken is the assignment of the 220 to 270 mL interval.
- **Shape** predicted which fractions merited assay independently of intensity, rejecting the faint shoulders of run 1 and the intense but overlapping peak of run 4.
- **Agreement with the activity read-out** held where it could be tested: the one run with a defined feature in the protein region gave the only two active fractions of the study, there and nowhere else.

The criterion is conservative in one direction only. A broad or shouldered feature establishes that the fractions cannot be assumed homogeneous, but it establishes nothing about the number of species present, since a single pure protein may itself elute as a shouldered peak under conditions that do not resolve its forms [5], and the profiles of species that do co-elute are recoverable only by deconvolution [3].

It is worth separating two things the word *validation* covers, because this entry does one and not the other. Calibrating the column with mass standards validates **the axis**: it converts an elution volume into a molecular mass. Assaying the collected fractions validates **the inference**: it tests whether the material assigned to a position is in fact what the assignment claims. This series validates the inference and does not calibrate the axis. The criteria were stated before the fractions were measured and the activity agreed with them in every run, which is the stronger of the two tests, since a calibrated axis with no determination on the fractions would establish where a protein of that mass should elute without establishing that the protein eluting there was the enzyme. The axis nevertheless remains uncalibrated, and that is the first item below.

**Against the expected outcome, the separation itself did not reproduce**, and this is the informative part of the result. Two of the eight purified preparations assayed across both routes were active, and both came from a single run. In the three runs with appreciable absorbance most of the signal elutes at or beyond Vₜ, the profile of a crude extract dominated by nucleotides and metabolites and consistent with the application of an unfractionated lysate. What the chromatograms demonstrate is a separation that did not reproduce rather than an enzyme that was absent, and the activity data settle that question, since the enzyme was strongly active in the extract and in the fractions of run 2. Returning to IMAC with the same active stock gave −1.41 mOD/min (R² = 0.928), so the difficulty is attributable not to either method in particular but to the survival of this enzyme through purification. The decision to abandon the route is set out in Engineering, Iteration 7.
For a team repeating the measurement, the modifications we would introduce follow from the criteria that failed.

1. **Calibrate the column.** A single run with Blue Dextran, vitamin B₁₂ and protein standards spanning the fractionation range would convert V₀, Vₜ and the DHAK interval from nominal figures into measured values, which is what would make the assignments of Table 1 defensible rather than indicative [1,2].
2. **Fix the load.** Inject a smaller, more concentrated volume well within the 13 mL recommended for this 320 mL column, since a load above 2 to 5 % of the column volume broadens every band and is a plausible cause of the broad features in runs 2 and 4 [2].
3. **Maintain and verify the flow rate between runs.** Partitioning is continuous, so resolution deteriorates if the flow rate drifts in either direction, and deviations of this order measurably alter peak shape and retention [3].
4. **Reduce the small molecule background.** Desalting or a partial purification before the column would prevent the nucleotide peak near Vₜ from dominating the trace, and this is in any case the condition under which FPLC separations are normally performed [1].
5. **Set the collector against the measured delay** between detector and collector before starting, and verify the first fraction against the trace.

One objection should be met directly: a method for reading chromatograms is here supported by a series in which the separation seldom worked — one run almost empty, one broad and unresolved, one lost to a mistimed collector and one overlapping much larger material. That is precisely what makes the series informative.

**A decision rule is tested by whether it predicts the outcome of the measurement, not by whether the measurement succeeds**, and in all four runs it did. A series of four clean separations would have confirmed the criteria far more weakly, since nothing in it would have been at risk of failing.

alginate encapsulation: Efficient bacterial encapsulation was essential to develop a biological module that combines biosafety and structural stability. Rather than relying on a single optimisation step, the encapsulation strategy was developed through a sequential experimental workflow in which the outcome of each stage guided the design of the next.

Upon contact with calcium ions, alginate rapidly forms a hydrogel through ionic crosslinking between its polymer chains according to the well-established egg-box model [1]. The relative proportion of α-L-guluronic acid (G) and β-D-mannuronic acid (M) residues strongly influences the mechanical properties of the resulting gel [2]. This property enables the formation of alginate beads by dripping an alginate solution into a calcium chloride bath under mild conditions, making alginate one of the most widely used materials for bacterial encapsulation [2-4]. However, obtaining beads with consistent size, shape and mechanical integrity requires careful optimisation of several synthesis parameters, including alginate concentration, drop height, flow rate and crosslinking time.

Building upon this optimised bead protocol, the system was then translated into a more advanced core-shell architecture, in which a liquid calcium chloride core is surrounded by an alginate shell [3,4]. Unlike conventional beads, core-shell capsule formation depends on the simultaneous control of two coaxial flows, making additional optimisation necessary. Parameters such as the concentrations of the inner calcium chloride and outer alginate solutions, the outer-to-inner flow-rate ratio, storage conditions and mechanical resistance were therefore systematically evaluated to obtain stable, reproducible capsules suitable for wastewater treatment.

Unless otherwise stated, all encapsulation experiments were performed using sodium alginate from brown algae (Sigma-Aldrich, A1112; lot 081M1381V), anhydrous calcium chloride (96%, extra pure, Acros Organics, 349615000; lot A0358796) and distilled water. Solutions were prepared immediately before use and delivered using programmable infusion pumps (KDS 200 dual-syringe pump, KD Scientific, and Fisherbrand KDS 100 single-syringe pump, Fisher Scientific) through plastic syringes (10 mL), connected via standard Luer connectors and flexible tubing to the dispensing outlet. Bead production used a single infusion pump, while core-shell production used both pumps and a coaxial injector (DMF-C01, Doxa Microfluidics; inner needle: 22G, 0.7 mm OD / 0.4 mm ID; outer needle: 17G, 1.4 mm OD / 1.1 mm ID). Capsule formation was carried out by dripping into a calcium chloride crosslinking bath under ambient laboratory conditions. When a parameter was investigated, all remaining synthesis conditions were kept constant unless explicitly indicated.

Together, these experiments provided the experimental evidence required to develop an encapsulation platform suitable for the safe immobilisation of engineered bacteria and its integration into the rePhlow bioreactor.
revalorisation: This set of experiments is the **conversion module** of rePhlow’s multi-enzymatic system for turning waste into high-value products (see Project Description). It couples two enzymes. **DHAK** (dihydroxyacetone kinase from *Citrobacter freundii*) phosphorylates dihydroxyacetone to **dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP)**, an unstable and expensive building block for the DHAP-dependent aldolases used to make rare sugars and iminosugars [1, 2]. **PPK2** draws energy from polyphosphate to **regenerate ATP** from a small recycled nucleotide pool instead of a costly stoichiometric supply of cofactor, and clears the ADP that inhibits DHAK as it forms. We use a bifunctional **BcPPK2-III** from *Burkholderia cenocepacia*, which carries AMP through to ATP in a single enzyme and stays active across pH 6 to 9 [3], the range a scalable cascade needs.

In the complete design, the phosphate stored inside the *Pseudomonas putida* beads is released by lysing the recovered beads, giving the inorganic polyphosphate that feeds this module. For the experiments we **decoupled the block from bead recovery**, which depends on the upstream hardware, and used commercial polyphosphate instead, so that the biochemistry of the conversion could be characterised on its own terms; substituting bead-derived polyP is a later integration step.

Obtaining a working module required two enzymes that are active, pure enough to be measured without interference, and able to sustain each other’s reaction. Rather than optimising a single step, the module was built through a **sequential experimental workflow** in which each stage produces the material and the information the next one needs: a gene designed *in silico* becomes a protein, the protein is purified, and only then can its activity, and that of the coupled pair, be measured. Most of the wet-lab route is shared between the two enzymes, which are transformed, induced, harvested and lysed through the same procedure; the differences appear where the two proteins behave differently, and the problems that caused them are developed in Engineering.

Unless otherwise stated, both enzymes were expressed in *E. coli* BL21(DE3) from genes supplied in a **pET-28a(+)** vector, codon-optimised for *E. coli*, grown in LB medium with kanamycin at 50 µg/mL and induced with IPTG. Purification used **Co²⁺-IDA-agarose** resin in disposable SPE cartridges, with all buffers prepared in ultrapure water (Milli-Q) immediately before use and filtered before application. Activity assays used α-glycerophosphate dehydrogenase and triosephosphate isomerase as coupling enzymes, read as the fall in absorbance at 340 nm and converted with the NADH extinction coefficient, **ε₃₄₀ = 6220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹**. Format was chosen by convenience rather than by assay, with the continuous DHAK assay run mostly in **1 cm cuvettes** and occasionally in microplate, and the endpoint coupled assay in **microplate** throughout, so the path length of the format used is applied in every conversion. Throughout this module, **one unit (U) is the amount of enzyme forming one µmol of product per minute** under the assay conditions, DHAP for DHAK and ATP for PPK2. The expected masses on a denaturing gel are **about 60 kDa for the DHAK subunit**, a protein of around 556 residues that is native as a **homodimer of about 118 kDa**, and **about 33 kDa for PPK2**, whose theoretical mass is 32 kDa, both including the roughly 1 kDa added by the hexahistidine tag. The polyphosphate used is a commercial sodium polyphosphate with a chain length of **12 phosphate units**, and all polyphosphate concentrations in this module are given as **millimolar chains**, so one millimolar supplies **12 mM of transferable phosphate**. That distinction matters because the reaction consumes phosphate residues rather than whole chains, and PPK2 can draw repeatedly on the same chain.

Together, these experiments provide the evidence required to show that the conversion module produces DHAP and that its ATP can be regenerated from polyphosphate, the step that makes the process viable for integration into the rePhlow system.

alginate encapsulation: This section builds the encapsulation platform of the rePhlow sphere: the raw alginate is characterised, a reproducible bead protocol is established, the system is translated into a core-shell architecture and validated against the chemical, physical and mechanical demands of the bioreactor, and the final platform is characterised structurally. This page reports the outcomes; the design and rationale of each experiment are on the Experiments page (see Experiments).
Each entry below reports the outcome of the corresponding experiment on the Experiments page, following the same order and titles.

Bead and capsule morphology is reported through two measurements. Size is given as the equivalent diameter, Deq = 2√(A/π), the diameter of a circle with the same projected area. Shape is given as the aspect ratio of the fitted ellipse, s = minor axis / major axis, referred to throughout as sphericity; it equals 1 for a perfect circle and falls as the object becomes elongated. Where capsules are compared under load, sphericity is expressed as a fraction of each condition's own unloaded value, since capsules do not all start out equally spherical and an absolute comparison would confound resistance to compression with initial shape.

enzymatic immobilisation::section 1 enzy: In this block we build and validate the enzymatic toolbox: we identify candidate phosphohydrolases by data mining, express them heterologously in *E. coli*, purify them by immobilised metal-ion affinity chromatography (IMAC) and characterise their activity under the operating conditions of the reactor (pH 5.0, 30 ºC).

Because heterologous expression carries inherent risks (insoluble aggregates, proteolysis, loss of active conformation), a parallel search for **commercial homologues** was kept for each activity as a contingency plan. The workflow runs from database mining, through in-silico construct design and cloning, to expression, solubilisation, purification and functional characterisation, aiming to reach **soluble, active and characterised enzymes with the fewest possible steps**.
enzymatic immobilisation::section 2 immo: In this block we establish **how to fix the enzymes onto the support** while keeping them active. Rather than testing directly on the more complex and costly alginate-chitosan-genipin sphere, the chemistry is first optimised on a simple, well-characterised **MANAE-agarose** model support, and the more reactive genipin of the final sphere is emulated by **glutaraldehyde**, which plays the same crosslinking role.

The model enzyme is **Lecitase Ultra**, chosen because it is the most demanding case: its active site is capped by a mobile lid that requires **interfacial activation**, and it forms **bimolecular aggregates** in solution. Mastering its immobilisation without losing activity is a strong indication that the more hydrophilic, structurally simpler enzymes of the panel can be accommodated afterwards. Two covalent strategies are compared, with and without detergent, and the results are rationalised by in-silico modelling of the enzyme's open and closed conformations.
genetic engineering::intro abstract: **RePhlow** aims to turn *Pseudomonas putida* KT2440, a robust, safe and very well-characterised chassis, into a **phosphorus-accumulating organism (PAO)**: a bacterium that captures phosphate from water and stores it internally as **polyphosphate (polyP)** granules. To do this we take inspiration from natural PAOs, above all *Candidatus* Accumulibacter phosphatis, the organism behind enhanced biological phosphorus removal in wastewater-treatment plants.
genetic engineering::section 0 polyphosp: This set of experiments establishes, in **wild-type P. putida KT2440** [1], how much phosphorus the **cells take up and store as polyphosphate, how fast, and under which operating condition**s this is maximised. Because the engineered strains will later be judged by exactly this read-out, the experiments first build and standardise a reproducible intracellular-phosphorus assay, then use it to **characterise growth, the kinetics of accumulation across media, and the two operating variables available in the real feed**. Two variants were used: t**he wild type (WT) and an mCherry-tagged variant (Cherry)** for growth tracking. The application target is a synthetic aqueous stream mimicking the phosphorus-rich effluent of biofuel production, the context in which polyphosphate-based phosphorus recovery would operate [2], [3].
genetic engineering::section 1 cloning: The goal of this set of experiments is a *P. putida* strain that stably expresses **ppk1** and **pstSCAB** from *Candidatus* Accumulibacter phosphatis. Because *P. putida* is far less amenable to routine cloning than *Escherichia coli* [1], [2], each plasmid is built and verified in an *E. coli* cloning host and only then moved into the final chassis. This keeps the iterative cloning steps in the fastest, most transformable host and reserves the slower work with *P. putida* for constructs we already trust.
genetic engineering::section 2 knocking: The goal of this set of experiments is to remove, in the same strain, three native activities that oppose accumulation: **ppx** (degrades polyphosphate), **ppkB** / **ppk2** (consumes polyphosphate to phosphorylate nucleotides) and **pitB** (low-affinity phosphate transport implicated in efflux). They are inactivated by **CRISPR base editing** [6], [7], [8] rather than by conventional Cas9 cutting, because a double-strand break in *P. putida* is problematic: the organism has limited non-homologous end joining, so cuts are repaired poorly and are often lethal, and scarless deletion would otherwise require a homology-directed repair template. A cytidine base editor sidesteps this, introducing a premature stop codon by chemistry alone, an approach already validated for gene inactivation in *P. putida* KT2440 [8].

We use the **pMBEC2** base editor [9], which fuses a cytidine deaminase, a Cas9 nickase and a uracil glycosylase inhibitor, and carries a constitutively expressed **msfGFP** cassette flanked by **BsaI** sites in place of the guide. The guide RNA is installed by **Golden Gate assembly** [9], [10], replacing the msfGFP marker, so that correct constructs can be picked by **loss of green fluorescence**.
