revalorisation::harvest: The induced cultures were transferred to pre-weighed 50 mL Falcon tubes and centrifuged at **6000 ×g, 10 °C, for 10 to 15 minutes**. The spent medium was discarded, the pellets were drained by inversion and weighed, and were then frozen at **−80 °C** until lysis. Freezing both stores the biomass conveniently and begins to weaken the cells, which assists the enzymatic lysis that follows. **The insoluble pellets were kept at −20 °C** after clarification, so that protein trapped in inclusion bodies could later be told apart from protein never made.
revalorisation::enzymatic lysis: The frozen pellets were resuspended in **50 mM potassium phosphate buffer (KH₂PO₄), pH 7.5**, with the buffer volume scaled to the pellet, **3.5 to 4 mL per tube**, so that all extracts entered lysis at a comparable cell density, and lysed enzymatically. Three reagents were added to each resuspension. **Lysozyme** at a final concentration of 0.5 mg/mL digests the peptidoglycan cell wall. **DNase I** at 10 µg/mL degrades the genomic DNA that would otherwise make the lysate viscous and hard to handle. **MgCl₂** at 2 mM supplies the magnesium that DNase I needs as a cofactor. The suspension was agitated at room temperature, 140 rpm, for 30 minutes, after which it visibly cleared. This lysozyme-based approach follows the method used for this enzyme by Bastida et al. [8].
revalorisation::clarification: The lysate was centrifuged (8500 rpm, 10 °C, 10 min) and the **supernatant was retained as the cell-free extract**. The soluble enzyme stays in the supernatant, while cell debris, membranes and any insoluble misfolded protein are discarded in the pellet.

**What we did not do.** Some reference protocols for this enzyme add two further steps, mechanical disruption by sonication and removal of nucleic acids by streptomycin-sulfate precipitation. Neither was used here. The clarified extract came out clear and only slightly turbid, so the streptomycin-sulfate step to precipitate DNA fragments was judged unnecessary, and enzymatic lysis with lysozyme plus DNase gave a workable soluble extract without sonication. These steps are noted only so our procedure is not confused with the fuller protocols in the source material.

enzymatic immobilisation::enzyme product: This block builds and validates the enzymatic toolbox. The phosphorus in the degumming effluent is not a single compound but a mixture of phospholipids, phytate and phosphomonoesters, so no single enzyme can mineralise it.

The block therefore has to deliver a small panel of complementary phosphohydrolases that are both expressible in *E. coli* and active in acid, and it has to do so without wasting effort on enzymes that cannot be made.

The thread that runs through it is the gap between making a protein and making a protein that folds: the first wet-lab steps go smoothly, the expression step then separates yield from solubility, and everything after it is a response to that split. Because heterologous expression carries inherent risks, a commercial homologue was kept in reserve for every activity.
enzymatic immobilisation::immobilisation: This block establishes how to fix an enzyme onto the support while keeping it active. Rather than testing on the complex and costly alginate-chitosan-genipin sphere, the chemistry is worked out on a simple, well-characterised **MANAE-agarose** model, with **glutaraldehyde** standing in for the amino-crosslinking role that genipin plays on the final sphere.

The model enzyme is **Lecitase Ultra**, chosen as the most demanding case: its active site is capped by a mobile lid that opens only on interfacial activation, and it forms bimolecular aggregates in solution, so a chemistry that preserves its activity should generalise to the simpler, more hydrophilic enzymes of the panel.

The block runs as one argument: a baseline is fixed, two anchoring strategies are compared, the detergent that separates them is identified, and the structural modelling then explains why the winner wins.
genetic engineering::section 0 polyphosp: The kinetics and yield of polyphosphate accumulation in wild-type *P. putida* KT2440 set the baseline that the engineered strains will later be measured against, so this is where the assay is standardised and the operating window established. The intracellular-phosphorus assay is first made reproducible; growth in the reference minimal medium is characterised; and the kinetics of accumulation are then compared across media and, finally, across pH and dilution in the synthetic stream, providing the operating conditions the rest of the project builds on.
genetic engineering::section 1 cloning: Building a *P. putida* strain that stably expresses *ppk1* and *pstSCAB* meant first building and verifying each construct in the faster, more transformable *E. coli* cloning host, and only then moving trusted constructs into the final chassis.
genetic engineering::section 2 knocking: Removing *ppx*, *ppkB*/*ppk2* and *pitB* in the same strain meant installing three markerless edits sequentially by CRISPR base editing, verifying each one before moving to the next.
revalorisation::conclusion: The activity work delivered an **active DHAK preparation** and a **coupled DHAK-PPK2 system that recycles its ATP pool**.

The working enzyme was the **CECT 4626 variant, 2012 stock**, reaching **~10 U/mg** as a purified preparation, close to the **10.7 U/mg reported for the fully purified enzyme** [10]. The **DSM 30040 reference** was too weakly active to serve as a control, which is what removed the comparison the module had been built around. Of the two PROSS-stabilised variants, **design 5 lost all measurable activity**, and the more conservative **design 1 was expressed but not assayed**, since it arrived too late in the season for the activity measurement. No conclusion is drawn here about whether PROSS stabilisation of this enzyme works.

The decisive test coupled **purified DHAK to purified PPK2** with polyphosphate as the phosphoryl donor. A first round on cell-free extract saturated the endpoint determination, so DHAP could only be bounded below rather than measured. The assay was redesigned with a smaller aliquot per well and repeated with both enzymes purified. With **1.7 mM ATP supplied**, the reaction formed **16.44 and 49.15 mM DHAP** at the two polyphosphate feeds, which corresponds to the nucleotide pool turning over about **10 and 29 times**.

**Two limits qualify this.** The determination was run **once per condition at a single time point**, with no replicates and no uncertainty attached to the figures. And the experiment **carries no condition lacking PPK2**, so the ATP recycling is inferred from the stoichiometry of the nucleotide supplied rather than measured against a non-regenerating control. Both are the first things a future round should close.

Within those limits, the **module works as designed**. **DHAK phosphorylates dihydroxyacetone, PPK2 rebuilds the ATP it spends from polyphosphate**, and conversion scales with the polyphosphate supplied.

alginate encapsulation: A key element of the rePhlow approach is the design and optimization of our alginate core-shell structures, which encapsulate phosphate-accumulating bacteria (PAOs) and are functionalized on their surface with phosphatase enzymes to accelerate phosphate uptake. These core-shells must meet several critical requirements: they need to be mechanically robust to withstand the treatment process, allow the diffusion of phosphate so that it can enter the core for absorption, and retain the bacteria securely without leakage.

We have carefully measured and adjusted their physical and chemical properties, tailoring composition and structure to balance protection, permeability, and functionality. This systematic characterization ensures that our bacteria remain active and effective, linking material design directly to efficient phosphate removal and resource recovery.
enzymatic immobilisation: Much of the phosphorus in the Bio-Oils effluent is not free phosphate but bound in organic molecules the bacteria cannot take up. Immobilising phosphatases on the outside of the alginate core-shells puts the enzymes that release it directly on the surface the water meets first, so phosphate is generated where it is about to be consumed. For that to work the enzyme has to be the most efficient candidate available under the acidic conditions of the effluent, and it has to keep working once it is fixed to a solid. The capsule provides the surface; this block decides which enzyme deserves it and how it should be attached.

Both questions are measurement problems, and neither is answered by looking at the solid. An enzyme bound to a support cannot be weighed out of the reaction or pipetted into a cuvette, so the quantity that matters, how much catalytic activity has become attached and how much is still loose in solution, is never observed directly. It has to be inferred from what the liquid phase is doing over time, which is only as sound as the controls behind the inference.

The second problem is that raw activity is an unreliable guide to which enzyme or which chemistry is better. Two preparations releasing the same amount of product are not equivalent if one of them is carrying twice as much protein, and in our panel that distinction reversed the ranking rather than merely shifting it. So the characterisation of this block rests on a pairing: every activity measurement is matched to a protein quantification, and conclusions are drawn only from the mass-normalised figure. The three techniques behind the buttons below are that pairing, plus the time-resolved version of it used to follow an immobilisation as it happens.
genetic engineering: The whole of rePhlow rests on one biological claim: that our engineered *Pseudomonas putida* pulls more phosphorus out of the effluent, and holds on to it, than the strain we started from. Everything else in the project is built around that claim. The capsules exist to contain and recover these cells, the hardware exists to circulate them, and the revalorisation module exists to spend the phosphorus they have stored. A genetic design that reads well on paper settles none of it.

What makes this hard to measure is that the phosphorus of interest is inside the cells, in a medium that is itself rich in phosphate. The signal we want and the background we must exclude are the same chemical species, so the measurement is only as good as the separation between the cells and the liquid they came from. Nor is the polymer we care about directly detectable: polyphosphate has to be broken down to orthophosphate before any colour chemistry can see it, which means the number reported is always one hydrolysis step removed from the molecule being claimed.

The assay behind the button below is built around those two constraints. It washes the extracellular phosphate away before lysis, releases the stored polymer by hot acid, quantifies the resulting orthophosphate against a calibration series, and normalises the result to biomass so that two strains can be compared on equal terms rather than on how many cells happened to be in the tube.
revalorisation: The revalorisation module converts the phosphorus recovered upstream into a defined phosphorylated product, and it does so entirely in vitro, with purified enzymes rather than living cells. Its central claim is that ATP regenerated from polyphosphate can drive a useful phosphorylation reaction, which means the module stands or falls on whether its components can be characterised reliably, and whether the activity observed for one enzyme translates into measurable product formation when it is coupled to another. Nothing about the sequences, the structures or the designs settles that. Only experimental evidence does.

The measurements we needed had to assess enzyme activity, evaluate the outcome of purification strategies and report the product of a kinase, which carries no colour and no absorbance of its own, in real time and in absolute units. We therefore built the module's characterisation around complementary approaches, combining protein purification with an enzyme-coupled spectrophotometric assay applied to individual enzyme preparations and to the coupled reaction. The assay was calibrated using a physical constant rather than an internal standard of our own, allowing the measurements to be interpreted on a defined scale. The techniques are described in full in the sections below, including the conditions and parameters another team would have to match to reproduce or adapt them.

alginate encapsulation: The characterisation runs in the order the decisions had to be made. Infrared spectroscopy came first, on the raw powder, because the mechanical behaviour of any calcium alginate gel depends on the composition of the alginate it was made from, and that varies by batch and supplier, so treating "alginate" as a known quantity would have put an unmeasured variable underneath every later result. Image analysis then carried the production work: the size and shape of beads and capsules under each set of conditions, the shell thickness in cross-section, and the deformation of individual capsules under increasing load. Thermal analysis established how much of a capsule is water and how stable the material is on heating. Electron microscopy and elemental analysis described the surface and confirmed that the polymer really is crosslinked calcium alginate rather than alginate that merely met a calcium solution. Ultraviolet-visible spectroscopy, finally, tested containment directly, by looking for the core in the liquid outside the capsule.

Two of these measurements only became possible after a change to the sample rather than to the instrument, and both are worth more than the numbers they produced. The shell could not be told from the core in an optical image at all until magnetite was incorporated into the alginate phase, which made the boundary visible and turned shell thickness into a measurable quantity. And a dried capsule is not a smaller version of a hydrated one, so the electron micrographs describe a collapsed structure, which is why the porosity visible in them is explicitly not used to say anything about permeability. Knowing which of our images describe the working material and which describe an artefact of preparation is part of the result.

The techniques also check each other, and that is the main reason there are five of them. The water content from thermal analysis, around 95% by mass, agrees with the volume loss measured optically on drying. And where one measurement could not answer its question, another was built to answer it instead: shell thickness turned out to vary more within a single capsule than between formulations, so the comparison that mattered was moved to the mechanical assay, which measures how the capsules deform rather than how round they are. Each technique page reports the parameters another team would need to repeat it, the controls and calibrations behind each number, and the point at which its own dispersion makes it stop discriminating.
enzymatic immobilisation: Three measurements carry this block, and they are layered rather than independent. A dye-binding protein assay gives the mass of biocatalyst in every reaction, calibrated each session against a standard series rather than assumed from a stock label. A chromogenic activity assay gives the rate at which an enzyme releases product, read as the appearance of p-nitrophenol and converted to absolute concentration through a known extinction coefficient and the actual optical path, which in a microplate is set by the fill volume and not by the cuvette convention of 1 cm. Dividing the second by the first gives specific activity, the only figure on which enzymes or supports are compared here.

The immobilisation measurement itself is differential, and this is the part that needed the most care. At each time point the whole suspension reports the activity of free plus bound enzyme, while the clarified supernatant reports only what remains free; the difference is the immobilised activity and its ratio to the total is the yield. That subtraction can go wrong in two directions, so both are controlled. Residual support particles scatter light and would inflate the apparent activity of the supernatant, so the sedimentation step is specified and the supernatant is required to be optically clear, while the same step must not carry down free enzyme with the beads. And an enzyme losing activity by denaturation rather than by binding would look identical to one being immobilised, which is why a support-free incubation runs alongside to confirm the enzyme is stable over the measurement window.

The technique pages give the parameters that change the answer rather than a general description: buffer and pH, reaction temperature, wavelength and why that wavelength was chosen, the extinction coefficient and path length used for the conversion, the quench and its timing for the discontinuous format, the sedimentation conditions, the number of replicates, and the dilution range inside which the protein assay stays linear. They also state the known weaknesses, namely that dye-binding quantification is intrinsically non-linear and sensitive to buffer composition, which is why standards and samples share a buffer and why the dilution with the lowest replicate error is the one carried forward. For another team, the transferable part is not our particular enzyme but the differential scheme: free versus total activity against time, with a scattering control and a support-free control, is how any immobilisation on a particulate support can be quantified without ever measuring the solid.
genetic engineering: Most of the work behind this block is construction and verification, and it is reported in Experiments and Results. The measurement that belongs here is the one that turns the engineered strain from a sequence into a phenotype: an intracellular polyphosphate uptake assay, run across a time-course rather than at a single point, because what distinguishes the two strains is a rate. Cells are primed by a phosphate starvation step, which de-represses the phosphate regulon and makes them take up phosphate avidly once it is offered, then resuspended in the operation medium at a defined optical density and sampled every fifteen minutes for two hours. Each sample is split: one aliquot gives the biomass, the other gives the phosphorus.

Three features of the protocol are what make the result interpretable, and each one exists to close a specific way of being wrong. The triple saline wash before lysis removes the phosphate-rich medium, without which extracellular phosphate would be counted as intracellular and every value would be inflated. The optical density measured on a parallel aliquot at every time point allows the phosphorus to be expressed per unit of biomass, which separates genuine accumulation from the appearance of accumulation caused by cells dividing. And the phosphate calibration series, run in duplicate alongside the samples, converts absorbance into absolute mass rather than into a relative signal, so the figures are comparable to those of any other laboratory using the same chemistry.

That technique page reports the parameters another team would need rather than a narrative of the afternoon: the growth and starvation conditions, the starting density, the sampling interval, the wash and centrifugation steps, the acid concentration, the hydrolysis time and temperature, the neutralisation, the dilution applied before colour development, the development time and the wavelength. It is also explicit about where the measurement is weak. The per-time-point values scatter, so the comparison between strains is taken from the slope over the linear uptake window rather than from any single point, and the most likely source of that scatter is incomplete removal of the external medium, which is why the next iteration of the protocol tightens the wash rather than adding more time points. The approach generalises directly to any team quantifying intracellular polyphosphate in whole cells, and the part worth borrowing is less the colour chemistry, which is standard, than the pairing of a biomass normalisation with a wash step aggressive enough to make the word "intracellular" mean something.
revalorisation: The module's characterisation combines protein purification and enzymatic measurements, with the coupled α-GDH/TIM assay providing a common readout for enzyme activity and product formation. In continuous mode it gives the initial rate of a single kinase, which helps distinguish an enzyme preparation with measurable activity from one that does not work detectably, and allows activity to be compared between preparations. In endpoint mode, run on stopped aliquots, the same chemistry measures how much product has accumulated in the coupled DHAK and PPK2 reaction over time. These measurements address different stages of the module, from evaluating individual enzyme preparations to investigating whether polyphosphate-driven ATP regeneration can support product formation.

Using a shared readout for both is a deliberate choice, not a convenience. Because the continuous and endpoint measurements share their reporter chemistry, extinction coefficient and wavelength, they can be interpreted within the same measurement framework. At the same time, each format has its own limitations, and the conditions under which a result is obtained determine what conclusions can be drawn from it. This is why the technique sections report the controls used to assess the assay, including the no-enzyme background that is subtracted from each session, the starting absorbance that confirms the set-up before any enzyme is added, and the conversion to absolute units through the NADH extinction coefficient rather than through a relative scale.

The characterisation also includes the purification strategies investigated to obtain enzyme suitable for further testing. Chromatographic profiles help identify candidate fractions, but absorbance alone cannot establish the identity or activity of the protein they contain, making independent activity measurements necessary for their interpretation. The technique sections give the buffer, final concentrations, temperature, path length and fitting window where relevant, since these parameters can affect the result. They also state plainly where our numbers are still volumetric rather than mass-normalised, since specific activity requires a protein quantification we had not completed at the time of measurement. The methods and their limitations are documented to make the results interpretable and the procedures reproducible, while the assay itself may also be useful to other teams studying enzymes that produce dihydroxyacetone phosphate, or coupled systems involving polyphosphate-driven ATP regeneration.

alginate encapsulation: The platform is characterised well enough to build on, and the limits of that characterisation are known. Production is controllable: alginate concentration and drop height set shape and reproducibility rather than size, flow rate can be raised several-fold without destabilising drop formation, and crosslinking time beyond ten minutes changes nothing until contraction appears at ninety. The capsules are approximately 95% water, thermally stable far beyond anything the process will reach, built from genuinely crosslinked calcium alginate, and continuous in their shell under the electron beam, with no capsule rupturing at any load tested. Storage in water for a week makes them stronger rather than weaker, which is the opposite of what we expected and the result with the most direct consequence for operation, since the bioreactor receives stored capsules rather than fresh ones.

Two findings are about measurement rather than material, and they are the ones we would pass on. Dispersion, not the mean, was the useful statistic in nearly every comparison: the conditions that selected themselves did so by being reproducible, and the one measurement that failed, shell thickness, failed because its spread exceeded the difference it was meant to resolve. And when a geometric quantity sits below the resolution available, measuring the function that quantity is supposed to serve can succeed where measuring the quantity cannot, which is how the flow-rate ratio was finally settled.

What is still missing is also clear. Permeability has never been measured, only bounded by the fact that phosphate reaches the cells; the dried-state imaging cannot supply it and transport experiments would be needed. Absolute mechanical properties, a modulus or a rupture load, are beyond an image-based assay. And every preservation result points at the same untested variable: the capsules degrade in media that compete for calcium, so the composition of the real effluent, rather than the mechanics of the capsule, is the thing most likely to decide whether the platform holds up outside the laboratory.
enzymatic immobilisation: These measurements changed decisions rather than confirming them. Mass normalisation inverted the ranking of our phosphohydrolase panel, so the enzyme that looked strongest by raw product release was not the one carried forward, and the differential yield measurement showed the two immobilisation chemistries responding in opposite directions to the same detergent, which is not something either could have been predicted into. That second result also separates a good yield from a useful one: both routes bound a similar fraction of the activity offered to them, while the amount of activity actually immobilised differed roughly ten-fold, so the chemistry was chosen on the absolute figure rather than the percentage.

What remains open is named in the technique pages with the experiment that would settle it: retained specific activity per milligram of immobilised enzyme, operational stability over repeated cycles, and whether the selected protocol behaves the same way on the genipin, chitosan and alginate matrix the project actually uses, which is the transfer this whole characterisation exists to inform.
genetic engineering: The measurement did its job: the engineered strain takes up phosphorus from the real operation medium at roughly 1.7 times the rate of the wild type, under the acidic conditions the process will actually run at rather than at a laboratory optimum. That is the functional validation the genetic design needed, and it is the number that justified carrying this chassis into the encapsulation and recovery work rather than redesigning it. The comparison is also the robust part of the result, because both strains were processed identically and share every dilution and normalisation factor, so the ratio between them survives uncertainties that the absolute values do not. What the assay has not yet established is the ceiling: the time-course stops while both strains are still accumulating, so we have a rate but not a maximum storage capacity, and we cannot yet say which of the individual genetic changes contributes most of the gain. Both are named in the technique page with the experiment that would answer them, a longer run to the plateau and a comparison of the modifications in isolation, and the second of those is the measurement we would most want another team to repeat.
revalorisation: The measurements provided a way to assess enzyme activity, investigate purification strategies and examine product formation in the revalorisation module. The activity assay distinguished preparations with measurable activity from those without it, while the purification work identified candidate fractions for further evaluation. Expressing activity through a defined spectrophotometric readout also allowed results to be compared under the same measurement conditions, rather than relying on relative signals alone. This helped turn the experimental work into evidence that could be interpreted and evaluated by others.

The limits are equally clear. Activities are volumetric until the protein quantification is in place, and the reporter chemistry is calibrated using a literature extinction coefficient rather than a local standard curve. In addition, the initial endpoint measurements of the coupled cascade reached the detection ceiling, preventing reliable quantification of product accumulation and therefore not establishing the extent to which polyphosphate-driven ATP regeneration supported the reaction. These limitations identify the next steps needed to strengthen the measurements, including protein quantification, further validation of the assay's quantitative range and optimisation of the endpoint procedure.

By documenting the methods, conditions, controls and limitations alongside the results, we aim to provide a transparent account of what the measurements establish and what remains unresolved. This also gives other teams a practical basis for reproducing or adapting the approaches, while making clear which parameters and limitations need to be considered when applying them to a different system.
